Soon, a pure white light covered my body. My vision immediately blurred but as time passed, color slowly returned. Staring blankly up at the sky, I ended up chuckling.
So it was gloomy here twenty years ago too.
Rafdonia’s sky was as gray as usual.
“Hey, are you going home right away?”
“Of course not. Let’s go have a drink first.”

Dimension Square was teeming with adventurers. Yeah, this was how it used to be. There had been so many incidents recently that the sight of it full was actually strange. It was slowly starting to hit me.
I really am twenty years in the past.
And I was going to have to live here for a while.

chapters.title: Chapter 285: Cause and Effect (1)
paragraphs: The sea was raging with violent waves.
“Bjorn? Is Bjorn not here yet?”
“No. He should be here soon...”

Arua Raven kept her eyes on the horizon, the coordinate transmitter clutched tightly in her hand. As was the case for everyone on the boat right now, an unfamiliar unease was beginning to fill her. Bjorn Yandel, their leader, was facing a rank-three monster alone to buy them time to escape.
“Something must have gone wrrrong. We have to go save him!”
“No! Didn’t you hear what he said? He said to absolutely not go near there.”
“That guy always says stuff like that and then does whatever he wants! I don’t carrre. I’m going to do whatever I want from now on too!”
“But how are you going to get down there? Mr. Yandel is fighting under the sea!”
“That’s...” Missha trailed off.
At that, Raven bit her lip and took care to be more patient rather than getting emotional and raising her voice. “Just wait. Mr. Yandel will surely come back in one piece.”
“Sorry for shouting.”
“It’s okay. I feel the same way.”
“The same way?”
Raven answered Missha’s question after a moment’s pause. “...We’re comrades.”
“Ah, right... yes.”

There was an awkward silence after that. All the while, everyone on the boat kept their eyes fixed on the point they had started their journey from. About five minutes later, the anchored ship began to rock violently.
“Th-the water is going down!” The elevated sea level was lowering as they spoke.
“W-What? But Bjorn isn’t here yet. Did he... fail?”
“I don’t think so! If the Storm Gush were alive, there would be another storm!”
“Oh, then...”
“Yes! Mr. Yandel defeated the Storm Gush!” Raven shouted, unable to hide her joy.

Missha was in the same boat. “Ahh, you barbarrrian bastard! You said you were just going to hold out! What the hell were you doing down there?!” In sharp contrast to the contents of her rant, Missha’s expression was filled only with bright relief.
“Mr. Patzran! Turn the boat around, quickly!”
“W-Will do!”
Raven hurriedly turned the boat around and headed for the island.
Flash!
Then, as if lightning had struck under the sea, a white light shimmered on the surface of the water before disappearing.
“W-What was that just now?”
“D-Do you think something went wrrrong down there...?”
The priestess and everyone else turned their eyes to Raven, but being a wizard didn’t mean you knew everything. “I-I don’t know either...”
That was what the labyrinth was like. There were more things you didn’t know than things you did. This was her first time seeing a Storm Gush too.
With time, the water level went down and the island started reappearing, starting from the center and highest point. However, the person they were looking for was nowhere to be found.
“W-Where on earth did they disappearrr too? And is that their equipment?”
All that was left in the center of the island was the equipment Bjorn and the woman named Amelia had been wearing.
“There’s a stake here. The rope is still attached, too, so it looks like Mister was just here a moment ago...”
“It looks like they tried not to get swept away by the current. But where...?”
“But wait, the equipment...? What’s with the equipment? There would be no reason for them to take it off...”
Nothing about this made sense.

“...Let’s search the area first. If they were swept away by the water, they couldn’t have gone far.” Raven’s head felt just as jumbled, but she doled out instructions as calmly as possible. Didn’t Bjorn tell her that she had to act as the leader when he wasn’t there?
“Here! There’s more equipment over here! This is the necklace Bjorn wears!”
“H-His underwear is here too!”
After that, the group split up and started searching. All the while, the sea level continued to drop and the island returned to its original state.
“Why... why can’t we find them anywhere?”
Even after they searched all over the island, Bjorn was nowhere to be found. Just what the hell had happened here?
“Did Yandel...”
They didn’t know anything for sure right now, but when Raven spoke, her voice was firm. “Mr. Urikfried, don’t spout nonsense. He’s most definitely alive.”
Being optimistic even when there was no evidence to back it up—yeah, that barbarian said that was what a leader was supposed to do.

“First, it’s clear from the circumstantial evidence that they killed the Storm Gush. They also had the mind to stick a stake into the ground to avoid getting washed away. I don’t know why they took off all their equipment, but it’s possible they were washed to a nearby island. Let’s go look around.”

After that, Raven got on Patzran’s boat and searched all the nearby islands. In the process, they threw around many theories and even had the occasional argument, but no one lost hope. Time marched on and in the end, they reached the labyrinth closing day without finding Bjorn.
“...We’ll meet in the city.”
Shaaaaaa!

The light of the labyrinth announced their return. Arriving in the city, Raven searched the empty Dimension Square for a barbarian. None were immediately visible. Thinking he could have wandered somewhere else before she could spot him, Raven even headed to the checkpoint, but it was just more of the same.
“Bjorn? Was he in the square? The staff here said no one matching his description passed through.”

“...I couldn’t find him in the square.” Raven continued to wait at the checkpoint with her comrades, who had arrived there before her. Even after all the other adventurers passed through the checkpoint, leaving the square empty, Bjorn didn’t turn up even though they should have reunited here no matter where he had ended up in the labyrinth. As long as he was alive, at least.
“Um... it’s nearing closing time.”
Even as the staff hinted at them to leave, Bjorn did not appear. That could only mean one thing, but no one could say it out loud.
A heavy silence fell, and his one and only warrior comrade, Ainar, was the one to break it. “So, Bjorn is dead,” she said bluntly.
It was time to face reality.

Conventional wisdom said that even mountains and rivers would change over ten years, but that wasn’t the case here, at least. Although enough time had passed for mountains and rivers to change twice, this city hadn’t changed much, just like the street in front of the checkpoint I was at now.
“Dad! Here! Over here!”
“Ramirion, I’m glad you came back safely again. Let’s head home. I prepared all your favorites.”

The acquaintances and family members of adventurers filled the checkpoint. Even the buildings around hadn’t changed much. The only slight differences I could find were the signs hanging on the first floors of the buildings.
So that was originally a bar, not a general store.
While I was busy being mildly fascinated by the differences between past and present and searching around for more, a woman came up next to me. It was Amelia.
“Ah, you’re here.”
“I kept you waiting. Were there any problems during the inspection?”
“I just handed over my ID and exchanged the mana stones like you told me to.”
“Really? That’s a relief. Then let’s move.”
“Where are we going first?”
“First, a clothing store.”
After meeting up with Amelia, we headed to a nearby store to buy clothes and found an inn in District Seven, the place I usually lived.
“Come to my room after you wash up. Let’s discuss some things.”
I first went into the bathroom and scrubbed myself clean, then I put on my new clothes and went to Amelia’s room. Fortunately, she was done washing up too and the door opened quickly.
“What did you want to talk about?” I asked as I sat down on the bed.
Amelia shook the water out of her hair and sat at the table across from me. “First, I have one thing to ask you.”
“Hit me.”
“Are you... thinking of going back?”
I’d wondered what she wanted to ask me, but wasn’t the answer to that obvious? “Of course. I’m going back no matter what.”
“Hmm, I see.”
“Did you really think I would want to stay?”
“I thought it was possible. You must be slowly coming to terms with the fact that you are in the past now.”
“What does that have to do with anything?”
“...This is twenty years ago. You may not have realized this, but if you take advantage of this time difference, you could lead a much more comfortable life than before.”
“I see.”
“...This isn’t an ‘I see’ kind of situation. Barbarian, you may not realize, but the opportunity you have now—”

I cut Amelia off before she could go on any longer. “That’s enough.” I got what she was saying, but I wasn’t particularly interested. There was no bitcoin mine here. Staying here would just mean my equipment, hard-earned nobility status, and diligently cultivated comrades were all gone. It was a total loss. For me, there was no reason to stay. “If there is a way to go back, I’m going right away. So don’t bring this up again. If it weren’t for you, I wouldn’t have gotten sucked into this in the first place.”
“...I’m sorry about that.”
Yeah, that apology was a little too late. “Never mind. So is that why you asked to see me?”
“No, the main thing I wanted to discuss was something else. If you were going to stay here, I wasn’t going to tell you.”
No wonder she kept feeling me out. “Stop beating around the bush and get to the point.”
“I want you to help me while you are here in the past.”
Huh, she never once answered any of my questions properly on the island but now she wanted my help? Did she think I was a fool? “And what do I gain from that?”
“I will help you get back in return.”
“You don’t even know how, so how are you going to help?”
“...There is one method worth trying.”
“Tell me.” If she said I had to give her my answer first before she would tell me what it was, I was going to leave immediately.
But Amelia readily told me the method she was referring to. “Using the Fragment of Records Stone one more time.”

I didn’t immediately understand. “The Fragment of Records Stone? That disappeared when...” I paused halfway through the question. “Ah...” It wasn’t actually gone, since this was twenty years in the past.
“Yes, the one I used is gone, but there is still one here. At this point in history, it would be in the possession of the lord of Noark.”
Suddenly, the Genesis Treasures came to mind. Just as the stone was still here, the stolen keys to the final floor also still existed in the present day.
What happens if I take them back with me? Would that mean there would be a way to clear the final level?

I entertained the idea for a second, but it was quickly put to rest. Not only did I already have more than enough on my plate just worrying about getting back to my original time, but it wouldn’t be possible to bring them back with me in the first place. Considering our foray back in time dropped me and Amelia on Farune Island naked, it was likely that the same thing would happen the other way around. It would be impossible to take an item from here into the present.
Ah, my thoughts were wandering. By the time I tuned back in, Amelia had stopped talking and started staring at me. Jeez, can’t a barbarian have a hard time concentrating?
“Ahem, I’m listening. Keep going.”
“...I’ll say the rest after I hear your answer.”
Ha, that’s how you want to play this?

My first thought was that she was being a cheapskate, but that didn’t really change my answer. Not only did it make sense to use the Fragment of Records Stone to go back, but if she didn’t help me, it’d be hard to manage on my own. To get that item, help from Amelia, who was from Noark, was essential, since I didn’t know where the lord of the castle stored it.
“Okay, then tell me. How can I help you?”
Once my consent was given, Amelia’s expression shifted. Strangely, she didn’t seem happy. Rather, she looked somewhat displeased.
“Is there a problem?”
“...No. There’s no way what that bastard said was true.”
“That bastard?” I asked, but Amelia went quiet.
After calming herself, she slowly parted her lips. It was quite a long story, and when it was over, I finally understood the woman named Amelia Rainwales—and the past she was so desperate to change.
The day after said long story, Amelia checked out of the inn.
“I might not be able to come for a while since I’ll be busy. I can’t stop you from doing anything, but try to avoid causing a scene as much as possible.”

Apparently, a scout was operating in the shadows who offered a helping hand to people who became criminals and tried to recruit them into joining Noark. She planned to make contact with them. That was because for both of us to achieve our goals, entering Noark was critical.
Man, I never thought I’d go all the way to Noark.

Anyway, the period of time Amelia said she’d be busy was about three weeks. She said she’d stop by from time to time to keep me updated on her progress, so I could hear about any changes to the plan then.
What should I do now?
Once I was alone in the room by myself, I felt restless. Maybe this was my gamer’s curiosity talking. After all, I was twenty years in the past.
Should I look around?

The moment the thought came to mind, I put on my clothes and left the inn. Although Amelia repeatedly told me not to attract attention, honestly, how could I just sit down and take that? What was the worst that could happen?

chapters.title: Chapter 286: Cause and Effect (2)
paragraphs: I didn’t have a specific destination in mind for this outing. I just walked wherever my feet would take me.
Oh, so that skewer shop was here twenty years ago too.

I didn’t particularly like going on walks, but this time I quite enjoyed it. It was like a spot-the-difference picture game. Each time I saw a shop that was still in operation twenty years later, I was glad to see it even if I hadn’t actually visited it a lot myself.
When did I get here? Force of habit really is a scary thing.
I raised my head absently to look at the beautiful exterior of the building in front of me.
[Ravigion Southern Central Records Archives]
This was the place everyone referred to as the library, and also the place I visited most in this world.
This place is exactly the same now as it is twenty years in the future.
It wasn’t like I had loads of stuff to do right now, so I entered the library without hesitation.
“Hello, welcome.” As soon as I entered, I was greeted by staff. To be honest, I was really taken aback.
The heck? This place was never like this.
The counters that were always empty except for Ragna were all filled with staff. The first time I ever came here, there had only been a single dozing librarian.

One of the many librarians approached me, a girl who appeared to be in her early to mid-teens. “Is this your first visit?” She looked very young. This couldn’t be her full-time job, then. Was it like a part-time job? But why did she look so familiar? “...Is this your first visit?”
“Ah, yes... that’s right.”
“Then I will briefly guide you through the rules and browsing process.”

As I listened to the woman’s explanation, it seemed to me that it wasn’t just the number of librarians that had changed. The administrative wizard was only one of the many people here. To find a book, a visitor had to give them a keyword so they could pull up the records with magic while the other ordinary librarians guided the visitor to the book’s location.
“...Why do you use such a complicated process?”
“Sorry?”
“Wouldn’t it be easier to cast a spell on the visitors and get them to search for books on their own instead?”

The librarian looked at me with eyes that seemed to ask, What the hell is this barbarian bastard talking about? and answered with a bright smile, “Haha, I guess you might think that way. But I heard bestowing magic on others increases the consumption of mana by several times.”
“Oh, so the problem is that there are too few wizards.”
“Yes. And I’ve never heard of a spell like that in the first place.”
Huh? What’s this now? That spell doesn’t exist?
As I tilted my head involuntarily, the librarian continued in a low, self-deprecating voice, “There’s no way those lofty wizards from the Tower would create a spell for us librarians.”
“...Uh, I see? Sorry. I’ll come back in a bit, then.”
“It’s all right. If you think of a book or a genre you would like to read as you browse, please feel free to ask us any time.”
The conversation ended and the librarian returned to her seat. But thanks to that, I caught sight of her nametag, which hadn’t been visible while we were talking.
[Apprentice Librarian – Shavin Emoor]
Ha, no wonder she looked so familiar. It was her. It looked like she had worked here until becoming an adult and getting a job at the administrative office.
That’s so interesting.
I had the sudden thought that given the time period I was in, I might get a chance to hear young Missha’s babbling.
Ah, I guess she still babbles in the present, though.
Anyway, that wasn’t important. The fact that I could see the childhoods of people I was acquainted with if I wanted to? That might be interesting, but what did it matter?
“Dwalkie... would be alive here.”
Riol Warb Dwalkie, the wizard who would probably be a raw nerve to me for the rest of my life.
If changing the future is possible...
Couldn’t I possibly prevent Dwalkie from dying with my actions here? The moment I had that thought, an electric current ran through my body—not metaphorically, but literally.
Bzzzzzz.
What is this? Who seared me with electricity?

When I glanced down in response to the stinging sensation prickling at my feet, I saw a child looking up at me arrogantly. I responded graciously like the mature barbarian I was. “What the crap are you doing?”
The child answered my question. “I’m a wizard.”
I was dumbfounded.
Yeah, what about it? What, did you think I would cower in fear or something?

“Human child, it seems you don’t realize that wizards can also die when their necks get snapped.” Since actually arguing with a six-or seven-year-old kid was ridiculous, I instead gave her some sincere advice. But was that not to her liking?
“Whatever, just get out of my way. I can’t get past because of you.” The child wizard glared up at me with attitude. Well, that answered the question of why she zapped me with electricity.
Ha, did she shock me just because I was in the way?
This was one rude kid, but I managed to hold it together, albeit narrowly, remembering Amelia’s warning not to make a scene. “Yes, go ahead, child.”
“What’s good about being big? You can’t even use magic.”
“What did you say? You wanna see a spell that breaks necks?”
When I stood to the side to make way, the child snorted loud enough for me to hear before disappearing. “...How barbarian.”
Yeah, that had no effect on a barbarian.
Tsk, tsk. Were all children like this twenty years ago? Jeez, it wasn’t like this back in my day... What is this world coming to?
After that, I took a quick look around the library and without taking out a book, sat down in an empty seat. There was something I needed to make up my mind about.
Yeah, it’d be too much of a waste to throw away this opportunity.
It was a twenty-year time difference, after all. Just as Amelia said, this was an opportunity, and it occurred to me that it would be a loss to just go back to my original time immediately.
Although I can’t do much since I only have three weeks left aboveground...
I made a list of things I could do during that time. A few things came to mind.
First, the Genesis Treasures.

The Genesis Treasures would be stolen in twenty years. I wouldn’t be able to stop that, and it would be virtually impossible for me to steal one in advance and bury it underground for safekeeping. I didn’t know where they were hidden in their respective holy lands.
But I can leave a warning.

Like that, the first item on my to-do list was decided: write an anonymous letter that someone would be coming to steal the Genesis Treasures on March 1, year 153 of New World. Of course, it was unclear whether this would change the future, but since it did not require much effort, it wasn’t like I had much to lose. On that note, I decided to include a word about the War of Sacred Relics. That had been the primary cause of the decline of the barbarian tribe.
It would be nice if they held as much power there as they do here.

I hadn’t spent too long looking around the Rafdonia of twenty years prior, but the most noticeable difference was the number of barbarians. There were quite a lot wherever I went. This had probably been normal in the past. The War of Sacred Relics decreased the population and the Magic Tower then announced that our hearts were valuable as magical ingredients, leaving us in the state that we were in in the present.
The Magic Tower... can I not stop them somehow?

Hmm, I decided to think more about that later. Nothing really came to mind right now. Anyway, onto the next item on my to-do list: create a future where Dwalkie doesn’t die. In the case of this item, there were a total of two methods that came to mind: either intervene and induce a scenario where he didn’t become an adventurer in the first place, or kill that Dragon Slayer son of a bitch. The former had too many variables, while the latter would be the most effective solution. It was also a deed that would benefit the world in more ways than one. In many ways, there were only pros.
But the problem is, there’s no way to know for sure if that bastard will even be in Noark.

According to public records, the guy first revealed himself about ten years after he stole the Dragon Sword. I heard he made his Orcules debut by single-handedly terrorizing the holy land of the elves after it was left in ruins by the War of Sacred Relics. Unfortunately, nothing was known about his past.
Then I should first meet with Dwalkie.

And so I chose to proceed with the plan to create a future where Dwalkie wouldn’t become an adventurer. Many things could go wrong, but it was worth a shot. Not to mention I even knew where Dwalkie was staying at this time.
If I go find him and only tell him bad things about what a hard and disgusting job it is, I’m sure he’ll be put off. Okay, then that’s how we’ll deal with that. Next up is...
Just as I was getting my thoughts in order, I heard the crackling of electricity from somewhere nearby.
Crackle!
Fortunately, this time it wasn’t coming from my body.
“Agh!” When I turned my head in the direction of the sound, I spotted the man who was screaming after being terrorized by lightning.

“Move, don’t block the way.” The little kid recited the same line she spat at me earlier. But unfortunately, the results were not the same. Well, how many grown-ups were as benevolent and understanding as I was?
Slap!
The man slapped the child on the cheek without mercy. Although he had the build of a stick figure, it was still hard for a six-or seven-year-old to withstand the strength of a full-fledged adult.
“Birhe Te—” The child who was thrown back quickly got up and began to cast a spell, but the outraged man did not allow her the chance to do so.
Smack!
Merciless kicks were directed at the tiny body.
“...Shouldn’t we stop him?”
“Librarian! Let’s call a librarian.”
People around us started to look, but no one stepped forward.
Ha, this is why I can’t deal with nerds who only study. I can’t concentrate.
“Who made that noise?” I had no choice but to head in the direction of the commotion and approach the still-angry man who was continuously stomping his feet. “Be quiet in the library.” I tripped him.
Boom!
“Ugh, who the hell are you!?” The man fell on his butt and huffed as he got up. He raised his voice in annoyance. “Unless you want to get hurt...” He trailed off as soon as our eyes met.
“Unless I want to get hurt...? Why did you stop there?”

The man couldn’t answer my question right away. I wondered if he was going to employ the number one method to piss someone off, but fortunately, that wasn’t the case. “...Just be on your way.” Stick Man tried to act tough even as his eyes slowly drifted downward.
Huh, that was weird. Given how mercilessly he had slapped a little kid, I had been so sure he was an egalitarian, too, like how barbarians didn’t discriminate between men and women.
But it seems he’s only tough when he’s facing someone weaker than him.
Well, I mean, this kid was 100 percent in the wrong this time.
“Why don’t you stop here? Can’t you see people are reading?”

“...Tsk.” When I laid out a justification for him, Stick Man clicked his tongue, turned around, and disappeared. He probably realized what a disturbing thing he had done once the anger subsided a little.
“Can you get up?”
“...Don’t worry about it.”
If you’re going to say a line like that, at least wait to say it when you’re a few years older and lose your baby fat.
Sigh.
I sighed and lifted the child who was curled up on the ground like a shrimp. “Do you have a mom?”
“I do.”
Eh? You do?
“But you’re alone?”
“...She’s at home.”
Oh, I see. You should’ve said that in the first place.
“Why did you leave the house alone without your mom? If you’re going to come somewhere like this, come with her.”
“...I can go places on my own.”
“Is that why you got beaten like that?”
When I hit her where it hurt like the barbarian I was, the child frowned. “...I could’ve won.”

“I see.” This was why I hated children. They were so stubborn for beings that were such a long way away from developing rational thinking. “Whatever, you figure this out yourself. If you’re going to pick fights again, do it somewhere I’m not.”
“...I wasn’t picking a fight. It’s his fault for blocking the way in the first place.”
What was she talking about? “It’s your fault for using magic just because someone was in the way too. You should have asked him to get out of the way first.”
“I did. I asked you and that man earlier. But both of you ignored me.”
Huh? Really? I really didn’t notice...
“So I won’t do it,” she said.
“What are you talking about?”
“I’m not going to say thank you.”
“Oh, really?” I hadn’t even expected her to. “Fine, just go.”
When I waved her off, the child huffed in anger for some reason, then turned around and disappeared.

It was then that the staff rushed over. Fortunately, without me having to say anything, the other visitors nearby filled the staff in on what happened. “...I heard you stepped forward to sort this out. Thank you.” They thanked me and disappeared. That was the end of the incident. I sat back down and got back to brainstorming.
Drag.
When I turned to look beside me at the sound, I saw that the kid from earlier had sat down diagonally across from me and opened a book.
“Hey, what are you doing?”
“I’m reading.”
“Why are you reading here?”
“Why can’t I read here?”
Ha, honestly... Let’s keep a cool head.
Employing all my patience as an adult, I switched seats. But what was this now?
Drag.
Not even a few minutes later, another chair was pulled up diagonally opposite me.
“Why did you follow me?”
“I didn’t follow you.”
“You did follow me.”
“No, I didn’t.”
According to my abundant experience as a volunteer, it seemed I’d somehow caught this child’s attention.
Indifference is key in moments like these.
If I didn’t respond, she’d lose interest and wander off on her own. So I stopped paying attention and got back to thinking, but this damn kid didn’t know how to stay in her lane.
“Why are you sitting there without a book?”
“Can’t you read?”
“Shall I teach you?”
Oh my god.
“Hey, kid.”
When I finally blurted something out after struggling to hold my tongue, the child frowned. “I’m not Kid.”
“Of course you’re a kid—”
“Arua Raven.”
“...Huh?” I froze. For a moment I wondered if I’d misheard her, but it wasn’t my ears that were wrong.
“Arua Raven is my name.”
...Wait, really?

She had flowy blonde hair, blue eyes, a small figure, and was human. That was all they had in common, but looking closely, I could see Arua Raven in her features. However, I couldn’t be sure like with Shavin Emoor. That was because there was a big difference between being six or seven years old and being in your mid-to-late teens.
So I asked again just to confirm. “Is it Arua? Not Aruna, Aruru, Aruberos, or anything like that?”
“What are those strange names? My name is Arua. So say it properly.”
Oh, so sensitive. In twenty years, there will be no one calling you just “Arua” anyway.
“So, how old are you?”
“Five years old.”
Wow, even the ages match up—I guess it really is her.

It seemed she had been tall for her age when she was young. I was surprised by the sudden encounter but slowly started to grow curious. “What is that book? It looks like a book on magic. I guess you’re doing some self-study?”
“Yeah.”
“Aren’t you going to the Magic Tower?” As someone who knew that Arua was associated with the Magic Tower in the future, I couldn’t help but wonder.
She clicked her tongue. “You think just anyone can join the Magic Tower?”
Uh, that’s true, but...
“Our family is too poor, so I can’t.”
“Is that why you’re studying alone?”
“Yeah, if I become an administrative wizard in the future, I won’t have to worry about making a living.”
I nodded awkwardly. “...Th-that’s true.”
What was I like when I was five years old? I was in and out of the operating room, and reading all day in the hospital.

I was pretty precocious for my age, too, but nothing compared to this girl. At least back then I hadn’t been worrying about the future. Well, I had also been at a crossroads between life and death back then, so it was mainly because I couldn’t afford to.
“Anyway, I’m leaving.”
“Huh? So suddenly?”
“It’s time for my mom to get home from work. If she finds out I’ve been at the library, I’ll be in trouble.”
“True, I’m sure she’ll be worried about you sneaking out like this.”
“...It’s probably something different from what you’re imagining.” With that, Raven set her book back on the return desk and left coolly without looking back.
Something different from worrying... what does that mean?
It could have been nothing, but Raven’s strangely dark expression as she said that bothered me.
Does she have some sort of problem with her family?
Come to think of it, she never talked about her family in front of us. This was my first time hearing she was a commoner too.
This piqued my curiosity.

chapters.title: Chapter 287: Cause and Effect (3)
paragraphs: After Raven left the library, I debated following her to her house, but I soon abandoned the idea. That wouldn’t be the respectful thing to do as her comrade. The reason why she hadn’t mentioned her family situation until now was probably because she didn’t want us to know about it. If I was really that curious, it would be better to ask her about it myself once I got back.
Then what do I do now?
I tried to get back to brainstorming once Raven was gone, but I eventually left because I couldn’t concentrate.
After I had eaten a meal and loafed around in bed for a while, Amelia came back from her earlier engagement. “...Have you been doing that all day?”
“Yes, and?”
You told me to stay at home.
When I stared back at her, Amelia shook her head and tossed something heavy from her pouch at me. “Here, take it.”
“...Money?”
“It’s money from selling the equipment and items from the plunderers. I divided it exactly in half, so find yourself some equipment in the city tomorrow.”
“Oh, it’s quite a lot.”
“There aren’t many forges in Noark, so it’ll be difficult to get equipment there. Only spend it on things that are absolutely necessary.”
Oh, you and your nagging.
“And your work? How’s it going?”
“It’s still a work in progress.”
Amelia told me she would let me know when she had results to report and then disappeared somewhere, saying she had something to do. Apparently, she’d only stopped by to hand me the money.
I’m going to grill some meat tomorrow.

Once the next day dawned, I left the inn early and headed to the commercial district of Kommelby, otherwise known as the Free Market. I headed to the forge I normally used and requested some custom-made equipment. They said it would take about three weeks.
Business was good here twenty years ago too.
Well, that made sense. There weren’t many forges in Kommelby that were both reasonably priced and handled top-quality equipment like this.
I should look around while I’m here.

I had nothing in particular to do after that, so I wandered around to sightsee. I went to the Central Exchange to check prices, asked nearby adventurers for recommendations to popular eateries from twenty years ago, etcetera. I made good use of my time until just before the last train, and then I headed back to the inn and had a drink before going to bed.
The next day, the third day, I visited the holy land.
Whew, I’m nervous.
I was slightly worried someone would come up to me and point out that I was an unfamiliar face.
Is it because of the larger population? The vibe in the holy land is also completely different here in the past.
Thankfully, my worries ended up being unfounded. Unlike my generation, which memorized the names and faces of everyone in our year and one above and below us, things here were very different.
Okay, I’m just going to leave the letter and bounce.

After hanging around the chieftain’s tent for a bit, I slipped the letter I had written the day before inside while the chief was away. Then I left the holy land and visited the Church of Reatlas. Coincidentally, a commission that was perfect for me had been announced. The job was repairing a building under the church. The only reward for this commission was achievement points in the eyes of the guild, and it was practically a volunteer job.
“Your application has been received.”

The commission started in three days, so I just submitted the application and stepped out onto the street. I had pretty much reached the end of today’s to-do list, but there was still quite a lot of time left in the day, so I headed to the library.
While I was sitting there quietly mulling over my plans just like I did yesterday, the chair across from me was pulled back with a scraping sound.
Drag.
So, you’re here again.
“Nice to see you, Arua.”
Although I greeted her and even called her by her name, Raven looked sulky. “Why didn’t you come yesterday?”
She made it sound like we’d had an appointment, even though she was the one who left without looking back the other day. “Did you already eat?”
“Yeah.” Raven explained that she ate a piece of bread she brought from home. How was that a meal?
“Let’s go grill some meat.”
“...Meat?”
“You don’t like it?”
“I don’t know.”
“You don’t know?”
“I’ve never had it before.”
Jeez, this girl was going to make a grown man cry. “Then you can try it today. What are you doing? Hurry, get up. You can study another time.”
“But—”
“I’m going to a restaurant right in front of the library, so don’t worry.”

“I wasn’t worried at all.” It seemed being treated like a child annoyed her because Raven closed her book and got down from her chair. Then she moved one seat down and sat a little farther away from me. “Don’t pity me. I can buy things like meat with my own money in the future.”
I guess trying to buy her something had hurt her pride quite a bit. Whoops, that was my bad. You had to approach people like her in a specific way. “Oh, sorry if you thought that way.”

When I offered her a genuine apology, Raven got down from her chair again. “I’ve never met an adult who apologizes. I’ll let it slide.” Then she moved back to her original seat. Was she a cat or something? “I’m going to read now, so don’t interrupt me,” Raven said firmly before actually beginning to read.
I was a little dumbfounded. When did I ever interrupt her? Anyway, with that sensible distance between us, we quietly passed the time.
Tap.
It was when she turned the last page of the book that Raven spoke again. “...Are you an adventurer?”
Honestly, I’d been wondering when she was going to ask. Kids were usually super excited about things like these. “Yes, I’m an adventurer.”
“What rank?”
“Rank five—no, rank six.” I quickly corrected myself. Just in case, I figured it was best to base all of my answers on Nivelles Enze’s life.
“Is that high?”
“It’s average. Most of the adventurers that appear in books would have passed rank four.”
“Hmm, I see.” Surprisingly, Raven didn’t try to pick a fight or say my rank was low or do anything else to look down on me. She just seemed curious. “Can you tell me about it?”
“About the labyrinth?”
“Yeah.”

Afterward, like playing make-believe with a kid, I told her somewhat exaggerated stories about things that had happened to me in the labyrinth and other interesting stories I heard while working as an adventurer. I left out the scary stories as much as possible. Raven’s case was different from Dwalkie’s. You needed to protect a child’s innocence.
“Interesting. Are all barbarians like you?”
“It’s Nivelles Enze, not barbarian.”

“Oh, sorry. I will call you by the correct name from now on.” In contrast to my first impression of her, where she seemed like a wild child, Raven was surprisingly down-to-earth. She was considerate and tried not to do to others what she herself wouldn’t want done to her. However, she was lacking in one area.
“Why do you keep picking fights with adults?”
“I wasn’t picking a fight.”
“I’m sure a kid as smart as you must know a better way to resolve things than by zapping people with electricity.”
“...I don’t know.”

Something I noticed while conversing with her was that Raven had a great desire to be acknowledged. Well, who didn’t have that desire? But hers was several times worse than the rest of her peers. Perhaps electrocuting passers-by who were blocking the way was an expression of that psychological need. She probably wanted to show off the fact that she was a wizard regardless of who she was showing off to. I doubted she ever received the reaction she was craving, though. Based on my experience, you generally only thought one thing after being suddenly electrocuted: Is this child out of her mind?
“Then I’m going now. Goodbye.”
It was a little earlier in the day than the last time we ran into each other, but Raven left the library as if fleeing from an embarrassing topic of conversation. And so I headed back to my inn.

Three more days passed in the past. At first, I had wandered the streets every day in fascination over the fact that I had really gone back in time, but I quickly lost interest. What was so special about twenty years ago? Everyone lived the same lives, after all. And so, except for chatting with Raven in the library these past three days, I spent most of my time at the inn.
Oh, come to think of it, I forgot to tell her I can’t come today.

After meeting up and talking to her every day for several days, I’d gotten quite close with Raven. Now I wasn’t just telling her stories about the labyrinth, but she voluntarily told me about her family too.
That was unexpected.

Raven was from a single-parent family, but not because her father was dead. Apparently, he left home a year ago after having an affair. Oh, for reference, her father was also a wizard. No wonder. I’d been pondering how it could be possible for a child, no matter how smart they were, to learn magic just by reading books in a library, but it seemed it was because her father had laid down the basics.
“Anyway, that’s why Mom doesn’t want me to learn magic. She even sold all the books we had at home. I guess it reminded her of him.”

I was a bit blindsided from being lectured on her family history out of nowhere like that, but Raven’s tone was utterly nonchalant. The way I saw it, it must have been some kind of defense mechanism. If she pretended to be okay in front of others, it’d convince her that nothing was wrong too.
Ha, honestly, breaking my heart...
And so I recently identified a new goal. The goal was none other than to help Raven get into the Magic Tower. Even without me, she’d join the Magic Tower one day but...
The sooner she joins, the better.
Perhaps when I returned to the future, Raven would have become an even greater wizard. Hmm, then would that change our first meeting too?
Ah, how different could it be?

That’d just make the Vampire battle a little easier, and it didn’t matter if it didn’t. The past had already been changed. I’d left a letter in the holy land. Not only that, but in three weeks I would have to head down to Noark with Amelia and save the life of a person who should have died.
If it’s going to change anyway, it’s better to induce a change that’s good for us.
Tap.
Arriving at my destination, I took a deep breath at the entrance.
I’m kind of nervous.
This was an orphanage under the Church of Reatlas, the place where Dwalkie had spent his childhood.
“Ah, are you Nivelles Enze?”
“That’s right.”
“If you wait here for a moment, the shift leader will inform you what you need to do today. Would you like something to drink?”
“No, it’s okay.”

I went inside the orphanage, announced that I was there to do volunteer work, then sat down and waited. A little while later, a tough-looking man came out and led me and the other volunteers to the site.

“As you can see, the building is quite old so some areas are uncomfortable and even dangerous for the children to stay in. We’ve divided the groups into a mix of experienced workers and first-timers, so let’s all work hard today.”

My role here for the next week was to help do repair work on the old building. It felt a bit strange. The last time I had been here, my job had been to carry boxes and furniture out right before demolition, not repairs.
“Hey there, barbarian! The morning shift is over so go and take a break!”

Anyway, I did what I was told and in my free time, I went to the vacant lot where the children were playing. Finding Dwalkie wasn’t difficult. Everyone was running around, but one kid was reading a book by himself in the shade of a tree.
So he didn’t have any friends back then, either.

Drinking water from a canteen, I casually walked over to the shade and sat down next to him. But I suddenly couldn’t recall the lines I’d composed to get close to him. All I could remember were his last moments. There were so many things I’d always wanted to say to him if we met again someday.
“I-I’ll get out of your way so you can rest...” My staring seemed to bother him because Dwalkie squirmed and stood up. Only then did I come to my senses.
Get sentimental later, do what you need to do now.
“Sit.”
“Y-Yes!”
“...You can relax. I won’t eat you.”

Dwalkie sat back down again at my words, but it was like he was sitting on a bed of nails. He was too busy watching me out of the corner of his eye to relax. Jeez, I didn’t realize he was this submissive.
“What’s your name?”
“Riol.”
“Last name?”
“...I don’t want to say.”
“I’m Nivelles Enze. Rank-six adventurer.”
“Okay...”
Huh, now it just looked like I was bugging him. Didn’t the kids usually like it when adventurers came to visit this place? Yeah, like these kids.
“Wow, a barbarian!”
“Is that a tattoo? Did it hurt?”

After I sat on the floor, the other children came up to me with curiosity. When I revealed that I was an adventurer, they begged me to tell them about the labyrinth. Dwalkie had moved to a corner before I could even blink, and I studied his face.
He could have left, but since he’s still here, I guess he’s curious too.

I figured Dwalkie wanted to hear about the labyrinth because he was looking my way from a short distance away. And so I cracked open the storybook in earnest. Oh, of course, I told them a different version of the story full of dreams and innocence that I’d told Raven.
“Goblins! Have you fought goblins too?”
“Of course I have. One time, after crushing its eyeball with my hands like this, I slammed down my fist like this. Their skulls are so hard that I had to slam down three times.”

“That reminds me of the one time I stepped on a goblin trap. I thought I was really going to die then. I couldn’t even use my leg because the muscles and tendons were all torn. I crawled in the darkness for several hours, not able to walk properly, looking for someone to rescue me.”

“Yeah. It’s still a difficult experience to think back on. I think a bone was protruding from my shin and oh, it was really painful each time the bone touched the floor. Halfway through, the goblin’s Paralysis Poison also left my system, so I thought I was going to go nuts from pain. I didn’t know it at the time, but later I found out that one of my molars was missing.”
“...Eh?” I guessed they weren’t expecting such a realistic story because the children’s faces darkened as the story progressed. True, who would have told them about stuff like this?

“Oh, and one more thing. Most people think monsters turn into mana stones as soon as they die, but that’s a misconception. They stare at you for about three seconds while gushing brain fluid through their noses and ear holes. With eyes just like these. Oh, is monster talk not fun for you guys? Then I’ll tell you a story about people this time. I once met a plunderer who used to wear human ears around his neck like a necklace—”
“Wahhh!” A trembling little girl in the front ran out crying.

Regardless, I continued telling stories. “I guess that one’s no good? Then this time I’ll tell you about the time my arm was ripped off... That’s no good, either? Then... Mm, how about the time the guild framed me and tried to get me killed?”
“Huh?”
Just as I was about to keep going, one of the kids spoke up in a shaky voice. “A-Are those all the stories you have?”
I nodded without a moment’s hesitation. “What else do you expect? I don’t know what you guys have been hearing up until now, but terrible things like this happen every day in the labyrinth.”
That was the honest-to-goodness truth. Even though you could still smile in those situations and say you were glad you became an adventurer, it was without a doubt terrible.
“Yeah, so...” I looked right at Dwalkie and said, “Don’t be like me, you guys. Got it?”

chapters.title: Chapter 288: Cause and Effect (4)
paragraphs: The week-long work on the repairs went by quickly. There were no notable incidents. All I did was engross myself in my work without getting sidetracked, and then talk about how hard it was to be an adventurer in front of the children. But even that was taken off the agenda starting the third day. Now, even if I rested under the shade, the other children didn’t come near me anymore. So, during the break, it became routine to sit quietly in the shade with Dwalkie.
Oh, of course, we chatted from time to time too. “How did you end up here?”
“...The director told me my parents couldn’t afford to raise me.”
“I see.”
“S-Still, I’m better off than the other kids. My parents will come back for me in a little while, so...”
“...Did you say that in front of the other kids?”
“Y-Yes, why?”
I think I know why he doesn’t have any friends here.

When I sighed, Dwalkie came up with some excuses. “I-I’m all right. It’s not like I’m going to be here for long, anyway... M-My parents are both merchants. So things are a little difficult for them right now...”
Difficult, my ass.

As soon as I heard that, I was overcome with bitterness because I knew his situation. The current baron had placed Dwalkie with some members of the collateral line as soon as he was born, and they’d abandoned him here without a care.
Only after his birth mother found out and told the baron did Dwalkie get to live with her in her annex...

For reference, he said he barely ever saw his adoptive parents over the ten years they spent living together. However, the financial support they provided wasn’t bad so he was able to live a normal life and learn magic as well.
“Sounds like you had a hard time. Have some beef jerky. You need to eat well when you’re young if you want to grow taller.”
“Oh, right... thank you.” We sat together and munched on jerky. My break ended soon after. “Um... is today your last day?”
“Yes, the repair work is now finished. The ceiling won’t leak now even if it rains.”
“...Thank you.”
At least you have manners. The other kids seem to think it’s only natural to have volunteers come and fix the house.
“If you’re really thankful, don’t ever become an adventurer.”
“Sorry? What do you—”
“Just promise.”

“Adventurer? I-I could never do that... And I don’t want to, either.” Kid Dwalkie’s face as he said that was sincere. Well, I was sure that was normal after hearing all the stuff I’d been telling them the past few days. The other kids were sick and tired of anything to do with adventurers now, so no one would be fanning the fire, at least.
...To be honest, I’m still not all that reassured. But I can’t stay here forever, so I can only leave the rest up to fate.
“Hey, Enze! If you’re done resting, come help me with this!”
“Then I’ll be on my way, Riol.”
“...Right. Goodbye.”

After that, I gave all the jerky and snacks in my bag to Dwalkie and headed back to the job site. The kid tried to refuse for a while, but what was he going to do against a barbarian who was insisting?
“Thanks to you, we managed to wrap up today’s agenda quickly as well. Now, good work, everyone!”
Anyway, after a few more hours of repair work, the chief announced that the week-long job was finally done.
“We’re going to have drinks later today, are you coming?”
“But I’m an adventurer.”
“Haha, we know you’re not condescending like the other adventurers, so it’s fine.”
The chief asked if I would attend the dinner and I replied yes after a moment’s thought. I had nothing else to do afterward, anyway. Raven wouldn’t be at the library at this time.
“The church has paid you generously for your hard work, so let loose and drink tonight!”
And so we moved to a nearby pub and had a drink. But was it because this was my first time attending something like this with non-adventurers?
It’s kind of awkward.
I couldn’t keep up with the topics of conversation. All we talked about was which forge had good quality equipment, who in what clan was going out with whom, and so on.
“Uhm...” While I was sitting alone, I heard a voice pipe up next to me. “My name is Warb Emirn.”
Oh, right, I knew her. Even with her small physique, she carried heavy loads without taking shortcuts and was a diligent worker. “Do you have something to say to me?”
“Well... I heard what you were saying to the kids.”
Ah, no wonder she had been giving me strange looks every time I spoke to them. “You mean about the labyrinth?”
Emirn nodded, looking slightly embarrassed. “Yes.” Then, after a moment, she carefully asked, “Is... that place really so terrible?”
“Not always.”
“Sorry? But...”
“The reason why I said that in front of the kids is because I don’t want them to get any weird ideas. It’s a difficult place to handle if you go in half-cocked and unprepared, that’s for sure.”

While I was at it, I told her about some other parts of the labyrinth, from the view on the third floor that Dwalkie especially liked, to the vast forest, to the snowy white field and various mysteries of Glacier Cave. The longer the conversation went on, the more I noticed the people around me growing quieter. Well, these were stories that children and adults alike could enjoy.
“Snow, huh? I’ve never seen it before so I can’t even imagine it.”
“Would it be like cold sugar?”

To people who had been confined within the castle walls all their lives, the inner workings of the labyrinth must have sounded like tales from another world. Just as their anecdotes felt unfamiliar to me, it would have been rare for them to spend time with adventurers too.
“It’s been a while since I’ve heard such a fantastical story.”
“I’ll have to tell my son when I get back.”
Of course, I didn’t spend too long rambling by myself. When I finished up my story, the topic naturally shifted to the stories of their own lives, and I just joined in on the topics I could.
This isn’t so bad...

As time passed and the sun began to set, the dinner came to an end and people returned to their homes one by one. Just as I was about to head back to the inn myself, the woman from earlier followed and stopped me. “Excuse me...!”
“Ah, Emirn. What is it?”
“I just wanted to ask you one thing. Is that all right?”
“Ask me.”
Emirn hesitated for a moment, and when she spoke, she sounded somewhat troubled. “You said there were times you felt afraid too, right?”
“I did.”
“I-I do too. There are times when everything seems impossible and just thinking about it scares me to the point that my heart might burst. How do you get through situations like that?”

This was kind of a tough question to answer, especially when the asker was someone who until a few days ago was a complete stranger to me. But I decided not to think too hard about it. Someone was standing in front of me asking for courage.

“As I said before, barbarians know fear too.” I knew it even more intimately as an ordinary office worker, but... “We just know that if we don’t do what must be done because of fear, it’ll only lead to ruin.”
“Ruin... Yes, I’m sure it would be...”
Afterward, an awkward silence followed. Giving her a moment to think, I then asked her, “Is it something you have to do?”
“Yes.” Her voice was small, but there was no hesitation, and so there was only one thing I could say to her.
“Then do it.” It was a pep talk only a barbarian could give.
It took a while for her to reply. “...Thank you for giving me the courage. I’ll try my best.”
“Yeah? Whatever it is, I hope it goes well.”
“Yes. The stories you told earlier were really interesting too.”
“Then I’m glad.”
“Especially the one about the place called the sea. I’ve only heard about it but I think it must be a very cool place. Although... someone like me will never be able to go there in my lifetime.”
I didn’t say anything to her self-deprecating remarks. What could I say? That she could go if she really wanted to? I knew very well that that would be a lie.
“...Then I’ll be on my way.”
“Oh, right. Go ahead.”
After exchanging one last goodbye, I parted ways with Emirn.
Warb Emirn...
I didn’t know why, but that name kept popping into my head all the way home.
When I returned from the dinner reeking of alcohol, I found Amelia in my room. “You were gone the whole day. Where have you been?”
“Oh, I went to do some volunteer work.”
“Volunteer...?”
Oh, you and that frown of yours. What, did I say something I shouldn’t have?
“People need to know when to give back.”
“...I see.”
“Anyway, it’s a good thing you’re here. I’m out of money. Lend me some while you’re here.”
“You spent all that money already?”
“Ah, after buying equipment and doing other things, there was nothing left.”
“...I see.” Amelia fiddled around with something on her waist and threw me a pouch. It was quite hefty.
I won’t have to worry about paying for meat for the next while.
“I’ll use it well.”

After expressing my gratitude, I told her about some of the good restaurants I’d visited. Judging by her reaction, I didn’t think she’d be checking them out, though. Yikes, I got the sense she was going to get pissed if I didn’t cut the small talk ASAP.
“Ah! So, how is the work going? You said you met with the broker or something last time?”
“We’re still establishing contact. Thankfully, everything is going as planned, so if there are no other hitches, we should be able to leave next week. You should prepare yourself.”
“I will.”
As soon as our brief discussion was over, Amelia left, saying she had something to do.
We’re leaving in a week, huh?
After washing up a bit, I lay down on the bed and mapped out what I had to get done during my last few days here. There wasn’t much to map out, actually.
If we’re leaving next week, I should wrap things up with Raven.
I should be able to pick up the equipment I ordered sometime next week, and then I just had to deal with Raven. Tomorrow, I should go straight to the library.
What’s important is what’ll happen after we head down to Noark, I guess.
From then on, I would probably have to live on high alert. Although I’d already discussed with Amelia how I should act once we got down there, when did things ever go as planned?
Man... I just want to go back already.
With a head full of hopes and dreams, sleep slowly came over me.
The location was a two-story rental house that Missha and I had found together. There, I was laughing and chatting with my comrades. I didn’t realize it at first, but I quickly noticed.
This is a dream.

What convinced me was the mirror. I glanced to the side while laughing to see that the person in the mirror was not Bjorn but Hansu Lee—something that could never happen in real life. The moment I realized this, the backdrop crumpled and the space changed.
“Bjorn, what arrre you doing? Let’s go!”

Now, I was in the labyrinth. I was climbing the floors and exploring as usual. But once again, I was Hansu Lee, not Bjorn. The shield was heavy, and my eye level had dropped so I was forced to look up. Maybe that was why...
“Why can’t you even stop that!?”
I kept making mistakes, leaving my comrades to suffer damage. At first, it was injuries, but it ended up leading to death.
“If it weren’t for you...”
It was Dwalkie. Only then did I remember this was a dream, and the space around me swirled again. I was once again in a familiar place—a quiet room reminiscent of a medieval aristocrat’s office.
“What, it’s the Round Table this time?” At first, I just laughed, about to move on, but I soon noticed something strange.
It’s a bit different...

The structure and feel of the room were similar, but the wall that should have been filled with clothes and accessories was missing. Well, it could have been that my imagination had just missed a detail while cooking up this dream.
“...But it’s too realistic for that.”
Numbly, I opened and closed my hand repeatedly. Every time I tightened my grip, I could clearly feel my muscles moving. Even my train of thought grew more natural and coherent.
Knock, knock.
The sound and sensation of knocking on a wall—all of it was indistinguishable from reality.
Slide.

Coming to a realization, I immediately checked the full-length mirror to the side of the room. As expected, there stood Hansu Lee, not Bjorn. But how did this happen? As I was assuming that this wasn’t a dream, a plausible hypothesis presented itself to me almost immediately, surprisingly.
Ah... today is the day the community opens.

I’d been summoned while asleep. That would explain the situation I was in. The community of twenty years from now had computers and masks, but this version must have operated differently. Considering this was the early days, that made sense. I might even be able to see the surprised face of the GM once I walked out that door.
I suddenly recalled a conversation I’d had with Baekho.
“There were already evil spirits in this city even more than a hundred years ago. On Earth, that was more than twenty years ago. So who were those people?”
Back then I told him to just tell me the answer because I didn’t know.
“The answer is they were from another dimension!”

Evil spirits summoned from another dimension, few in number compared to the people from Earth, but each possessed unique powers. Apparently, one of them created this space, and the GM we knew in the present had just inherited it.
Could it be...?
One very plausible possibility popped into my mind.
Knock, knock.
Someone knocked on my door.

chapters.title: Chapter 289: Big Fish (1)
paragraphs: There was no second knock. As if the first knock was just to alert me that someone was coming in, the door opened right away without the knocker even asking for permission.
Creak.

It was an old man who entered. He had thick gray hair and wrinkled skin, but he didn’t carry the characteristic air of fragility that usually accompanied an elderly person. There was no shakiness in his gait, and his back was straight with no hunches.

“Hmm.” Even without words, the distinct temperament conveyed in his movements and the look in his eye were telling me that this old man was dangerous. “Judging by your outfit, you must be from Earth,” the old man muttered curtly, giving me a once-over. “How did you get here?”

For a moment, my mind went blank. How should I answer? Judging by his outfit, it seemed he was definitely an evil spirit from another realm. I chose silence for now. Rather than hastily open my mouth, I decided to get the other side to speak first so I could get a better grasp of the situation.
Well, that was the plan, but...
“Incredible. Three rank-three essences already. It’s been a little over a year since you people were brought here.” This old man was reciting my personal information even though I hadn’t said a word.
Damn it, where the hell do you get an ability like that?

“This is piquing my interest for the first time in a long while. Forget about how you got here, tell me this first: who are you?” I didn’t respond. “Are you just going to keep staring at me like that?”
Anyone else might have been wary of a visit from an uninvited stranger, but the old man instead sounded friendly as he urged me to answer.
Jeez, what do I say?

Should I just tell him I was from the future? I did have that thought, but it remained just a thought. It wouldn’t be wise to give out too much of my own information while I still didn’t know anything about the other person.
“I’ll ask the questions first.”
“Oh? Then will you answer my questions too?”

“To some extent.” I took advantage of my opponent’s curiosity and seized the upper hand. As confused as I was, he must have been equally as curious about who I was. I was going to use this to obtain as much information as possible.
“Go ahead.”
As soon as the old man gave me permission, I asked this question first: “What is your name?”

“Haha, my name, huh?” The old man laughed like he found the question anticlimactic, but his name was important to me because I had the advantage of coming from twenty years in the future. A name that was unknown now may not be in my time. With the right questions, I might even be able to find out what this guy was doing in the future. “Seeing as you want us to introduce ourselves, it seems you know your manners.” The man then laughed welcomingly. “I am—”
But the moment he was about to speak, the old man suddenly frowned and shut his mouth. The frown only lasted a moment, though.

“Sorry. Something has come up out there, so I will have to resume this discussion later.” The old man put a dignified end to our conversation and proceeded to make an unexpected proposal. “It would be rude to leave you here. Hmm, what to do... Will you come with me?”
I thought about this for a moment and replied that I would. What was I going to do in this room alone? If I followed this old man out there, I might be able to obtain more information.

“All right, you skinny fellows have courage. Anyway, going out like that will attract the attention of the other members, so here, put this on.” When the old man waved his hand, an outfit suitable for a person from this era appeared out of thin air. But was that not good enough for him? “Ah, it would be best to cover your face too.”

The old man even made me a white mask on the spot. What was this convenient ability? It could probably only be used in the spirit world, right? With that thought in mind, I put on the clothes and mask.
“Is it uncomfortable?”
“No, it fits just right.”
“Haha, I should equip this place with something like this next time. There may be some people who don’t want to show their faces. Now, then. Let’s go.”
After that, I followed the old man out of the room. As we walked, he gave me a few words of warning.
“Whoever you see inside, don’t show any surprise or let them know that you know them. No, if possible, just keep your mouth shut like earlier and observe.”
“What if someone talks to me first?”
“That won’t happen, but even if it does, I will take care of it.”
Well, if you say so.

Even as I walked behind the old man, I continued to inspect my surroundings. The more I did, the more I felt a strange sense of déjà vu. I’d gotten the same vibe from the room I was in earlier, but it really did feel similar to the mansion where the Round Table was located.
The fact that there are no windows is the same too.
Of course, details such as the decorations on the wall, the location of the room, and the width of the hallway were all different.
But something about writing it off as pure coincidence doesn’t seem right to me.

I didn’t dismiss it as just a flight of fancy and continued to scan the area. After who knows how long of that, the old man stopped walking down the hallway and slowly opened a large door. “We’re here.”
What is this place?

Surprisingly, there was a round table inside, the same Round Table that sat in the room I’d been in and out of countless times while wearing the mask of Lion. When I took a closer look, though, there were quite a few differences from that place. First of all, there was no jewel in the center of the Round Table that distinguished truth from lies, and the room was also a bit smaller.
But it’s similar.

Other than that, it was almost identical. From the pattern engraved on the edge of the Round Table to the obscure picture frames hanging on the wall, most details were consistent with the room where the Round Table met twenty years from now. But how?
Is this old man the Master?

Perhaps that was the identity of the old man standing in front of me now—the mysterious man whom I’d met just once before and who created the Watchers of the Round Table. Well, there was also the possibility that one of the other people here had simply modeled the Round Table after this place.
Anyway, let’s think about this later.

Momentarily flinching at the familiar sight of the Round Table, I quickly came to my senses. The Round Table wasn’t important right now. What was important were the four people sitting around it—three men and one woman. They looked our way as soon as the door opened.
“Who is that man behind you?” They showed a strong interest in me and the mask I wore. In a way, it was kind of similar to the first time I participated in the Round Table.
Geez, look at those eyes.
It was as if there were thorns in their eyes. Every time their gazes honed in on me, my skin stung and it felt a little like getting stabbed.

“You do not need to take an interest in who this man is.” Unlike how he spoke to me earlier, the old man was firm and harsh with these guys. Everyone instantly settled down as he laid down the law, and he got straight to the point. “I heard there was trouble while I was gone. Of course, I trust that you lot are not foolish enough to forget the rules of this place, but I should hear this out first. What happened?”

The old man spoke in the same tone one would use to scold small children and an awkward silence fell in the hall. Given the fact that they were all averting eye contact every time his eyes passed over them, it seemed like they were trying to figure out who was going to take one for the team.

The first to step forward was a middle-aged man built like a mountain. “I’ll say this in advance, but we have no intention of feuding with each other. However, this man keeps encouraging us to take outrageous action. “
At the man’s criticism, a nearby man in black frowned. “How is suggesting killing the king outrageous?”
“Ha, you think I don’t know why you want to kill the king? Do not try to drag us into your personal, greedy plans.”
“Kagureas, are you still holding out hope of returning after decades of fruitless attempts?”
“Of course. As is everyone here. Oh, though you should be removed from that list now.”
“How funny. If you wish to go back, shouldn’t that make you all the more willing to help me? The palace likely holds the big secret that would be the final answer to all our questions.”
“...Laying a hand on the king is too dangerous. There isn’t even a guarantee that the palace holds any clues as to how to return.”

It was obvious what the conflict was about—on one side there were the fanatics who wanted to kill the king to obtain clues, and on the other side were the fence-sitters who thought that was too dangerous and wanted to find another way. The conversations of evil spirits twenty years in the past were quite fascinating, and I was listening intently when my mind went blank at the next thing the middle-aged man said.
“I don’t care what you do on your own. Whether you establish Orcules or not doesn’t affect me.”
What? Establish Orcules? Could this be the founder?

I had stumbled on an unexpectedly big fish. Suddenly, I remembered what the old man had said earlier. What was it again? Something like, don’t be surprised about who you see inside. If this was the leader of Orcules we were talking about, that warning was warranted. After all, this was a legend shrouded in mystery that no one knew anything about. I never expected to run into him here.

“But Lord Ruingenes is different.” Just then, the middle-aged man glanced at an individual with the appearance of a child and then continued speaking. “If you attempt to persuade him with your nonsense, I will not stand idly by.”
My mind temporarily went blank again.
Huh? Ruingenes is...
Belbev Ruingenes was the true name of Fallen Scholar, who was once the head of one of the greatest magical schools but had become a criminal after tampering with forbidden magic.
“Do you really believe he can perfect dimensional magic?”
“I do. I believe in that much more than a foolish plot to kill the king.”
Staring at the child who was calmly sipping tea without paying any mind to the people discussing him, I clenched my fists.
Slurp.
Seriously, this kid is Fallen Scholar...? Jeez, what is this lineup?
After learning the identities of the two giants, I naturally became interested in the two people who remained.
I’ve never heard of the name Kagureas.
To start, this was my first time hearing the middle-aged man’s name. The woman hadn’t talked at all so I had no information on her. Just who the hell were these people?

Just then, the old man opened his mouth and quieted the hall. “I understand the situation now, so stop it, all of you.” He wasn’t particularly charismatic or anything, but the members were instantly cowed when he spoke. “Leave, everyone. I have more pressing matters to deal with today so let’s discuss this at a later date.”
“Pressing matters?” The woman who had only been listening the whole time finally opened her mouth at the old man’s words. “Is it related to that person behind you?”
“It is.”
When the old man readily affirmed that, all eyes focused on me again. He’s more important than us? That was what their looks seemed to be saying.

But while everyone else kept those thoughts to themselves as they waited for the old man to elaborate, the woman spoke up again. “Who is that person? I think this is the first time you’ve brought someone here. And why are they wearing a mask for no reason?”
The old man answered the same way he did before. “Never mind that. Will you all step outside now?”
When the old man issued another order for them to leave, everyone got up one by one starting with the woman.
“Haha, we’re finally alone.” When everyone left, it was like a mask slid off the old man’s face. His benevolent smile instantly returned. “Then let’s continue our conversation. How far did we get?”
“...You were about to say your name.”

“Oh, right.” He laughed like an old man who lived next door, the kind that talked about how you’d feel the same when you got older and introduced himself without hesitation. “If you’re from Earth, my name might be one you’re already familiar with. Nice to meet you. I am Auril Gavis.”
Auril Gavis, the author of the Complete Book of Rifts—and the creator of the game Dungeon and Stone.

chapters.title: Chapter 290: Big Fish (2)
paragraphs: Thump.

My low, steady heart rate gradually shortened. “...You’re Auril Gavis?” He was perhaps the one person who could answer all the questions I’d had since waking up in this body. “Are you... really the one who made that game?”
“I’m pretty sure we agreed to alternate who asked the questions but since I understand how you’re probably feeling, I will answer this one.” He nodded. “That’s right. I made that game.”
Jeez, so it really was him. Assuming he wasn’t lying, of course.
“Now, since I revealed my name, it’s your turn. What is your name?” Now that the ball was in his court, he asked a question of his own.
He must be asking for the same reason I did.

Names were important, especially in a spiritual world where appearances meant nothing. As could be inferred from the fact that the Fallen Scholar wore the appearance of a child here, in this place, we took the form we considered our own. But that anonymity disappeared the moment we revealed our names. It opened up an opportunity for him to find me on the outside.
“Hansu Lee.” I revealed my real name, which I hadn’t told anyone aside from Baekho.
Of course, the old man wasn’t satisfied with this. “Oh? I guess that means you’re from Korea? But my question was the name you use here, not that.”
“The name I use here, huh?” Okay, I figured he would ask that. “Nivelles Enze.”

That was technically a name I used here too, right? Since I’d already dealt with Baekho, who was able to distinguish between truths and lies, I deliberately threw in a trick. This could be the creator of the Round Table, after all. If this was the man who created the jewel system that formed the basis of the gathering, I didn’t think it’d be weird to assume he might have an ability like that.
It doesn’t hurt to be careful...
At my answer, the man gave me an unreadable look. “Hmm...”
“Is there a problem?”
He just stared at me for a moment before announcing the end of his turn. “No. Then it’s your turn now.”
My head was spinning. What should I ask first? There were so many things I’d always wanted to ask if I ever met this man so it was hard to prioritize.
Yes, let’s ask that first.
I picked one of the questions from my list. “Why did you call us into this world?” This was the root of all action: motivation. Why had he done something like this?
Instead of answering, Auril Gavis made a strange remark. “...You certainly are special.”
“What does that mean?”
“I have met a few people from Earth, but most believe they are just inside a game.”

Oh, so that was what he meant. To be fair, I used to think that way too. However, after going through so many hardships here, I’d managed to obtain plenty of clues. To think they could still be so deluded. This place was its own separate world. If my theory was correct, Dungeon and Stone was simply a game based on said world.
“So, your answer?”

“Fair, as far as you’re concerned, there would be nothing you’d want to know more than that.” Soon, Auril Gavis opened his mouth and gave me the reason these people had had to bring beings from a distant realm to this world. “Because you are the only ones who can open the door to the Gate of the Abyss.”
“What? The Gate of the Abyss? What could that possibly be—”
Auril Gavis cut me off. “Questions are asked one at a time. Wasn’t that the rule?”
“Ah...” Yeah, that was true. “Ask me.”

When I relinquished my turn, the man grinned. “You... Did you use the Fragment of Records Stone?” The eyes of the wrinkled old man twinkled with eager anticipation. The Fragment of Records Stone was a family heirloom passed down through generations of Noark’s royal household, and a treasure with the incredible ability to reverse time.
The heck, how did he figure that out?

The moment he brought it up, my heart skipped a beat. And rightfully so, because I hadn’t imagined for a moment that the question he would ask after my name would be one that cut straight to the heart of my entire situation.
Shit, what do I answer?
It was already too late to casually brush the question aside by asking what the Fragment of Records Stone was. He would have already noticed that I was flustered too.
“You can take your time,” Auril Gavis said.
I quickly made up my mind. “What made you think that?”

Of course, I knew that asking this was no different from half-confirming his suspicions, but what else could I do? Not only was this someone on whom lies didn’t work, but there must have been something I did that made him think that in the first place. Auril Gavis had already skipped straight to certainty. If he weren’t certain, he would never have mentioned the Fragment of Records Stone in front of me.

“I have three reasons.” Auril Gavis smiled as he explained the basis of his suspicions like he was explaining something to his grandchild. “One, you are too strong to have only been here a year. Two, you weren’t one of the people I invited to this place. Three, you may be strong, but not enough to invade my territory without permission.”
“Just with that...?”
“Haha, it’s not ‘just.’ For all those things to be true, there’s no other explanation but that one.”
I still don’t understand, though...
“So can I assume the answer to my question is a yes?”
It would be ridiculous to deny it now, so I just coolly admitted to it. It was a pity I’d been exposed in two questions, but what could I do? I just had to do damage control from this point on.
“Haha, since you’re from Earth, you wouldn’t have come from the past. What year are you from?”
“The questions were one at a time, I believe.”

“Ah, that’s right. Go ahead.” Auril seemed to be in a good mood. “So, what are you curious about now? What the Gate of the Abyss is? Whether the witch is alive? Hmm, or you might be wondering if the outside world is really hell, like the king claims.” He sounded like he would answer anything I asked.
It’s oddly getting on my nerves.
Was it because I’d seen him coldly dismiss the other members earlier? Auril Gavis’s strange kindness was rousing my rebellious side.
Should I just abandon ship now?

I even started to wonder if it would be wiser to end the Q&A session here and ask to be sent outside. There was no rational reason for me to feel that way, but it wasn’t the kind of thing I should overlook. Based on my experience, ignoring these gut feelings usually led to disaster.
But if not now, I may never get another chance to find out these things.
I couldn’t deny that this was too precious of an opportunity to pass up simply because it was a bit uncomfortable. This old man would have all the answers. Soon, I made up my mind.

Let’s forget all the little curiosities and ask about what’s important. Are you from here? Then how did you shift dimensions? Do you have comrades who share your objectives, and for what reason did you create this spiritual world?

Swallowing back the many other questions I had, I asked, “Why are you trying to open the Gate of the Abyss?” When it came to people, motivation was one of the easiest things about them to grasp. What drove this man’s actions?
Auril Gavis answered after a brief pause. “Why do you ask that?”
“I thought we agreed to one question at a time.”
“Haha, don’t look so cold. I was just wondering if you shouldn’t ask what the Gate of the Abyss is first.”
His question was justified. It was just that it wasn’t a reasonable one in my opinion.
“Haha, I think I’m starting to understand what kind of disposition you have,” he said.
“So, what is your answer?”
“I planned to answer any question you had for me, but this seems a bit unfair.”
“Are you saying you won’t answer?”
“I still don’t know who you are very well. Everything has a proper order.”
Ha, I didn’t expect him to take that stance. Then would we have to end the question-and-answer session here?
