When I glared at him demandingly, Auril gave me a Zen, riddle-like answer. “I both created and did not create this space.”
What kind of wordplay was this? “Are you being serious?”
“...The light is green now, is it not?”
“Speak clearly. What do you mean by that? Does that mean you have a collaborator?”
Auril answered after a brief pause. “I guess you could see it like that.”
What do you mean, ‘could see it’?
Although this was outrageous, the green light did in fact appear.
Then I guess I can interpret this as him wanting to hide the fact he had a partner. The red light earlier must have been because he felt remorse for trying to answer me half-heartedly.
I’d gained an unexpectedly decent amount of information from this.
“Then this makes your third. Go ahead,” Auril urged me, sounding somewhat drained.
Oh, don’t rush me.
“The witch...” I smirked and corrected myself. It was best to be clear here. It would only be right to refer to her by her proper title. “Is the Earth Witch really dead?”

Though it may not have been an urgent matter right now, this was something I had to address at least once. Even if you weren’t particularly interested in history, the Earth Witch was a name you couldn’t help but hear countless times while living in this world. Now that I was thinking about it, I’d always been curious just how many of the stories about the witch that were considered common knowledge among the citizens of Rafdonia were true.
“...From the first question to the last, you couldn’t make a single one easy, could you?”
“Your answer?”
Auril smiled unhappily at my prodding and replied, “She is alive.”
Woah, really...?
Suddenly, I had a lot to think about.
If that’s the case, not only does that mean that the palace intentionally hid this fact... but no Easter egg hinted at this in the game, either.

This old man was the creator of the game, but he didn’t include that information even though he knew it. The same man who flooded players with all kinds of unnecessary information and settings and topped it all off with “Tutorial Complete” at the end? This, again, didn’t make sense. It would be more reasonable to assume he intentionally hid this in the hopes that it would not reach players’ ears.
But why did he want to keep this a secret?

I played around with a few guesses, but I wasn’t sure yet. I didn’t have enough clues at this point, but I had the feeling that by digging into this, I would be able to learn what this old man’s—and the palace’s—ultimate goals were. Put simply, this question provided me with the basic roadmap.
While I was getting my thoughts in order, the old man, who had had to persevere through my questions, burst into hearty laughter. “Haha, then it’s finally my turn.”
Geez, what kind of question is he planning on asking?
I was starting to get anxious by the time the old man opened his mouth. “Do you wish to return to Earth?”

The implication behind this question was obvious. Although he expressed it in a roundabout way, I was sure there was something else he wanted to know. What he really wanted to ask was probably whether I was determined to open the Gate of the Abyss.
“I don’t know,” I said, releasing a breath I had been holding in, and before long, the jewel began to glow green.

“You don’t know, huh?” Auril laughed like he had mixed feelings about that, then schooled his expression as if nothing had happened. Then he gave me advice, which was unlike him. “I hope you make your decision soon.”
“Why?”

“Because that will be better for both of us.” I asked him what he meant by that, but he just responded like the old fox he was with, “Is that your question?”, marking the end of that particular discussion.
It was my turn again. Without wasting any time, I asked straight away, “Does the Witch’s Poison really exist?”
“...Were you always so curious about her?”
Well, actually, not really. It was just that the more we talked, the more it occurred to me that the Witch might be the key to all this.

“Hah...” Auril took a sip of his tea and answered like he was recounting a story from a distant past. “That much isn’t made up. This world was almost destroyed once because of her. If not for the existence of the labyrinth, it would have definitely come to an end.”

The light on the jewel was green. Hmm, then had the outside world really returned to normal because of the passage of time? I moved on to the next question. “If the Witch is alive, where is she now?” This was the only subjective question among those I’d asked today. Since I had nothing to go off of, I figured I wouldn’t be able to get an answer to this with a yes or no question.
However, Auril was ready. “She is where everyone’s hopes go.”
Ugh, those goddamn riddles. I sighed and checked the jewel. Seeing as the green light was on, I didn’t think he’d give me an answer even if I tried to argue.
“Are you really going to act like that?” I decided to at least give it a try and glared at him.

Auril placed his hand on the jewel. “But there is really no more appropriate explanation than this.” The green light came on again. Given his haughty expression, I didn’t think he would change his stance even if I pressed further, so I just gave up.
Well, at least I confirmed one thing.
Auril knew the witch’s location and he didn’t want to tell me where it was. Simply put, what I could learn about the witch had the potential to interfere with Auril’s goals.
“We’re already at three.” The old man laughed an easy laugh like this round of questions hadn’t been all that tough.
Ugh, so annoying.
It might have been time to check that out, the thing that might be much more important than any of the questions I’d asked about the witch until now.
“Now, go ahead.”
After a moment’s thought, I said, “Do you even feel sorry?”

There was a brief pause. I knew Auril was a wizard. He also seemed to be knowledgeable about the secrets of this world, including information about the witch. He was the game’s creator, and I also knew that he had a hostile relationship with the palace. So, it was time to see for myself. Just what kind of person was Auril Gavis?

“Haha, you’re asking another tough question.” The old man’s distinct, hearty laugh brought the short silence to an end. “You responded to my question of whether you want to return to Earth with, ‘I don’t know,’ correct? That would mean your life here hasn’t been so bad.”
This was not an answer to my question. Not bothering with any long explanations, I just stared straight at him without a word.
“Why are you looking at me like that? You should know. To achieve a goal, there are times you must forgo all emotion.”
Although I agreed with this, it was also not an answer to my question. “If this question is that difficult to answer, I will change it.”
Auril consented to my concession. “Ah, will you?”

I nodded and changed the question since it seemed he was having trouble with my original one. To help him out, I made it a bit more specific. “Auril Gavis, do you feel the slightest bit of remorse for the deaths of countless ‘evil spirits’ who were brought here as a result of your greed?”

Again, there was no response, only awkward laughter, but that was enough answer for me. “Haha! Hahaha!” Auril began to loudly crack up. To an observer, it was a very disturbing sight, so much so that chills ran down my spine. “You know, you make it very hard to see you in a friendly light.” He looked at me with eyes that were devoid of all laughter. At that moment, the air around us grew heavy.
Tap.

Then Auril placed his hand on the jewel at the center of the table and spoke in the same friendly voice he’d been using up to this point. “How could I ever be at peace? Of course I feel sorry for you. I feel responsible as well. I will probably live with and atone for this for the rest of my life.” Auril smiled. “Was that enough of an answer for you?”
“...More than enough,” I responded, glancing at the jewel.
Shaaaaaa!
The light emanating from the jewel was a vivid red.

chapters.title: Chapter 309: Round Table (3)
paragraphs: The silence that had fallen several times throughout our conversation once again stretched between us. Auril Gavis watched me cooly, and I met his eyes without looking away. Although I tried not to show it, I felt like I couldn’t breathe.
“Now then...” Auril calmly opened his mouth, acting as if nothing had happened. “Is it my turn?”
My heart pounded at those words. This old man was like the abyss a famed philosopher had once spoken of. Through this conversation, he was able to gaze beyond the darkness back at me.
“How many people clear the original in the next twenty years?”
With his first question, this man had checked to see if there was a replacement for me.
“Do you wish to return to Earth?”
With his second question, he had checked whether I had flaws. So what would the third question be? The answer was coming out of his mouth now.
“What is the name of the body your soul came to dwell in as it passed through the Gate of the Abyss?”
Bjorn Yandel—my name. A concrete way of finding me outside this anonymous, spiritual world.

“Do not say Nivelles Enze. I had a strange feeling about that last time and already looked into it.” I recalled the mysterious look in his eyes when I gave him the name Nivelles Enze. At the time, I thought I’d done a good job of clearing that hurdle. “The question I asked at the time was what name you use here, correct?” But, noticing my trick, Auril had begun investigating. “Did you know? There are a total of seven people in Rafdonia who use that name. I was able to visit six of them to confirm they were ordinary people but...”
“But you were never able to find the last one.”
“Rank-six adventurer Nivelles Enze. Surprisingly, he was a barbarian, even though I was sure his name followed a human naming convention.”
The longer the conversation dragged on, the more it felt like the walls were closing in on me, and suddenly it hit me.
“...Are you perhaps a barbarian?”

Even that seemingly joking question from earlier had been part of a plan to reveal my true identity. Despite the fact that I gave him the name of a false identity, he must have concluded that the races, at least, must be the same.
“Let me ask again,” Auril repeated his question once more. “What is the name of the body your soul came to dwell in as it passed through the Gate of the Abyss?”
There was no way for me to use a different name. By wording the question in that specific way, he ensured that the only answer I could give was already set in stone.
God damn it.

I didn’t know about anything else, but I had to hide my name now that I knew what kind of person Auril Gavis was. Although it may have been too early to conclude he was an enemy, at least one thing was for sure.
“How could I ever be at peace? Of course I feel sorry for you. I feel responsible as well. I will probably live with and atone for this for the rest of my life.”
This old man could never be my ally.
“I will not answer that.” I proudly exercised my right to remain silent.

“Hmm...” Surprisingly, Auril didn’t argue. He simply studied my reaction like he found it interesting. “I guess that was a tough question for you. Well, it makes sense for you to be wary of me. Let me change the question then.” He did not get hung up on the fact that I wouldn’t tell him my name and instead changed tacks. “How long has it been since you woke up in that body?”

He questioned the length of my stay here. Since he knew I came from twenty years in the future, obtaining that information would allow Auril to guess when in the timeline I would open my eyes in the body of a barbarian.
“I will not answer that.”
“Really? Then another question—”

“No, question and answer time is over.” I ended our game of twenty questions with no regrets. There were still many things I wanted to ask, but this old man was not running a charity. If there was something I wanted, I would have to pay the price for it. And I made the call that paying any more here would be dangerous.
“...Wait, it’s over? What do you mean by that?”
“It is as I said. Since you were the one running the game, there shouldn’t be any issues, right?”

Auril licked his lips in disappointment at my one-sided declaration, studying me. I knew for a fact he couldn’t logically refute me. It wasn’t like we had decided in advance how many questions we would be asking.
He made his regret obvious. “That’s unexpected. I was sure you still had a lot of questions for me.”

“Well.” There was no doubt the list of questions I had for him could fill numerous pages. In fact, my next question was going to be whether the Fragment of Records Stone the lord of the castle had in his possession could return me to my original time.
Good thing I didn’t ask that earlier.
Now that I thought about it, I was glad I’d put off asking that question. If he worked backwards, that one question could expose the fact that I was currently in Noark.

“I guess you won’t change your mind?” The old man stared straight at me for a while longer before letting out a deep sigh and praising me instead. “The more I talk to you, the cleverer you are. So what will you do now? Will you go back?” Contrary to what I expected, Auril acted like a gentleman and offered to send me back whenever I wanted.
What should I do?
I didn’t expect our game of twenty questions to end so early, so I needed time to figure out what was next.
It’d be a waste to just go back like this...
After thinking it through for a moment, I finally decided to go with an earlier plan. “Why don’t we do as you suggested earlier? Have our conversation with the others present.”
“Hmm? I thought that our conversation was already over?”
“I think it’s a good idea. Although it needs a few tweaks.” Since I’d come all the way here, I should at least see their faces.
Twenty questions with Auril Gavis was a lot like Russian roulette, especially in that each turn that passed left me on pins and needles.
So that’s enough limited-edition information.

There was tons of stuff I didn’t know, anyway. Auril wouldn’t be the only one here with useful information, especially considering these people were evil spirits from another realm who were brought to this world decades before me.

It would be a free exchange of information rather than a question and answer session, but all of the information given would have to be true, and it would have to be something at least half of the participants didn’t already know. When I explained the rules of the future Round Table to him in their entirety, Auril laughed joyfully. “Hmm, what an interesting idea you just came up with. That sounds logical. The system is well-structured for something you developed on the spot. What did you used to do in your original world?”
The answer was that I was an ordinary office worker. Of course, I wasn’t going to give him an honest response. “I thought I said the question and answer period was over?” I replied sharply.
“I was just curious,” Auril muttered, aggrieved. “And it’s not as if I asked for a great big secret, no?”
He wasn’t wrong. But since he was the one asking, it felt like there had to be some kind of hidden motive behind it.
“Anyway, give me a moment. To add the capabilities you mentioned, I’ll have to imbue it with more of my power.” Auril then placed his hand on the jewel and closed his eyes in concentration.
Whooom.
Although it wasn’t visible to the naked eye, the air around the gem distorted a bit, kind of like the haze that appeared above a hot road in the middle of summer.
“It’s all done.”
“That looked easier than I thought.”
“Haha, it hurts my feelings when you say things like that. Whether you believe me or not is up to you, but I lost a significant portion of my power over this space by doing that.”
Hmm, I’m still not convinced...

When I glanced at Auril, the old man launched into an explanation I didn’t even ask for. “The main casualty was my ability to materialize things here. I still have enough power to create an object if I use all my concentration, but the results will be different from the real thing.”

I wasn’t paying much attention to what he was saying, but that last part made me flinch. Materialization, concentration—whatever. But different from the real thing? “Wait, is that why the Sprite earlier tasted so bland...?”
Auril nodded without hesitation. “That’s right. Is there a problem?”
Of course there is. That means I can no longer experience the refreshing taste of Sprite from here on out.
“That is a serious Sprite addiction you have, my friend. But seeing as you miss it so much, I guess that means it’s been quite a while since you came over from your world?”

What was this old man talking about? The fact that he was trying to dig for information at a moment like this was, well... That thankfully brought me to my senses. “Forget that—why are you doing all this? It’s obvious that power is a very important one.”
Auril laughed as if he had read my mind and found whatever he saw very cute. “You once told me that you received an invitation from someone nicknamed the GM.”
Ah, I did say that once. “And?”

“That means that ownership of this space will be transferred to them sometime in the future. I don’t know how that transpired, but if it’s going to happen anyway, there is no reason to hand over the substantial potential this space has to them as well.”

I thought I could understand his logic. Even if this was something you would never do under normal circumstances, if the service termination date had already been announced, that was a different story. No amount of stacking the deck was a waste. But there was one thing I was wondering.
“Why don’t you ask more about the GM?”
“Haha, you told me you don’t know much about them, other than their nickname.”
Ah, that’s true.
While I was busy nodding, Auril added in a low voice, “And even if you did know more, I do not particularly want to ask.”
“...Why?” I asked, genuinely curious.
Auril’s tone was somewhat forlorn as he answered. “I told you. A future that has already come to pass cannot be changed no matter what.”
Hmm, are you trying to say ignorance is bliss?
Just as I was starting to get where he was coming from, Auril stood up and I followed his lead. “That’s enough chitchat. Let us go. I think they will enjoy this too.”
We headed to the room with the Round Table, which I was far too familiar with.
Creaaak.
When Auril stepped through the door, the three men and one woman seated inside turned to him.
“...Master.”
Their reactions were all identical. I didn’t know what he did after he sent me off the other day, but everyone was looking at Auril with fear in their eyes.
“And... that man is here again as well.”
They also showed interest in me. But was it because Auril firmly put his foot down when it came to my identity last time? None of them were bold enough to open their mouths and ask.

Just like that, a strange silence descended over the Round Table for a beat. The one to end it was Auril. “Haha, everyone is so tense today.” He spoke like an all-powerful being who, out of consideration for the little guy, wanted to assure them they could relax now.
The woman whose name I didn’t know parted her lips in an exhale. “Understandably so, considering how you were at the end of our last meeting...”
Auril chuckled apologetically. From there, the atmosphere started to loosen up.

“Anyway, it’s good to see everyone together. You see, I made something very interesting during my conversation with this man.” Auril proceeded to place the jewel down at the center of the Round Table before continuing. “I summoned you all here for the purpose of exchanging information, but we haven’t managed to have a proper conversation yet, have we? Perhaps this will solve that problem.”
“Could you please explain in more detail?” The man who I presumed to be the head of Orcules asked.
Auril briefly explained the rules of the meeting. Once the explanation was over, there were mixed reactions.
“Information that more than half of the members are unaware of... That’ll be difficult.” The woman seemed somewhat worried.

The middle-aged man named Kagureas, on the other hand, seemed to welcome the idea. “But it has to be at least that compelling for this to turn into a proper exchange. Since everyone has been busy hiding things from each other so far.”
The child, Fallen Scholar, who spoke in a dignified manner despite his young appearance, asked only one thing. “Will you be participating, Master?”
“Of course I intend to participate. The same goes for my friend beside me.”

At Auril’s response, the four people turned to me again. They seemed somewhat displeased. I was sure they didn’t want to reveal any information to a strange outsider who had suddenly intruded on their meeting.
And while I may look like I have Auril’s favor, they must be wondering if I’m really on the same level as them.
Hmm, so what should I do? I think it would be best to prove how qualified I am first.
After taking a moment to think, I called Auril’s name. Actually, I was about to call his name, but I stopped myself just in time. “Um...”
“Ah, just call me Master. As it stands, you are the only one here who knows my name.”
Uh, you’re just gonna drop that on us out of nowhere?
The moment the old man cut me off, the eyes of the other four people in the room went wide.
What the hell is this?
To be honest, “baffled” wasn’t a strong enough word to describe how I was feeling right now. Just how did this old man treat these people?
“He knows... your name...?”

I had no idea he hadn’t even told them his name. Well, maybe this would be useful for establishing my credibility. As I was processing my shock and trying to look at this positively, I noticed Auril smile so that only I could see.
Jeez, he’s so transparent.

It was obvious why this old man was helping me. If it weren’t for me, he would have had no reason to participate in this meeting. The reason he’d said yes to my proposal in the first place was probably because he wanted to obtain as much information about me as possible. And that wasn’t all.

“Now, now. Sit yourselves down. It’s only natural that you’re wary of him, but that can all be resolved by him going first.” Auril smoothly set things up so that I’d be forced to share an important piece of information.

“...Shouldn’t you ask if everyone will participate first?” I didn’t hide my disapproval at the old man’s trick. But what was this now? The eyes of the quartet widened again like they couldn’t believe what they were seeing.
“How could he speak in such a way to Master...?”
“...But Master isn’t reprimanding him.”
Ugh, it’s like I can’t say anything here.
It was so ridiculous that it wasn’t even funny.
Drag.
I just pulled out a chair wherever and sat down. As soon as I did, everyone at the table expressed their intent to participate one by one.
“I will participate.”
“I will too.”
“...Who would refuse a seat at a table like this?”

The number of people who opted out was zero. Auril didn’t bother to hide his satisfied smile and took on the role of emcee. “Then we’ve reached a unanimous agreement. There is no need for introductions, so let’s get started. Once you go first, we will go around the table clockwise.”

With that, everyone’s attention turned to me again. Even I couldn’t help feeling the heat, and rightfully so, because I was the first speaker of the very first Round Table summit. Depending on the quality of the information I gave them here, the quality of the information they would provide me would go up as well.
Even if it weren’t for that, it would be best not to let them look down on me.

There was something I’d learned from my time at the Round Table twenty years in the future. First, acting cool was the way to go. Just like how people applauded celebrities for so much as taking a poo, there were many moments I’d passed my turn with insignificant information that the others simply assumed held some hidden meaning because I was the one sharing it.
Hmm, what should I go with?
Even as I continued to think it over, I studied each face sitting at the Round Table. Everyone was showing a strong interest in me, and among them, Auril was the most enthusiastic.
So, you’re dying to know what information I’ll drop in a situation like this, huh?
Thanks to that, my anxiety vanished. I knew what this old man was waiting for.
Not a chance.
This wasn’t my first rodeo. Coming to a decision, I opened my mouth to share something that would be useless to Auril and also satisfy the other members. “The Earth Witch is alive.”
[Lion Style Form 1: Juggling Information]

chapters.title: Chapter 310: Round Table (4)
paragraphs: The Earth Witch was alive. I had several reasons for recycling this information. Among them, the top one was that it was a way to screw over Auril Gavis, who had been looking forward to the information I was going to provide.

“Ha...” He seemed to be at an actual, literal loss for words given the way he could only groan, an incredulous look in his eyes. The sight instantly warmed my heart. Well, that wasn’t the only reason that I threw out that piece of information, though.

That brought us to the second point: this tidbit was quite useful. My source? Me. I had been very surprised when I first heard it. At the risk of being dramatic, I actually felt my heart drop when he told me, although I hadn’t let it show, unlike these guys. Put simply, it was the best piece of information to make me look impressive.
Flick.

I slowly studied everyone’s reactions. They were uniform. At first, their faces seemed to say, Huh? What is he on? Then they processed what I was telling them and all turned toward the same spot—the center of the Round Table where the jewel was situated, the place where the truth was stored. Soon, the jewel glowed green.
“It’s green.”
“Then that must be the truth...”
“At least, that’s what this man believes.”
At the sight of their astonishment, I chuckled. Yeah, that should be enough to prove my credentials.
So, you never told them about that, huh?

That was my third reason. By asking this question, I could discern how much information Auril had offered his members. If Auril had been sharing this kind of high-quality information with them this whole time, the light wouldn’t have turned green.
Well, I expected that to be the case when I realized they didn’t even know his name.

There was also a fourth reason: sharing this information with the members. After all, there was no mention of the Earth Witch being alive in the game. I interpreted this to mean that the old man had intentionally hidden this information for some reason.
Yeah, secrets are best when exposed.

I’d pretty much just spilled poison on this group. Although I didn’t know the side effects of this poison, how lethal it was, or whether it would pass with nothing more than a slight sting, judging by their sour expressions, it seemed I had succeeded. I had learned a secret that Auril was trying to hide from the four veterans in this gathering. This would definitely set off a chain reaction that wasn’t in Auril’s favor.
“To think the Earth Witch was alive... I will start researching this from now on.” Fallen Scholar, who took the form of a child, pondered this bit of news with a studious glint in his eyes.

“I’m sure the palace knew about this yet kept it hidden. Perhaps this could serve as a weak spot in their armor.” The face of the head of Orcules was bright with determination, like I just handed him a powerful weapon.
“If the witch really is alive... where is she now?” The woman echoed the same question I had asked Auril.
Oh, you even look smart.
“What is your name?”
The woman in fancy dress frowned at my question. “...Ravi,” she said softly.
Ravi. I couldn’t even be sure if that was her first or last name. Actually, I couldn’t be sure it was her real name at all. Well, I would look into it later.
“But why are you asking that?” she wondered aloud.
That was obvious. She was the only one here whose name I didn’t know. Of course, I couldn’t say something as boring as that though.
“Because you ask foolish questions. Is there a reason I should answer your question?”

It would be strange for me to speak respectfully to these people when I didn’t even use honorifics with Master, so I just treated her as an inferior. But did that piss her off a little? Ravi bit her lip and glared at me. My year of experience as Lion told me that this was the perfect time to offer her a carrot.
“However, if you say something interesting, I could be moved to give you the answer you seek.”

My arrogance made her pause before she nodded in apparent understanding. Then she closed her eyes for a beat and looked at me. “You want us to prove ourselves too. All right.” There was a competitive fire in that glare of hers.

I expected this reaction. These elites had all been gathered by the Master, after all. Their egos wouldn’t be run-of-the-mill, and it made sense to get frustrated hearing something like that from a mysterious man you were meeting for the first time. The other members seemed slightly fired up by my challenge as well.
Okay, I think this should be enough bait... Huh?
Sensing eyes on me, I turned in that direction to see Auril staring right at me. The look in his eyes seemed to ask, Who the hell does this bastard think he is?
Starting with me, the meeting proceeded clockwise.

“I guess it’s my turn now?” The second person to go was Auril, who was to my left, so I kept my ears open. Information that half of these experienced veterans had to be unaware of? Whatever he said here would have to be useful. “Then allow me.” Auril then imparted his knowledge to the group. “Ms. Ravi, the Earth Witch is where everyone’s hopes go.”
Oh, you clever old man. I was going to use that on my next turn. Well, it’s probably because he knew I was going to that he said it first.
Auril would have realized by now that stopping me from recycling information was his only way of getting to see what cards I really had.
Shaaaaaa.
Naturally, the green light came on. The members each muttered to themselves as was the custom at this point.
“Where everyone’s hopes go...”
“That must mean the labyrinth, right?”
“You could interpret it like that, but it could also be referring to outside the castle walls.”
So these guys couldn’t pinpoint a place, either.
“Now, now. We can talk more later so for now, let us continue.” Auril prodded the conversation along and the meeting resumed.
The next person to speak was the middle-aged man, Kagureas. Amelia had never heard the name, either. Perhaps it was a pseudonym.
“Haha, I’ve never done anything like this so I’m not sure what to say.”
“Speak freely. Someone like you is bound to have at least one piece of information. Something important that other people don’t know about.”
“Yes, but...” The muscular man seemed to ponder if it was worth sharing the information he had here before letting out a sigh. “I must take this seriously since Master is here. Here I go.”
“Go ahead.”
“There is a portal in the palace’s basement.”
When the green light came on, questions burst from everyone’s lips except Auril’s.
“A portal? Is it connected to the labyrinth?”

Although he had no reason to reply since his turn had already passed, Kagureas shrugged and even provided an answer. “I learned about it by chance so I can’t be sure, but I do not think the portal is connected to the labyrinth.”
“This... is very interesting.”
“Then where in the world does the portal lead...?” Fallen Scholar muttered, sounding more like an old man than a child.
In unison, the four men and women naturally shifted their gazes to Auril Gavis and me. Everyone kept their mouths shut, but the hunger in their eyes was clear as day.
You two know, right?
That hunger for answers was a sight I’d encountered countless times while living as a Lion.
“...Haha.” Auril simply laughed it off.

I just kept silent like I wasn’t at all affected by what was going on. This was something that had been drilled into me over and over again through experience, and it always got me halfway to wherever I wanted to go—Lion Style Form Two: Sit Tight. Of course, even in Form Two, my gears were frantically turning as I tried to get my thoughts in order.
A secret related to the palace, huh? Perhaps he’s on the palace’s side.
Kagureas—what kind of man was he? The fact that I knew next to nothing about this guy, unlike the head of Orcules and the Fallen Scholar, made me even more interested in him.

However, it seemed someone didn’t want to let this pointless silence drag on. “Then it’s my turn.” With that, Fallen Scholar dropped his bomb without delay. “That which keeps the labyrinth’s mana circulating is vitality.”
As soon as I heard that, a question mark formed in my head. But it seemed I wasn’t the only one drawing a blank.
“...Lord Ruingenes, could you explain in simpler terms? Unlike you, we know little of the ways of magic.”

“Simpler? All right.” Fallen Scholar provided further explanation at Kagureas’s request. “Contrary to what’s commonly believed, the labyrinth is not sustained by mana. For mana to continue to circulate through it like it does now, it requires a different resource.” To me, this all sounded like an alien language.
However, it seemed the woman named Ravi knew a thing or two about magic. “And you’re saying that that resource is vitality,” she said in apparent understanding, and Fallen Scholar nodded.
“But so what?” Kagureas asked, sounding disgruntled. “I don’t think anyone here is all that curious about how the labyrinth works.”
Actually, I felt the same way. Where were we supposed to use this information?

“Tsk, how annoying.” When Fallen Scholar clicked his tongue, Kagureas clammed up. Seeing a muscular man tiptoe around a kid wasn’t as strange a sight as one would think. Although he looked like a child, Fallen Scholar gave off the aura of someone who shouldn’t be trifled with.
“Then may I explain instead?” Ravi said.
“Do as you wish,” Fallen Scholar said, seemingly sulking.
“Vitality as the resource needed to create mana stones means that the labyrinth is sustained through life force. If I understood that correctly... this changes everything.”
“What do you mean?”
“This means that humanity was not revived and this city was sustained by the discovery of the labyrinth. The labyrinth was sustained by the existence of this city and its people.”
The back of my head tingled.
Wait, hold on... Is that true? If what she said is correct...

“...So the adventurers who die inside the labyrinth essentially serve as its fuel. Which the palace must be aware of.” Thinking along the same lines I was, the head of Orcules verbalized the same conclusion I had just come to.
“Well, that’s how I understood it, anyway.” Ravi shrugged and glanced at Fallen Scholar.
“There is no doubt that vitality is the resource that maintains the circulation of the labyrinth. And suspicions about the palace are logical and can be derived from this fact.”
“I-I see...”
“Now, is that enough? I think this is just as valuable as a vague declaration that an unidentified portal exists under the palace.”
Kagureas laughed sheepishly at Fallen Scholar’s sharp remark. “Haha, don’t get angry. People like me don’t understand stuff unless they get everything explained to them.”
...Is this guy a barbarian?
I felt a strange sense of déjà vu from his manner of speech, but determining his race from that would be too much of a leap. There were plenty of adventurers who talked like him.
“Now it’s Ms. Ravi’s turn.” All eyes turned to the woman at Auril’s words.

I had some hopes riding on her too. Not only were the previous two pieces of information extremely interesting, but this woman had met my challenge earlier head-on. Even if it wasn’t to put me in my place, I was sure she’d want to prove we were all on a similar level.

“I guess it’s my turn.” She opened her mouth and then shared a completely unexpected piece of information. “The ancient elder dragon is dead. You all may not know this, but it happened over ten years ago.”

I was stunned. I had just been wondering what incredible piece of information she was going to reveal with that determined look on her face, but that was it? I almost wanted to laugh, but the light on the jewel was green. Auril would definitely have known this already, so that meant the other three were hearing it for the first time.
“...I see. No wonder the dragon tribe has been quiet recently.”
“So that’s the situation.”
“It’s a shame that he who lived through the age of the Immortal King has died.”

The trio took in this information like they were hearing a hard truth. At first, that seemed strange to me, but it made sense when I thought about it. From what I remembered, it was only after the Dragon Slayer, Regal Vagos, killed the ancient elder dragon that the new elder dragon was elected.
So that was roughly around this time, right?
Since I hadn’t studied the exact history, I couldn’t remember the exact year, but that seemed to be the case.
But I didn’t realize the secret was so well-kept that even these guys didn’t know about it.
I pursed my lips in disappointment, but I guessed she didn’t notice.
“What do you think? Was that interesting?”

“I don’t know.” I didn’t really get why they were reacting to the death of the dragon tribe’s chief like this in the first place. I couldn’t believe that she was acting all pompous over something like this. Wasn’t the information that was shared before hers clearly much more useful? So I just gave my honest opinion. “I don’t think it’s particularly valuable.”

“...You’re saying you’re vetoing it.” Ravi glared at me like I had hurt her pride. I also noticed a hint of suspicion mixed into her expression. She was probably wondering if I was putting on an act to intentionally put her down.
If you’re going to act high and mighty, bring me something more interesting.
For the sake of information quality, it was necessary to kill her spirit a bit.
Is it time to bring out Form Three?
I tapped my fingers on the arm of my chair absently and said, “It’s not my turn yet, but I’ll say this now.”
“What do you—”
How dare you speak when the Lion is speaking?

There was a chance I might be able to pass through the next round for free, so without leaving any room for interruption, I continued in one breath. “The one who killed the ancient elder dragon is a dragon man named Regal Vagos.”
“...Huh?” The woman stopped mid-objection. After a short pause, the jewel turned green.
Shaaaaaa.
The silence was all too familiar to me. As it fell, I looked at Ravi and spoke like I was kindly explaining something to a bug crawling on the ground. “What do you think, is that explanation enough?”
[Lion Style Form 3: Disrespect for the Weak]

chapters.title: Chapter 311: Round Table (5)
paragraphs: “Regal Vagos...?”
“I’ve met him once before. He was an adventurer with a very useful form of Dragon Speech.”
“An adventurer who betrayed his people... this piques my interest.”

After I was done speaking, Kagureas and the head of Orcules had a brief exchange. Even those short comments were significant. Piqued his interest? I couldn’t describe the discomfort I felt at hearing those words come out of the head of Orcules’s mouth. However, I took my eyes off them and directed my gaze somewhere else.
The woman in the fancy dress, Ravi, who had been looking at me with belligerence, now stared at me with her jaw slightly dropped. Her eyes were filled with shock. “H-How could you possibly...?”

Since she was even stuttering, it seemed my announcement had been shocking enough to pull the rug out from under her. But I had no room for sympathy. This was a cold-hearted, dog-eat-dog world, after all. If you missed an opportunity to strike, you couldn’t become the king of the jungle.
“N-No way. The number of people who know that information is still less than ten...”

At the sight of Ravi’s deep confusion, I chuckled. “You’re young,” I said, treating her like a naïve child who’d only ever seen the world’s good side. Her actual age would be much higher than mine, but that wasn’t my business. She didn’t know a thing about me, anyway.

Ravi’s reaction was instantaneous. Her lips clamped shut. It seemed being treated like a child pissed her off, as her face turned red and her eyes drilled holes into my head. There was one question carved into those eyes, though, and Ravi blurted it out. “Who... who are you?”

Name, identity, whatever it was—it was as if anything was fine with her as long as she learned even a little bit about me. She had asked a question that was all too vague. The other members watched the situation unfold with interest, not interrupting our conversation. Well, I was sure no one wanted to step forward to save face. They were just as curious about who I was as Ravi. The question she just asked probably scratched an itch for all of them.
Okay, the mood is just right.

My answer to her question was already decided. Although it may have felt a bit cliché, all cliché meant was that this had worked well so far. “Well,” I said unhurriedly, “that’s nothing I can’t answer.”
At that, I could see the level of focus in the room rise sharply. Really? Is he really going to tell us something? Their expressions filled with anticipation.
I studied each of those faces, relishing in them, and then continued. “For those who are worth it.”
“Ha...” When my words rang through the Round Table, Orcules’s commander released a scoff.
“You mean we have to prove ourselves to hear your name?” muscular, middle-aged Kagureas asked coolly. “We have to show you whether or not we are qualified to be associated with you?”
I didn’t keep quiet this time. “Thankfully, you understood correctly.” Instead, I agreed with him. This was the age of self-PR, after all. Why bother being humble? Nothing good ever came out of that.

“...Where did someone like this guy come from?” Fallen Scholar burst into laughter at my arrogant words. Come to think of it, this was the first time I’d ever seen him smile. Most of the time, he was just sipping on tea disinterestedly.
This definitely drew aggro.
I was smiling to myself behind my mask, satisfied with my handiwork, when I suddenly felt eyes on me. They belonged to Auril Gavis.
Jeez, so uncomfortable.
He was staring at me blankly, his gaze once again containing the same question: Who the hell does this bastard think he is?
Despite the slight hiccup, the meeting continued with Auril as the moderator.

“Three months ago, an envoy from the king visited the lord of Noark’s castle. Unfortunately, this matter was handled with the utmost secrecy, so it is unknown what they discussed.” The last person to speak this round, the head of Orcules, revealed this information and received a green light.
“Hmm! Interesting. I think this is the first time the castle has interacted directly with the palace.”
“Perhaps that’s why...”

Unlike Fallen Scholar, who was muttering to himself like he found this illuminating, this was not a very significant piece of information to me. What use did I have for politics from twenty years ago? There was only one thing I learned from this information—not only did the palace know about Noark at this point, but everyone who knew anything knew about the existence of the underground city.

“Then up next is...” After round one came to an end, Auril glanced at me. Then he pursed his lips in disappointment. “I guess we’ll have to go around again without this fellow this time. Is there anyone who would like to go first?”
The person to raise their hand was Kagureas. “I will go first.”
“Ah, will you?”
“I think going first would put me more at ease. I also have something I’d like to share.”
“Go ahead.”
The muscular man revealed his information, marking the start of the second round. “Um... Another one of the Genesis Treasures has been obtained.”

For something said while scratching his cheek, the information was far too shocking. My mind went blank for a moment. That was because twenty years from now, these items disappeared without a trace. But now he was saying another had been obtained?
Then that means he already had more than one.
I almost screamed, but I held it in. I wasn’t the only one who was shocked.
“What? Is that true?!” Fallen Scholar jumped up from his seat.
Ravi was also worked up. “F-From which tribe?”
“I cannot tell you that.”
“Then at least tell me how it was obtained...?”
“As for the how... I can only say it was luck.”
“How can you get an item like that out of luck?”
“Ah, don’t be like that, everyone. To be more precise, it’s more like I got the right to borrow it once in the future.”

Wow, it turned out this man was no ordinary guy. It was then that I realized I had entered the world of veterans. Obtaining one Genesis Treasure was doable in the game. All you had to do was clear the main character’s tribal storyline and become a chieftain. The real trouble started when you got to the second Genesis Treasure. You had to either clear the storyline of another tribe and obtain the right to use it or turn one of your comrades into a chieftain.
That means it really is possible to unlock it.
The moment that thought occurred to me, I glanced at Auril. His expression remained unchanged. Put simply, he already knew about this turn of events. Why did this old man call these kids failures?

As I was pondering this, Kagureas continued, “Anyway, there is only one reason I’m revealing this here. As Master has said, we have spent much time together, yet never spoken openly. But that needs to change. I have two now. Since the ancient elder dragon is dead, Ms. Ravi should be able to bring us another as long as she works at it.”
“Why are you saying that at a time like this?” Ravi scolded Kagureas sharply, shooting me a glance to see how I would react. But I’d already heard everything I needed to hear.
So, she is from the dragon tribe.

“Ah, my mistake. That was thoughtless of me.” Kagureas apologized like a true man and then wrapped up what he wanted to say. “Now there are three left. And if we really work together, I believe it’s doable... What do you all think?” He seemed to be asking everyone, but Kagureas’s eyes were fixed on the head of Orcules.
Ah, come to think of it, those two were fighting about this last time.
In a way, this could be seen as a peace offering. So how would the commander respond?

His answer was silence. Kagureas continued, trying to persuade him. “I know you have a grudge against the king. But think rationally. That relationship was built in this world, anyway. If you think of the family you left behind in the real world—”
“Stop.” The head of Orcules cut him off, voice cold. As if Kagureas had pulled a trigger of his, he suddenly exuded vicious murderous intent.

At this, the smile disappeared from Kagureas’s face as well. “As expected, you were trash all along. I thought your goals, at least, would be aligned with ours. You say the palace should be the target of all of our suspicions? That if we wish to return, we must help you? I feel like a fool for even getting my hopes up at your words.”
“Kagureas, please stop...”
“You heard it too, Ms. Ravi. This man has no desire to return.”
“That can’t be true. Otherwise, why would he show his face here every month?”

“Isn’t that obvious? Because if he makes good use of us, we can be helpful in his mission of killing the king. He probably only thinks of us as consumables he can use up before discarding. Am I wrong?”
At Kagureas’s belligerent demand, the leader of Orcules responded in the same acidic tone. “Aren’t you also hiding your true intentions?”
“What?”
“Lord Ruingenes said he believes the dimensional spell can be completed, but in truth, you were just going around collecting Genesis Treasures.”
“...What’s the problem with that? It’s obviously better to have more than one plan in place.”

“However, there has to be another reason why you opposed me when I tried to persuade Lord Ruingenes to help me. If your goal is to collect all the Genesis Treasures, you’ll inevitably come into conflict with the palace. Yet you keep interfering with my work.”
“Ah, you mean that?” Kagureas spoke confidently like he had nothing at all to hide. “I have good instincts. And I had a strong gut feeling that you are a charlatan and a piece of trash.”
The head of Orcules no longer opened his mouth. He just met Kagureas’s eyes and exuded an even thicker murderous intent. At this, I almost let out an exclamation of admiration.
His murderous intent is on another level.
You couldn’t compare the members of the Round Table twenty years from now to these people. Even though the murderous intent wasn’t even aimed at me, my skin burned and my breathing stuttered.

“Haha, it seems everyone’s fired up.” Auril, who had only been watching up to this point, stepped in and said something unexpected. “We’d better call it a day. Everyone go rest and we’ll meet again next time.”
...What? Wait, we’re ending it here? We haven’t even properly gotten started yet. If you’re going to end it, at least finish this round. I manipulated the last round for nothing, then.
“Wait—” Just as I was about to say something, my vision flickered like the sputtering of a light bulb.
Flash!
When I opened my eyes again, I saw Amelia’s familiar face. “...You’re back already?”
Ha, he really kicked me out.
“How long has it been?”
“About three seconds since you closed your eyes.”
Three seconds, huh? It was natural that Amelia was giving me a strange look. To her, it had only been a moment. It probably didn’t even feel real to her.
I was thirsty, but when I reached for the cup on the nightstand, Amelia handed it to me instead. “Here.”
What the...?
“Ah, oh... thanks.” When I thanked her, not able to hide my bashfulness, Amelia averted her eyes awkwardly.
“So, what happened inside this time?”
“Oh, that...”
Man, where do I start?

Too much had happened to summarize what I’d been through in a few short sentences, so I just told her everything from the beginning. I figured she might be able to notice anything I might have missed.
“Wait, Auril Gavis apologized? For such an unreasonable demand?”
“Yes?”
“...Nothing, keep going.”

The story, which started with the battle of wits between me and Auril, soon reached the Round Table. The increasingly peculiar look in Amelia’s eyes became clearer and clearer. It was a look I’d seen several times at the Round Table.
“You... what did you used to do in your original world?”

chapters.title: Chapter 312: Inheritance (1)
paragraphs: Arua Raven stopped by a rather well-known, high-end restaurant in District Seven to meet up with her clanmates for the first time in a long while. Of course, this was her first visit here. If they had set this meeting up at one of the places they normally went to, they would only have ended up more depressed.
“Aren’t you going to order?”
“We’re not all here yet.” At Raven’s short response, Abman looked somewhat uneasy.
As an awkward tension began to descend, Ainar spoke. “No, everyone is here. Missha said she’s not coming. I hoped she would change her mind, but if she’s not here by now, that means she hasn’t.”
“...I see. Then it’s just the three of us.” Raven let out an involuntary sigh. As she did, similar sounds came from beside her. All of them were feeling despondent.
“Raven?”
“Yes, Mr. Urikfried?”
“What happened with Erwen? Have you been in touch?”
“I did send her a letter. I told her that we’re going to be discussing the loot from the last expedition, and Mr. Yandel’s... estate, so we’d like her to come.”
In truth, she had only contacted Erwen out of a sense of duty. She didn’t expect the elf to come in the slightest, considering how she left them last time.
“Did you receive a reply?”
“No, I didn’t. But once we’re done dividing the loot, I’m just going to send her share by mail.”
“I see.”

“Anyway, enough about that elf. I never imagined Miss Karlstein would be absent too. I didn’t expect that at all. I thought for sure that the person who was most central to this discussion would come.” Raven sighed and looked at Ainar. Then she asked carefully, “How is Miss Karlstein? Is she doing all right?”

Raven was genuinely worried about her. The last time she saw her was during the funeral procession held by the palace. At the time, they were far apart and it wasn’t the right moment to have a conversation. She wondered how she was.
“Of course she’s not doing well. She’s holed up in her room all day and won’t even eat properly. I once force-fed her food and she threw it up.”
“I see...”
“That’s why I don’t go home often these days. I think she feels more uncomfortable when I’m there.”
“Then where are you staying right now, Miss Ainar?”
“I’m staying in the holy land. But it seems like Missha eats at least the bare minimum when I’m not around. So I just bought a bunch of food for the house.”
“That’s a relief.”
“Raven, what do you think? Is it okay to leave Missha alone like this?”
“That’s...” Raven spoke based on her own experience over the past month. “First, I think the reason she can’t eat is because of guilt. You know. The act of eating itself... brings discomfort...”
Raven’s explanation was vague, which was unlike her, but Ainar and Abman nodded in apparent understanding. “Ah, right.”
“I think I get what you mean too. But what does that have to do with anything?”
“...I don’t know. How to help Miss Karlstein, that is. I don’t think it’s a bad idea to give her some time alone, but I also don’t know if that’s the right answer.”
“True, it’s not like you have all the answers.”

Ainar hadn’t said that in a mean way, but Raven felt her chest tighten and a wave of sadness wash over her anyway. Ainar wasn’t wrong. If he were here, he definitely would have been able to figure out the best way to handle this.
“Before that, let’s order. If we keep loitering like this, we’ll get kicked out.” Abman must have sensed something was off because he changed the subject.
Raven shifted gears from the heavy conversation to choose something from the menu as well. “Oh, I’ve never been here before but the food is very good. What are you two doing? Eat.”
“Ah, right...”
After the food was served, they chatted as they ate, and then they officially started talking about work.
“There are no issues with the loot settlement. All there was to do was divide everything into five equal parts. The problem is the inheritance... Have you all seen Mr. Yandel’s will?”

“Ah, I saw it. Other than the allocation ratio, there was nothing to it. Well, what else would you expect from that guy...?” Abman laughed a bit before trailing off. Then he carefully posed a question. “But isn’t it strange?”
“Strange?”
“The ratio. To be honest, I don’t understand why he split it like that.”
“Ah, about that...”

Raven nodded slightly in sympathy. She had been surprised at first too. She never imagined all of them would get an equal 20 percent share of his inheritance. She thought for sure that most of his wealth would go to Missha or Ainar. However, Bjorn Yandel wasn’t that type of person. Because the only thing he’d written down was the ratio and not which exact items would go to whom, they would have to reach an agreement on that amongst themselves, but everyone’s share was the same size.
“Since you didn’t finish your sentence, I suppose you have a guess?”

Raven smiled sadly. “It’s obvious why Mr. Yandel would do that.” That clever barbarian warrior had wanted to ensure that even after his death, they wouldn’t hurt each other by arguing over money and could continue to support each other and themselves without issue.
“...I don’t think we should leave Miss Missha alone like this.”
Yes, if he were here, this is what he would have wanted.
Three days after my return from the Round Table, Amelia and I put on our full equipment and visited the castle.

We met up with a man at the designated rendezvous point. “Nice to meet you. You’re Iron Mask, correct?” His nickname in Noark was Felic Barker, the leader of the clan to which the young Rainwales sisters belonged. There were thirteen or so members in total.

“Nice to meet you. I’m Iron Mask.” I also went by Bjon, son of Thor, but I used my new nickname when introducing myself instead. There was nothing particularly wrong with that. In this city, many people used pseudonyms and titles.
“Let’s go in.”

When we followed the man into the clan base located inside the castle walls, the smell of alcohol immediately hit my nose. Inside the well-decorated interior, rough-looking clan members lounged around, drinking and smoking cigarettes. This wasn’t some kind of criminal hideout.
“Would you like to drink?” When we sat on the sofa across from him, Felic Barker offered us alcohol by the bottle.
“No,” Amelia said sharply.

I just accepted the bottle, as it’d be weird if both of us refused to drink. We came here to join the clan, after all. In this city, refusing to drink with someone was the same as saying, “I don’t trust you.”
Click.

Touching the base of the helmet, I raised it to just above my chin and chugged down the drink. Felic Barker grinned. “Good, good. I like it. Ah, but there’s one thing I want to ask you. Is that okay?”
“Ask.”
“Why did you choose our clan?”

The answer was simple: because the Rainwales sisters belonged to this clan. This was our best way of ensuring we would have a valid reason to be around them when that incident occurred in five months. We couldn’t tell him that, though.
“Emily said you guys made us an offer first.”
“But if even half the rumors about you guys are true, you would have had better offers.”
I provided the answers I had prepared in advance. “Because having a clan seems more convenient, but if we go somewhere like that, we’re bound to get a lower share of the loot.”
“You’re saying you’d rather have a Troll head than an Ogre claw.”
“Yes, is that a problem?”
Felic Barker stared at me like he was trying to gauge my true intentions, but there was no way that would work. How was he going to look into my eyes when I was wearing an iron helmet over my face?

Just as I was thinking this, the guy suddenly burst into laughter, his eyes sparkling. “Ha! Hahaha!” Unlike Auril, this guy was a joke. His high-and-mighty act was full of nothing but hot air. His tone sounded strangely fake too. “Good, very good.”
“What’s good about it?”
“It makes me like you guys more.”
“Then do we pass?”

“No, not yet.” Felic wagged his finger at us slowly like some kind of mafia boss. “We operate on a merit-based system. There are three ranks someone in the clan can have, excluding me, and the share of the loot you get is determined by your rank. But we don’t know what you’re capable of yet. Have you ever heard of the term ‘law of the jungle?’”
“I have.”
“Then this will be quick. If you want the Troll’s head, take it. And prove yourself. In this world, that is how you stand out—”
Ah, I had been wondering what he was talking about. “Fine.”
“You’re saying you want to know whether the rumors are true or not.”
“Yes, but—”
“Then why are you talking so much?” When I stood up from my seat, Felic blinked up at me, startled.
What, you thought if you acted tough I’d get scared? These kinds of cutscenes are meant to be skipped over as quickly as possible.
“Enough talk—tell me what I should do. What, do I need to kill you?”
“...Fights are only allowed between members. And I didn’t necessarily mean kill—”

Ah, so boring. “Then who do I need to destroy?” I glanced around at the clan members in the area, at which point one of the big guys who made eye contact with me flinched. “Looks like he’s my opponent, then.”
“That’s right. But the fight doesn’t have to be to the death—”
Ugh, stop making so much noise.
When I stomped over with murderous intent, the large man scrambled out of my way and glanced at Felic with the distinct look of someone begging for help.
At that point, Felic came to his senses as well and spoke up. “W-Wait! There’s a vacant lot out back.”
“Ah, then let’s move there.”
“A-And special abilities are prohibited during a duel.”

Ha, I didn’t think there would be a rule banning skills. That meant the fight had to be conducted with just our passives and our default stats. It seemed Noark really was a macho kind of place. “Destroy him without using special abilities... Well, that won’t be too difficult.” After a moment’s thought, I gladly accepted the rules.
But what was this? “I’d prefer if no one dies, if possible...” Felic said in a very small voice.
I turned to him in shock. “But then I can’t get promoted!”
“All you need is their surrender.”

“What? I can get promoted even without killing anyone?” Weren’t bloody power struggles the norm in the underground world? Besides, he was the one who brought up the ‘law of the jungle’ earlier. “What is going on? How does that make sense?” I stared at him like I genuinely didn’t understand.
Coincidentally, he was also wearing a similar expression on his face. “You... didn’t you say you’ve been in Noark less than a month?”
“And?”
“Nothing...” Felic was the first to avert his eyes.
In a dark room with windows covered by thick cloth, Missha Karlstein lifted her upper body off her mattress, deep bags under her eyes. Another day has begun.

Peeking through the curtain just enough to check that it was daytime, she lay back on the bed again. Sleep did not come, and her unwashed body was still covered in sweat from last night’s nightmare. More than that, her stomach was empty to the point of pain, to the point that it ached.

Missha dragged her haggard body out of the room. She stopped in front of Bjorn’s room, which hadn’t been touched since that day. It almost felt like if she opened that door, she’d find the person she’d been longing for sleeping inside. But she once again couldn’t bring herself to check.
Turning away weakly, she headed down the stairs to the first floor, which was as dark as the second. The curtains were drawn because of the people coming to leave flowers.
“She came again...” Missha murmured distantly.
On the table was a note left by Ainar written in crooked letters. It read that the pantry had been refilled and that she should check it out.
Rattle.
Missha checked the pantry. It was mostly filled with things she used to enjoy eating, like rye bread, vegetables often used for cooking, and meat and fruits.

Just looking at it made her nauseous. She couldn’t even bear to smell it. The rye bread was Bjorn’s favorite, not to mention the meat. Vegetables were something she always kept in stock since Bjorn was a picky eater, meaning she often ended up having to eat his share.
In the end, Missha almost ran away from the pantry, but she was well aware that she still had to eat. If she didn’t, her body would fail. Bjorn wouldn’t have wanted that.
“Bjorn...”
In the dark kitchen with the lights turned off, she collapsed into a chair and sobbed for a while before finally getting back up again and heading to the pantry. Which was when it happened.
“Oh, you’re here. I thought no one would be home.” An unfamiliar male voice rang out behind her.
A thief?
Missha grabbed the knife that was on the cutting board and whirled around. The action was so nimble that it was hard to believe it was performed by someone who looked so haggard.

“Woah, woah. That’s dangerous.” The unidentified man had no trouble grabbing her wrist to subdue her. Even when she strained against his grip, he would not budge. “You’re going to start off swinging a knife at me when it’s been so long since we last met?”
“So long...?” Missha looked up at the face of her assailant. It was too dark to tell, but it looked somehow familiar.

He was human with skin that was white as snow, and not a single scar could be seen on his body, which seemed to indicate he’d been raised in a wealthy household. His platinum hair, a symbol of nobility, was well-groomed and slicked back.
“Red Cat, are you a player?”
“Hmm? F-Frayer?”
“An evil spirit.”
“N-N-No, I’m not!”
Thanks to that distinctly light, yet creepy manner of speech, she immediately remembered where she knew this man from. “You’re that—!”

“I guess you remember? I’m Baekho Lee. I’m going to let you go, so stay calm.” After introducing himself with a strange-sounding name, the man released her arm as promised. Missha cradled her sore wrist and took a step back. The platinum-haired man then smiled in what he probably felt was a reassuring way. “Don’t be so on guard.”
Goosebumps crawled down her spine. Unlike his wide, curved lips, his eyes were not smiling at all.
“I just came to ask you a question.”

chapters.title: Chapter 313: Inheritance (2)
paragraphs: Her body froze like she had just come face-to-face with her natural predator. Her heart pounded like it was malfunctioning. Despite wanting to die every single day, Missha suddenly craved life.
Almost like he could read her mind, Baekho’s smile grew bigger. “You know that Bjorn Yandel was a player, right?”
“I don’t know. I have no idea what you’re—”

Although Missha immediately denied it, Baekho didn’t even hear her out to the end. “Oh, so you really did know?” He didn’t sound like he was merely feeling her out—he sounded like he was already sure. Missha looked into Baekho’s eyes, trying to gauge his ulterior motives.
Flinch.
Without her even realizing it, her breath caught. Eyes so empty that they were practically bottomless turned her way. It felt like he could see right through her insides.
Seeing as Missha was unable to speak a word, the man opened his mouth. “Bjorn Yandel. How did he die?”

His tone was calm and asked nothing more of her than for her to verify the facts, but Missha detected a strange undercurrent of anger beneath the surface. She had no idea why. Could it be that he and Bjorn were close? No, that made no sense. Then why was he taking out his anger on her?

“Word around the city is that he died while giving you guys time to escape...” At that moment, the air in the kitchen grew heavy. “Did you guys kill him?” The oppressive feeling was so intense that it became hard for her to breathe. At the same time, the anger seeping into Baekho’s voice grew clearer. “Makes sense, since you knew he was an evil spirit. Did you stab him in the back to steal his fortune? I heard he even left his estate in your names. That’s more than enough reason to kill him.”
“What kind of nonsense—”
“How is that nonsense? You guys don’t even see us as real people.” His tone was mocking yet cynical.

At those words, Missha realized this man had had a similar experience in the past. Was that why? It suddenly felt like a blade was digging into her heart, not just because she was afraid of the man in front of her. Could it be that Bjorn thought the same thing when he looked at her? Was he anxious and hurt, fearing she would look at him with disgust if his identity were revealed? Had he been building up a wall all alone to protect himself?
In his final moments alone, what were the thoughts running through his head?

Just thinking about it made her lungs tighten. Even he would have been anxious and scared. That was probably why he didn’t leave any words for them in his will. Though he always smiled in front of them, a deep loneliness would have lay behind that smile.
“Answer me. Did you guys do it?”

One thing was for certain, though: despite it all, he cherished them more than anyone. That was why Missha met the man’s eyes without flinching. “There’s no way we would do that.” Even though she knew this man would never truly hear her, she said, “Don’t see him as a person... Bjorn...? How would that ever be possible?”

She, at least, could never see him as anything less. She regretted the fact that she hadn’t told him that herself sooner. Then Bjorn wouldn’t have been anxious around her. Missha closed her eyes, no longer afraid of this strange man. She waited out the waves of emotions that washed over her.
“He had a good comrade, then,” Baekho said. “Unlike me.”

Contrary to his previously tyrannical personality, his voice now sounded oddly sad. Missha opened her eyes again. A moment later, the pressure that pressed down on her skin to the point of pain disappeared without a trace.
“Was it Missha Karlstein?”
“Y-Yes...?” Missha replied in confusion at the drastic change in attitude.
Baekho smiled. “What if I told you there’s a way to bring Bjorn Yandel back from the dead?” And this time when he did, his eyes crinkled too.
Two weeks had passed since we first joined Felic Barker’s clan.
Whoosh.

I sat in front of a blazing campfire on the second floor’s Rock Desert. Behind me, four men and women were busy preparing camp. Oh, for reference, they were doing so per my orders. If all the work was left to the herder as usual because they couldn’t be bothered to help, it would just end up taking way longer.
“Ugh, why do we have to do this?”
“Be quiet, he’ll hear you over there.”
I already heard it, punk.
I smirked and glanced at the four people preparing camp. When I did, I made eye contact with a lump of muscles.

To prove my qualifications to Felic Barker so I could join his clan, my first bloody battle to climb the ranks—no, what they called a duel—had been against this guy. He was a rank-six adventurer by overworld standards. After getting his head bashed in within the first three seconds of our no-skill fight, he narrowly escaped with his life thanks to potions. His name was...
“Dumbo.”
“...It’s Durbon, not Dumbo.”
Oh, right.
I may have made a mistake, but the sight of his arrogant poker face pissed me off a little. Durbon had to be a pseudonym, anyway. I didn’t see how it mattered.
“Haven’t come to your senses, have you?” I jumped up from my seat and headed toward Dumbo. Then, as if the memory of getting beaten up had finally come back to him, he began to tremble.
Jeez, if you’re going to end up like this just from me standing in front of you, why are you acting so tough?

“Dumbo.” I placed my hand on his shoulder and spoke with all my authority as the third team leader of Clan Barker. “Do I look like a joke to you?” My grip tightened. “Your name is now Dumbo. That’s easier to pronounce. Got it?”
Silence.
“Answer.”
“...Sure.”
Tsk, should’ve said that from the start.
I patted Dumbo on the shoulder and praised him for accepting the name change, then sent him off to finish preparing our camp. I, on the other hand, returned to the campfire and took out some jerky.
Chew.

Having fought three separate duels on my first day as a clan member, I became one of the clan’s three team leaders with the approval of the clan’s head. Since Noark was a faction of real men, the team leader’s authority was absolute, especially inside the labyrinth.
Whew, is this the taste of power?
While I goofed around as everyone worked, one of the weaklings came over to let me know the preparations were complete. “Please, rest. We will take watch...”
This scrawny guy’s name is... What was it again?
Anyway, he was our team guide—not a scout, and his navigation skills were slightly below Rotmiller’s. But perhaps because he’d been looting for so long, he knew all the good places to plunder.
“I’m not tired now. Later. That kid is on first watch, right? If I’m tired, I’ll leave it to him and go to sleep. You guys rest first.”
“Ah, right...” When I gave them permission to sleep, Scrawny relayed the news to his friends and got into his sleeping bag.
“Can I sit?”
“Of course.”
A red-haired woman sat in the chair across from me. Although she gave off a mature air despite her age, the young woman was our team’s herder, Amelia’s older sister.
“What was your name again?”
“Laura Rainwales.” Laura obediently answered, her clipped tone implying she was wary of me, the newly appointed team leader. Which felt strange.
They look so alike—how can they give off such different vibes?

Their overall facial features were similar but the sister had a much gentler air about her, even knowing she once slaughtered a famous adventurer to save her younger sibling at the age of twelve, and even though she was speaking in a stiff tone.
“Is there a problem?”
“No, I just figured you must be having a hard time as well.”
“Ah...” Laura’s lips parted a bit in surprise. I guessed she never thought someone who hounded his subordinates as much as I did would say something like this.
“Your sister is a herder too, right?”
“Yes, she is working under Team Leader Martis.”
“Aren’t you worried?”

Laura clammed up in response to my question and glanced at me. She seemed suspicious of my intentions, but it seemed she decided it was not wise to ignore a question from the new team leader. “I’m not worried at all. I believe Team Leader Martis will take good care of my younger sister, so I am unconcerned.” Laura gave me a fake answer.
Yikes, this makes me feel like a snake or something.
“You can tell me the truth—it’s okay. You’re sisters. It’s normal to be worried.”
When I pressed, Laura couldn’t help but confess some of her feelings. “I am worried, but I don’t believe Team Leader Martis will maliciously bully my sister or send her to her death.”
“Your rationale?”
“...Because I am worth that much.”
“Hmm? Explain that in more detail. I’m the leader of this team, after all. I should know the situation.”
Laura seemed to ponder whether or not to tell me this before opening her mouth. “I may be a herder, but after many years of expeditions, I’ve grown strong enough to pull my weight.”

This was an established fact. Though low-ranking, I heard she had four essences too. But Laura was still a herder. Though she was treated well by the team, no matter how hard she worked, she was no different from a slave to the clan and couldn’t even claim her share of the loot.
“In exchange for giving up your share, you asked him to take good care of your sister.”
“Just because I earned it doesn’t mean I can have it. To be honest, when my father tried to sell my sister off as a herder, I was the one who brought her here.”
“Your reason?”
“At least in this clan... she won’t have to go through the things most others do.”
“You’re kind.”

Laura didn’t respond to that, and a brief silence ensued. It wasn’t particularly awkward. I sat there quietly staring into the fire to organize my thoughts, and when I got tired enough, I got up from my seat.
“I’m going to sleep now.”
“Sure.”
“That should have been about an hour of your watch. After another hour, switch shifts.”
“Pardon? But my shift is—”

“If you take a double, how are you going to fight tomorrow? You just said earlier you can pull the weight of one person. So, after an hour, hand it over to the next person and go to sleep. If they argue, tell them I ordered it.”
After that, I went straight to my sleeping bag. Laura seemed uneasy and tried to say something, but when she heard my snores, she fell silent.
Laura Rainwales, huh?
I had one thought on my mind until I fell asleep.
How can I save this girl?

After our first day of camping in the Rock Desert, we hastily resumed our journey the next morning. On the second day, we were able to arrive at Pilgrim’s Path on the third floor. Passing through Twilight Slope on the Rock Desert route, we continued traveling to the clan’s gathering place, Thorn Reed Field. This was a hunting ground that spanned from the Witch’s Forest, which lay in the center of the third floor, to parts of the western field.
When we arrived there on the fourth day, the rest of the teams had already arrived. After briefly acknowledging Amelia with eye contact, I headed over to the clan’s leader.
“Any trouble on the way?”
“None. Everyone is skilled.”
“Haha, they may not be as good at fighting as you, but they can each pull their own weight.”
Did this bastard have trouble distinguishing empty words from actual compliments? I smirked and sat on the empty chair next to him.
“Now, it would be best to move straight away since we’re all here, but since some of our friends are here for the first time, I will explain how this works again.”
Clan Leader Felic Barker smoothly briefed us on our plans, but there was no real strategy to speak of. The only plan was to split up and loot people, using this forest of reeds as our base.

“I’ll say this in advance but if you encounter an enemy that looks like they’ll give you even the slightest amount of trouble, make contact with the other teams through your guide. They will drop everything and rush over to help straight away.” The clan leader finished the briefing as quickly as a flash and asked if there were any final questions, to which I immediately raised my hand.
“But isn’t this a very inefficient method?”

“...Inefficient?” The leader of the clan looked at me like I was some sort of strange creature. I guessed that word sounded out of place coming out of a barbarian’s mouth, but that was a bit unfair. What other race out there valued efficiency as much as the barbarians did? “If you wish to say something, say it.”
As soon as permission was granted, I confidently opened my mouth. “The first problem is using the herders. Why do such a thing?”
“As I said before, planting an ally on the inside is a huge advantage in an ambush. It can reduce the need to use consumables too.”
“What are you saying? I’m not talking about that.”
“Huh?” the clan leader demanded, his eyes narrowing.

I spoke slowly like I was trying to explain something to someone particularly thick. “If you do that, you will only kill the adventurers who are nice enough to let the herders into their group. And those nice adventurers are usually poor.”
“...What on earth are you trying to say?”
“We should hunt those who plunder, just like us. Then we can seize all the equipment they’ve looted!”
When I explained my plan in earnest, a momentary silence fell. Then, before long, laughter broke out.
“Hahaha!”
“Why are you laughing?”
“Ah, sorry if that offended you. I’ve lived in Noark for over ten years but I’ve never heard an idea like that before.”
“So, your answer?”
“On the surface, your idea has merit, but your suggestion fails to take into account a key factor. We’re not all-knowing. How can we identify plunderers?”
Haha, I thought you’d say that.
I grinned. “Okay, hear me out. I have a way.”

chapters.title: Chapter 314: Inheritance (3)
paragraphs: Rank-six adventurer Droff Itoms was like any other run-of-the-mill adventurer in the labyrinth. Not affiliated with a large clan, his current party was intermediated by the Adventurers’ Guild. If there was anything a bit odd about him, it was that he was taking over for his previous team leader who had died recently. But that didn’t change the fact that he was ordinary.

Their party was active on the fourth floor. His teammates were of mediocre talent and their attitudes and mentality were no different from most others. They normally worked hard to collect mana stones, but like any other adventurer, they did not hesitate to get their hands dirty if the right opportunity arose, which was why Droff and his team were currently in a dilemma.
“Oh, you guys are so kind!”

Running into this barbarian was pure coincidence. As they were passing through the field of reeds on their way to the Witch’s Forest, they discovered him crying for help. Apparently, he got separated from his party trying to drink in secret during their break.
What kind of blockheaded bastard...?

It was almost unbelievable at first, but the man didn’t seem to be faking it. After all, he was a barbarian. Something completely illogical like this was more than possible for someone like him. More importantly, their race did not lie often, nor did they do it well.
Then that means he really is lost...
“Droff, what are you going to do?”
“You’re not going to just send him away, right? I think the ring that guy is wearing is a sub-space.”
“He said he left his weapon behind too. If we’re going to do this, let’s do it fast. His teammates might come looking.”

Everyone’s eyes gleamed with greed. This was only natural, because a sub-space ring sold for pretty much the same price it was bought at. It wasn’t like it came with an expiration date, nor was it like other equipment that could only be worn by someone of the same size as the original owner.
