She would definitely have realized that Ragna was a noble from her outfit and the air she gave off. Hyeonbyeol must’ve intentionally approached Ragna to get close to her.
Having pieced together what was going on, one thing still worried me.
“Recently, I’ve made a connection with a powerful person. I can use that to support you.”
This “powerful person” that Hyeonbyeol mentioned the other day...
Tap, tap.
Was she really referring to Ragna, or...?
...No. I don’t think she was lying when I asked who she was working under.
I shook my head. I was confident that I knew Hyeonbyeol well. Instead of assuming she was trying to deceive me, the more reasonable assumption to make was this:
Ragna Litaniel Peprok has a secret.
A massive secret that I didn’t know yet.

chapters.title: Chapter 449: Expanding (2)
paragraphs: When I returned home after my meeting with Ragna, I had an unexpected visitor. In fact, I had two of them.
“Oh, Mister! Welcome back! Your friends are waiting for you.”
“My friends?”
I tilted my head and entered the living room. On the sofa were two men enjoying a few light refreshments. The moment they saw me, they leapt to their feet with open arms.
“It’s—! It’s—! Bjorn Yandel, it’s really you! You’re really here!” sputtered the dwarf, Hikurod Murad.
“It’s been a while. I heard that you were alive not too long ago, but to think it was really true...” Even Brown Rotmiller had come.
It was great to see them after so long. Though technically, I had already seen the dwarf back in his forge. The memory of that encounter still had me reeling a bit, to be honest.
“Ugh, tsk... how unlucky. And he seemed like he had a lot of money.”
I never expected to hear something like that from him when I went to check out his shop.
“It’s great to see you two again. I’m sorry, I was going to visit you guys soon.”
“Haha! What’s there to be sorry about? We all know just how busy you’ve been lately.”
“How do you know that?”
“That’s because wherever we go, your name keeps coming up like you’re a celebrity or something! Even when I’m working at the forge, I still hear your name.”
“...I-Is that so?”

I couldn’t help but feel a bit embarrassed by that news. It turned out that they knew I had been going around and meeting with the bereaved families in person. They also knew about the recent banquet to celebrate my change in status and even my meeting with the other squad members in Kommelby. Was there an article in the newspaper that the heroes got together to celebrate with a welcome-home party?

“That’s why we took the initiative to come here. I wanted to do it a while back, but Rotmiller stopped me. He kept saying that we needed to give you some time so you could take care of some of your business first.”
“I see...”
I nodded my head at Rotmiller in thanks before settling down on the sofa. Erwen, who had been watching from the sidelines, came over to us. “Is there something I can get you?”
“Water, please. Oh, make it cold.”
“All right!”

As Erwen headed to the kitchen, the dwarf slowly scooted toward me to whisper in my ear. “Ah, that’s right! Do you have any idea how shocked I was? That girl, look at her welcoming you home with that big smile. And even going out of her way to get you water!”
“Oh, is this your first time meeting Erwen?”
Rotmiller nodded his head, but the dwarf shook his. “I’ve actually met her once before. When the party disbanded, she came to me all anxious, asking what happened to you.”
Ah, come to think of it, I could remember hearing something like that before.
“Hah, back then I had no idea that little elf would become such a famous adventurer... You never can guess what the future holds.”

“True...” I’d always thought that Erwen had incredible potential and talent, but even I couldn’t have predicted her meteoric rise. I especially didn’t expect her to end up with a nickname like Blood Spirit.
“By the way, Yandel,” Rotmiller interjected. “Have you... seen Miss Karlstein yet?”
Yeah, I was wondering why no one had mentioned her yet. “I haven’t yet.”
“I see...”
“Have you?”
“Only once, after you were presumed dead. I was worried, so I went to check on her, but I never got the chance to meet up with her after that. It was like she vanished into thin air.”
“What about you, Hikurod?”
“That goes for me too. Damn. With the news of your return spreading around the city, I was sure she’d come to see you... Surely nothing bad happened to her?”

The dwarf may have been a rambler, but I could understand why he was concerned. Fortunately, Missha was safe. Well, I couldn’t speak to how she was doing emotionally, but I at least knew she was alive. “I’m also looking into what Missha is up to. I’ll make sure to find her and bring her back safely, so don’t worry.”
“Well, if you’re on the case, I’m sure things will work out, but I wonder... Is Missha perhaps acting like this because of Blood Spirit?”
“...Why are you suddenly bringing up Erwen?”
“Well, there’s a rumor you two are in a relationship... Is that true?”
I sighed. He always was a gossip fiend. “No, it’s not.”
The dwarf immediately exhaled in relief. “Oh, well, that’s good...”
It was only a passing comment, but it made me hesitate. “That’s... good?”

“Ultimately, it’s up to you and your feelings. But you and Miss Karlstein have spent so much time together, haven’t you? And Dwalkie, it was his final wish before he passed... Honestly, I’d been watching you two for a while, and I secretly always thought you were a good match—”
Crash!
Just as the dwarf was ramping up to launch into one of his usual rants, the teacup sitting in front of him on the table shattered into pieces.
Step.
Erwen walked out of the kitchen.
“Oh my. The teacup broke,” she remarked with a smile, the cold water I’d requested in hand. “Mister, here’s your water.”
Fwooosh!

As Erwen set the cup down in front of me, the broken pieces of the other cup and the liquid that had spilled onto the carpet floated into the air. “There. Now everything’s clean.” She used the power of the spirits to clean everything in an instant, then quickly turned around and left after announcing she would be going back to her room.

The dwarf sat there as Erwen headed upstairs, and though he no longer had a teacup, he couldn’t seem to find the voice to request another one. He always did have a habit of talking too much, but it wasn’t like he was completely tactless.
“Why didn’t you watch your tongue? We’re guests here, after all.”

“...Hahaha, yeah. I made quite the m-mistake.” The dwarf let out a heavy exhale but plastered on an awkward smile, clearly wanting to move on and not dwell on what just happened. He really was quite the nosy blabbermouth.

Everything had gotten pretty awkward, so as the owner of the house, I took the liberty of changing the subject. “Well, how have the two of you been doing? Hikurod, I saw that you haven’t been doing much blacksmithing these days.”
“Huh? How did you know that?”
“I’ve actually visited your forge before. But you didn’t recognize me since I was much smaller back then.”
“Huh! Did that happen? Was I really not able to recognize you just because you were a little smaller?” the dwarf asked, sounding incredulous.
Well, it was the truth, so I filled him in on what happened that day. “I have to admit, I was surprised.”
“Oh, well, business has been good lately, so—”

“No, not about that. I was surprised because you told me that I was taking up so much space that other customers couldn’t come inside. And since I wasn’t planning on buying anything, you kicked me out. Anyway, I’m glad business is good these days.”
The dwarf flushed red like someone who’d been caught in the act, then laughed sheepishly. “Haha. I can’t believe you saw me like that. That’s rather embarrassing.”
“I didn’t say I blame you. There’s nothing wrong with trying to make some more money. I just realized you’d changed quite a bit.”
“True. You must find it pathetic that I left the party to chase after my dreams but ended up becoming a merchant.”
Huh, that wasn’t what I meant at all. Still, I was rather curious where he was going with this, so I let him continue.
“But you know what, Bjorn? I have another dream now. One that’s bigger than holding a hammer and pounding iron through the night.”
“Is your dream to make a lot of money?”
The dwarf smirked. “Something like that. After all, it takes a lot of money to sponsor an orphanage.”
“What?” Wait a second. “...Are you actually?”
“I still lack the funds, so I haven’t been able to do much. But just the other day, I was able to increase the number of orphanages I support to two.”
Damn, that made me feel like a scumbag. I sighed inwardly, momentarily lost in thought.

“Bjorn, I plan to make a lot of money. No matter how pathetic it makes me seem. At this point in my life, I don’t have much left to offer, but those kids are different. I’m doing this so those children can achieve their dreams in a way I never could. That’s my new dream.”
The dwarf seemed to stand a little taller today. Still, he looked quite embarrassed about having spilled his dream so openly. At a loss for words, I awkwardly sipped at my water.
Then, Rotmiller opened his mouth to tell us his story. “I’m not working right now.”

In a way, that update was more shocking than the dwarf’s. I couldn’t believe that such a hardworking man like him was unemployed. “What about the teaching center? Weren’t you using your scouting skills to teach other adventurers?”
“Unfortunately, I don’t have what it takes to run a business.”
So, in the end, the venture had failed. I wanted to offer him some words of consolation, but the dwarf abruptly jumped to his feet. “Hey, Rotmiller! The school failing wasn’t your fault—”
“Stop. Just stop it, Murad. We’re not here to talk about that.”
“B-But still! Bjorn is Baron Yandel now! With one word, he can—!”

“Didn’t I tell you to stop it?” Rotmiller’s harsh tone reverberated through the house. His voice was so cold and resolute that the dwarf immediately swallowed whatever he was going to say next. I wasn’t much better myself.
For him to speak like that...

I’d only seen Rotmiller angry once before. During Team Half-Wit’s final quest, he’d been furious with himself when confronted with his limits as an adventurer. He was a good person who didn’t direct his anger at others, only himself. Looking at him now, I couldn’t help but think that this was why people said it was the nice ones who were the scariest when they got angry.
Considering the dwarf was trying to console him, something must have happened.
I’d have to ask him later when the dwarf wasn’t around.
Anyway, the awkwardness quickly returned. I didn’t want to waste any more time sitting here broodingly, so I got straight to the point. “Hikurod.”
“Huh? Oh, uh, what is it?”
“I have a business proposal for you.”
“A... business proposal?”
“Yeah.” If he hadn’t come to see me today, I’d been planning to see him soon anyway as I had an important matter to discuss with him.
“It’s just you, yet for some reason, I feel kind of nervous... All right, lay it on me.”
“I plan to increase the size of my clan going forward.”
“What do you need me for, then?”
“I want your forge to be our clan’s personal forge.”
“Oh! That’s something that only the big forges get offered!” The dwarf was extremely happy about the offer, just as I’d expected.
All right, now onto the next steps. “Okay, then let’s draw up a contract.”
“Hm? Contract? We don’t need something like that between the two of us, though.”
“When it comes to work, things like this need to be ironed out and set in stone.”
“Hmm... That makes sense. But aren’t you rushing things? Even after we draft a contract, it’s still going to take some time for me to go over it.”
“What’s there to go over between friends? Let’s just finalize things here and now. All you have to do is stamp the palm of your hand here. Just for formality’s sake.”
“Hmm... Okay, then.”
After getting his approval, I quickly jotted down a contract. I then concentrated some of my Soul Power in the palm of my hand to stamp the paper alongside the dwarf.
“Done.”
In short, I’d procured myself a partner in crime going forward. I wondered what kind of look he’d shoot me when I gave him the equipment from the Order of the Rose.
The day after the dwarf and Rotmiller’s visit, I received my keepsakes back from Mr. Bear and Ainar.
It’s kind of strange to call them keepsakes, though...
Whatever the case, I put on the equipment I hadn’t worn in years.
[You have equipped a Large Adamantium Battle Shield. Your total Item Level has increased by +1750.]
[You have equipped a Lithinum Breastplate. Your total Item Level has increased by +270.]

First came a shield made of grade-five metal alongside my signature piece of armor. Whenever the latter broke, I made sure to get it repaired, and whenever it couldn’t be repaired, I always went to purchase one of equal size and value.
[You have equipped Idium Gaiters. Your total Item Level has increased by +400.]
[You have equipped No. 8667: Outlaw of the Wilderness. Your total Item Level has increased by +315.]
[You have equipped No. 8820: Iron Wall. Your total Item Level has increased by +310.]
Next were the gaiters that had been useful in escaping Doppelganger Forest, a belt, boots that doubled your Physical and Mana Resistance for three seconds when used, and...
Why did Mr. Bear take these? I feel kind of weird about it.

Lastly came some special magic underpants that were imbued with Automatic Repair, Shape Change, Acid Immunity, and Cleaning Maintenance. The slang term for it here in Rafdonia was an egg guard—aka a jockstrap.
Actually, now that I have Union, I don’t really need them, but...
They were relatively expensive, so even though I no longer had a need for them, I kept them anyway.
Raven also gave me back the Soul of the Dead I purchased and the Orb of Fire, so all that’s left is the necklace from Missha...
That was a funny way of thinking about it. It wasn’t like I was going around collecting wish-granting balls to summon a dragon or anything.

When I equipped my gear and looked in the mirror, I was glad I’d refused to take back the money they received from my will. The equipment they’d held onto was all in great condition. I would have been grateful purely for the fact that they didn’t sell it, but they’d even repaired and cleaned the parts that had been damaged during my fight with the Storm Gush. Considering the base quality of the equipment, I was sure the repair costs were quite steep.
Missha only took the necklace...
I sighed. That was the most precious thing I owned.
All right. Let’s see if there’s anything else that needs fixing...

After checking over the condition of my equipment, I left the house. I’d taken off my helmet, but still, it had been a while since I’d walked through the city streets in full, battle-ready armor. Since there was no reason to fight in the city, I usually only wore the breastplate. Which meant that today, I was planning on fighting.
Stomp, stomp.

I finally reached the outskirts of District Seven hours after beginning my early-morning walk. The gate that connected to the other districts was sealed shut. The guard on the wall looked down at me like he was waiting for some sort of signal.
Hmph, can’t he tell at first glance?
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
Thankfully, the doors that led to the holy land opened up without any need for identification.
Stomp, stomp.
I walked along the same forest path that I once trod with my fellow barbarians after the coming-of-age ceremony.
“Bjorn, son of Yandel! It’s really Bjorn, son of Yandel!”
“The strongest warrior, the one they call the Giant!”
The barbarians I encountered along the way all dropped what they were doing and began to follow me. I could feel it in my bones like a true barbarian—something fun was about to happen.
“Waaaaaah!”
“Bjorn, son of Yandel, has returned!”
Eventually, the forest path opened up to the barbarian’s village. By the time I arrived, without even lifting a finger, there were already hundreds of warriors following behind me.
“...So the rumors were true.”
All the barbarians staying in the residential area had heard I was coming, and they ran over barefoot to get a look at me.
Stomp, stomp.
Step by step, I walked forward without stopping or saying a single word while the other barbarians made way for me, pounding on their chests.
Whoo! Whoo! Whoo! Whoo!
If a human were watching right now, they would assume this was some sort of festival.
Whoo! Whoo!

As I followed the path they’d made for me, I eventually arrived at the hut of the chieftain. In front of the hut was Ainar, who was standing there waiting. I had heard she was training under him. So she really was spending all her time here.
We made eye contact, and I asked, “Is the chieftain inside?” She stepped aside, clearing the way into the hut. Was she telling me to head on in? Well, that was what I was planning on doing anyway.
Stomp, stomp.

When I entered, a massive barbarian was waiting for me. It was the chieftain. On the day I first woke up in this world, he was the one who brutally cut off the neck of Oreum, son of Kadua, after declaring him an evil spirit.

“You are late, Bjorn, son of Yandel.” The chieftain stood before me, looking down at me with a large axe slung over his shoulder. “I thought you had forgotten your tribe while you were busy messing around with the palace.”
He was extremely tall. Even though my body was back to normal, I still had to look up slightly to meet his gaze. “As if I would ever forget.”

At my answer, a bright smile appeared on his face, like that single statement had erased any feelings of frustration he may have been carrying. “Then welcome home, young warrior!” he said, welcoming me with open arms. “Bjorn, son of Yandel!”

The moment he finished greeting me, he asked me a question. The question, however, was distinctly different from what everyone else in my life had asked upon reuniting with me. Where had I been the past two years and six months? Was the royal family’s announcement about me being an evil spirit true? Was I caught up in some sort of political power struggle? He didn’t bother asking such human questions.
Instead, he got straight to the point. “So, what brings you here today?”
“I came here to tell you something,” I replied. This wasn’t a normal thing to say after being gone for such a long time, but I, too, was a barbarian.
“What is it?” The chieftain didn’t hesitate as he responded to me in the straightforward manner typical of our people.
“Let’s unwind with a fight. With the position of tribal chieftain on the line.”
His reply was swift and short. “Good.”
The second he accepted my request, all the barbarians began to cry out.
“B-Behel—aaah!”
“Behel—aaaaah!”
“Behel—aaaaah—ghk!”

chapters.title: Chapter 450: Expanding (3)
paragraphs: All nobles were first and foremost servants of the king. Given that, was it possible for a noble to also serve as the head of their race?
No matter from where or by whom that question was asked, the answer would always be simple: Nobody knew.
Because there’s no precedent.

Of course, if it were to actually happen, it would cause an uproar among the court. As nobles were meant to be mere servants of the king, every action they took should be for the sake of the king and kingdom rather than just one particular race. Even if there were no laws against it, the lack of precedent made it an unspoken rule.
“Let’s head outside.”

The chieftain, however, made no mention of such politics. I couldn’t tell if it was because he was unaware of the unspoken rule or simply didn’t care. However, now wasn’t the time to worry about such things. Why would it even matter if the chieftain knew? At the end of the day, the chieftain was a barbarian in his own right, just like the thousands of warriors around us shouting their hearts out. And that was good enough for me.
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
“Behel—aaaaaah!”

It’d be no exaggeration to say that all of the warriors in the holy land had gathered at the Grounds of Testament. It was the place where warriors went to settle their small quarrels or train or duel each other, rolling around in the dirt and trading blows.
Well, it’s more like a giant hole in the middle of the forest, though.

The Proving Grounds wasn’t a well-kept arena. The land was uneven and even covered in gravel, and when it rained, it often flooded, making it impossible to hold any duels until the water levels went down.
Thump-thump!

Yet as soon as we arrived, my warrior’s heart began to race. So what if there was no fancy marble flooring or tall statues? All that mattered was that the chieftain had brought me here himself. And unlike when I fought him in the past, I could tell he wasn’t going to just half-heartedly swing his ax at me this time.
It feels... like he’s acknowledged me.
How strange. I wasn’t even a real barbarian.
Thump-thump!
So why was I so excited?
Thud!

The chieftain stood opposite me and then jumped into the pit more than seven yards deep. He landed with a loud thump, sending a cloud of dust into the air. Before I could jump down to join him, my eyes met Ainar’s.
What’s wrong?
She nodded at me in support when our eyes locked, yet her smile didn’t contain its usual enthusiasm. A sudden thought struck me.
...Maybe she feels like I’ve taken something from her?

It would make sense for her to feel that way. After all, while I was missing, Ainar had been reading books in the library and making a real effort to become the next chieftain. So maybe my challenge to the chieftain today wasn’t welcome—
“Bjorn...” Ainar walked over to me, her tone and expression both quite serious. “Hey, make sure you win! You got it?! I’m putting my trust in you!”
Man, I felt shallow. What was wrong with me? Why was I getting all worried and stuck in my own head for no reason?
Thanks to you, I’m no longer nervous.
I smirked as I brought my fist up to hers. “I got it. Trust me.”
With that, I jumped down into the pit... or rather, into the Proving Grounds.
Thud!
A jolt rattled through my feet up to my legs as a thick cloud of dust flew up into the air. From up above, I could hear Ainar’s voice rising above the roar of the crowd.
“The great warrior has promised us victory!”
“Behel—aaah!”
I was so embarrassed at this point, there was no way I could lose.
Not that I ever planned on losing in the first place.
I stared straight ahead. Through the settling dust, I could see the chieftain slowly approaching.
Step, step.
For some reason, his footsteps rang loud and clear in my ears, slicing right through the thunderous shouts outside the pit.
Step.
The chieftain stopped a short distance away and drew the large ax he had strapped on his back. I tightened my grip on my hammer and shield as I quickly got into position.
Fwooosh.

Unlike a duel amongst nobles, we didn’t state our names or houses. No announcer was there to give us an introduction, nor was there any priest around to say a prayer before the duel began. There also wasn’t any of the banter that was typical of a fight between adventurers, who often sparred with empty words in an attempt to deceive or intimidate each other.
The moment we looked into each other’s eyes, we simply yelled out, both ready.
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
And with that, we ran toward each other without another word.
His ax and my shield collided.
Claaaaaang!
The chieftain, who was only an inch or so taller than me, struck me with his massive axe. I pushed back against him, and our contest of strength began.
Back then, I had to use Giantization just to hold off his ax.

Memories of our past fight flashed through my mind, but this battle was clearly building toward a different outcome. Our previous fight had taken place before I’d received the Earth Dragon’s Blessing from the dragon kid, and before I got the essence of the Bayon, the essence of the Storm Gush, the essence of the Vol-Herchan, and the essence of the Deep Sea Giant. Now, there was no way I would be pushed back in a battle of brute strength.
[You have cast Giantization.]
First, I’d grow in size and knock the chieftain’s ax back. I didn’t want to stay in this position any longer, honestly.
Screech.
It felt like he was still looking down on me.
[You have cast Wild Outburst. Your Threat Level has temporarily increased by 3x, and your Physique stats increase in proportion to that value.]
As I forcefully shoved the chieftain back, I wielded my hammer and smashed it down.
[You have cast Swing. The damage you deal with blunt weapons has increased significantly in proportion to your Muscle Strength.]
Instead of evading, the chieftain managed to block it with his axe.
Boom!
There was a roar as our weapons clashed.
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Frictional Heat.]
There was a sudden burst of heat like a bomb had gone off right in my face. However, a mere burst was all it was.
[The target weapon’s impact has been partially absorbed. Heat has been generated.]

It was a stacking skill, meaning its effects strengthened as more heat built up. At the end of the day, however, it was a skill that couldn’t do more than reduce the impact of an attack by a set amount, so the chieftain’s large body gradually bent back under the weight of my hammer.
Okay, I can work with this angle.
I slammed my massive foot against his stomach. He curled inward as he was sent flying like a soccer ball, now fully airborne.
Whooosh!
I couldn’t pass up on the opportunity to attack my opponent while he was stuck in midair. I grabbed my hammer and went to swing it like a baseball bat.
Fwooosh!
However, as I readied my swing, the chieftain stomped down on empty air and managed to jump even higher, out of my reach.
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Flame Leap.]

Flame Leap was one of the most effective high-rank movement skills there was. While a Manticore could travel farther with its regular Leap, a Flame Leap could be used in midair. More importantly, its additional effects were vastly different.
[The Fire damage dealt by the next skill used by Gudnulf Olga will be increased by 200%.]

This particular movement ability came with a rare-to-come-by double damage multiplier. Because of that, I always made sure to have the skill in my final build when I chose to go down a fire-type character route.
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Thunderspark.]
The chieftain landed behind me as he swung his axe.
Boooooom!
An explosion rocked my shield, sending a shock straight through me down to my bones. It’d been a while since I’d felt anything like this.
[Heat has been generated.]
It was like fighting a massive monster. But, like the warrior I was, I focused solely on the battle and swung my hammer to meet his attack head-on.
Thunk!
Yet somehow, when my hammer struck his chin, the chieftain was only sent stumbling a few steps back.
Ah... This old man is strong...

Was it because I’d only been fighting against weaklings recently? It was a strange feeling, landing a blow on the chieftain at full power and having it be nowhere near as effective as I’d expected. In the end, the strong truly were in a realm of their own, even when it came to tanking.
Clang!
I swung my hammer once more before he could recover, but the chieftain was faster as he quickly regrouped, raising his ax to block me.
[Heat has been generated.]
Was that three stacks now? It was somewhere around there, but there was no real need to keep a precise count. After all, it would be obvious when he reached ten.
[Heat has been generated.]
[Heat has been generated.]
[Heat has been generated.]
I continued to exchange blows with him as he continued to charge up.
[Gudnulf Olga’s next attack will be strengthened by the accumulated heat.]
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Flame Leap. The Fire damage dealt by the next skill used by Gudnulf Olga will be increased by 200%.]
The chieftain leaped high into the air and struck down at me with his axe. How was I supposed to deal with a combo like that?
Jump.
I could have blocked his attack, but given the condition of my shield, I decided to jump back and put more distance between us instead.
Boooooooooom!
His ax struck the ground, creating a massive crater large enough to bury three people inside.
He must be at ten stacks by now.
I had to be mindful of the sheer amount of strength and power at his disposal when he hit a multiple of ten stacks. Getting struck in the head by one of those blows would be pretty—
Huh?
While I was busy strategizing, the chieftain struck the ground once more. What followed was a skill from the rank-three monster Hellsmith.
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Pounding. The flames within the earth awaken.]
It was a fascinating spectacle. I didn’t expect him to whip out his finishing move already before he was even able to build up enough stacks.
Boooooom!
The ground cracked open as flames erupted from the earth, engulfing the chieftain’s body. Well, maybe the more appropriate term would be “cloaking.” Pounding was a buff skill.

[The damage dealt by all Fire-type skills has significantly increased. Gudnulf Olga’s Physique stats rise significantly in proportion to his Fire Sensitivity level. His surroundings will constantly catch fire.]
The chieftain, now covered in flames, immediately kicked off the ground and rushed straight at me.
Fwooosh!
I managed to block his ax with my shield, but a stinging wave of heat still burned my skin. Its effects were thankfully reduced because I had equipped the Orb of Fire.
[You have activated the Orb of Fire. All Fire-type damage within a radius of 15 yards will be reduced by 50%.]
I was glad that I brought it with me.
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
“Bjorn, son of Yandel, is pushing back the Flame Warrior!”
“Wooooooh!”
We exchanged several more blows. The barbarians watching shouted my name, sensing I had the upper hand in this fight. That was only because this matchup was a favorable one for me, however.
Clang!
I could easily block his ax with my hammer, and since my strength was on par with the chieftain’s, he couldn’t push me back or break my stance.
Fwooosh!
The continual fire damage I was being bombarded with was reduced, and my healing factor handled any damage that managed to get through.
[Gudnulf Olga’s next attack will be strengthened by the accumulated heat.]

Whenever the chieftain gathered enough stacks to land an even slightly dangerous blow, I made sure to step back and avoid it. From the chieftain’s point of view, this must have felt unfair and frustrating. This battle might have gone much differently had I been a pure tank and not part damage dealer.
Whack!
However, I was a warrior who wielded a shield for protection and a hammer to deal damage, a vexing foe to face. Of course, that wasn’t to say I had an overwhelming advantage over the chieftain.
Fwoooooosh!
Sure enough, he would not be an easy opponent.
[Gudnulf Olga’s next attack will be strengthened by the accumulated heat.]
The chieftain cast Flame Leap in a feint then smashed his ax against my adamantium shield.
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Resonance of Mother Nature.]
[Gudnulf Olga has cast Ignite.]
These were all fairly dangerous skills that suited a fire-type warrior.
[Gudnulf Olga’s stats have temporarily increased due to the accumulated heat.]
Now that he had built up fifty stacks, he was starting to get even faster.
[Gudnulf Olga acquires Natural Regeneration in proportion to the Fire damage inflicted by the innate ability, Ember.]
[All of Gudnulf Olga’s stats have increased in proportion to the resources consumed by the innate ability, Heat.]

The other effects he’d gained from going down the Golden Sun Imprint route were unexpectedly difficult to deal with. Since Heat was active, he must have gotten to the ninth stage of his imprint, at the very least.
Ha. He’s not even a tank, yet he’s this tough.

The chieftain was an ideal high-rank barbarian warrior. I could only imagine the number of times he’d been praised for his strength. Not only could he deal large amounts of damage, but he also had a sturdy body, an impressive healing factor, and a lack of fear.
However, one thing served him better than all of that.
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
The more cornered he was, the more violent and powerful he became.
That nickname... The Flame Warrior...

I was finally seeing with my own eyes the man from the story I’d heard so long ago. He’d been personally scouted by the largest clan in the city, and they came to see him as their leader after an attack on the Frostlord’s Palace in one of the eighth-floor Rifts. At the time, I thought I roughly understood how strong the chieftain was based on that tale.
It makes sense... With this much power, he could definitely pull that off.
Though he was considered to be one of the weakest chieftains in our clan’s history, he was still incredibly strong. Still, it wasn’t enough to overcome the difference between us.
I guess it’s about time.
It was finally time to end this duel.
Three, two, one...
As I counted down inside my head, the flames wrapped around the chieftain’s body slowly started to die down.
[Pounding has been deactivated.]
The buff, which served as his finisher, was finally deactivated. Now, it was my turn to go on the offensive and push him back.
Boooooom!
With every attack, I made sure to use Swing in combination with Transcendence and Eye of the Storm to not give him any time to breathe. Of course, that also meant I was quickly running out of MP...
I haven’t even used Soul Dive yet, though.
Sensing my intention to bring this duel to an end, the chieftain began to fight back even more fiercely.
Crack!

My shield, which had been struck by his ax several times already, completely shattered under his next blow. Even in the heat of the moment, I couldn’t help but feel depressed thinking about how much it would cost to fix. Still, the fact that I’d lost a shield and not my arm was worth the price.
Smash!
Using my now-empty hand, I drove a fist into the chieftain’s jaw. Even as his head snapped back, he glared right at me and swung his axe.
Clang!
I was barely able to block it with my hammer.
[The maximum amount of heat has been stored.]

The chieftain’s ax began to emit a reddish glow like it was fresh out of a blacksmith’s forge. I sighed inwardly. He’d now maxed out his stacks. I was hoping to finish this before it got to this point.
[All of Gudnulf Olga’s stats have significantly increased due to the accumulated heat.]

Of course, even with a full stack, the chieftain wasn’t in the best condition. Blood dripped down his forehead, and his entire body was badly bruised and swollen. His arms and legs, his stomach and head—every part of him was injured. To be honest, I wasn’t sure how he could possibly still be standing right now.
Oh.
Only then did it hit me—this must have been the same feeling others got when they looked at me.
“Bjorn, son of Yandel,” the chieftain called.

If he wanted to talk, he might as well go and put that red ax away already. Still, I decided to hear him out as this was the first time we were speaking mid-battle. I made sure to not take my eyes off of that axe, though.
“You’ve grown stronger.”
I’d been wondering what he was going to say, but was that really it?

“If it’s you, I think I can pass on the position of leader of this tribe.” Despite his words, his eyes looked nothing like those of a warrior who had accepted defeat. The declaration that followed only confirmed that. “But!” the chieftain bellowed. “I still hate losing! And that’s why I am going to win!”

With that, the chieftain let out a roar, ignoring the shouts of the other barbarians watching as he charged at me with determination. My response would be the same as always. Avoid what I could, block when I needed to, strike when I could, and wield my hammer until my enemy fell.
The time seemed to pass in a blink of an eye.

I couldn’t hear anything around me. It was like I was wearing earplugs. The other barbarian warriors watching from above must have been shouting something, but all I could hear was our battle. This sensation wasn’t new to me, though. Why hadn’t anyone made a saying for it yet? Something like, a barbarian only hears what they need to hear.
Right now, I could only hear the breaths of my opponent, the sound of his feet dragging across the ground...
Fwoooooosh!
And the sound of the wind rushing past me.
Step.

My eyes were glued to him. My body moved forward as I kicked off the ground. But in a flash, the moment I entered his range, that red ax brushed up against my upper body, slicing at me from the bottom up.

What was that just now? How did I dodge that? If I’d gotten hit by that, I wouldn’t have even had time to realize what had happened before it took me out of this fight. No, how did he even manage to swing his ax from that angle?
A chill shot down my spine as a flurry of questions whipped through my mind. Meanwhile, my body had already completely adapted and was taking action before I could think.
Slam!
My hammer swung down to strike the hand he had holding the axe. Even though his wrist was broken, the chieftain never let go of the handle. All I could do was strike it again.
Slam!
Only after his wrist was completely mangled did he release his grip on his axe. However, I was mistaken in hoping that that would be the end of our battle.
The chieftain stared at me with his one remaining hand clenched. It was an unspoken sign that this duel was not yet over.
Ha... So this is a real barbarian...

A wave of emotion rushed through me. Part of me was sick of his barbarian tenacity, but another part of me admired it. And yet another part felt a sense of disappointment. I wanted to deliver a clean KO to the chieftain with everyone watching.
Well, whatever...
I knew my fellow barbarians would enjoy watching this just as much.
Thud!
I threw my hammer aside as I deactivated Giantization—
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
—and decided to fistfight the chieftain until he was satisfied.
Punch! Punch! Punch!
I wasn’t meant to be the star of today’s show.
“Th-the winner has been decided!”
“Bjorn, son of Yandel! He will be our new chieftain!”
In the end, we didn’t finish our duel for the title of chieftain until long after lunchtime.

chapters.title: Chapter 451: Expanding (4)
paragraphs: Once my duel with the chieftain came to a close, I climbed out of the pit. Outside were countless warriors staring at me in excitement, mouths hanging wide open. They all looked at me like they were waiting for me to say something.
“Behel—aaaaaah!”
I bellowed, and the warriors let out answering shouts, satisfied with my speech. Hearing them up close hurt my ears.
Step.

I stepped to the side and glanced back down into the pit. The chieftain still lay at the bottom, forgotten as the warriors cheered my name and my name alone. It was a pitiful sight, but here, no warrior cared about the loser. Some may think it heartless, but it was a part of their culture. It was nothing more than the law of nature that winners were to be rewarded and losers were to be forgotten. That was all there was to it.
Woo! Woo! Woo! Woo!

Even though no preparations had been made in advance, a festival immediately began. Warriors who could play the drums pounded on their instruments as loud as they could while the warriors who couldn’t simply pounded on their chests. Everyone danced as they raised their cups high. They had cut down a few trees to make a large campfire and start grilling meat, though I wasn’t sure where they got all the meat from in the first place. The celebration continued even past sunset.
“Great Warrior! Where are you going?”
“To pee.”

I eventually managed to escape from my role as the center of attention in this rowdy celebration. As I headed over to the residential area, the warriors I passed on the way exchanged a few words with me. Regardless of whether they were simply having a good time or genuinely congratulating me, I didn’t pay them much attention.
Step, step.
The further away I got from the festival, the darker and quieter my surroundings became.
Woo! Woo!
The drums and cheering faded into the distance as I walked down the forest path. Without warning, Ainar, who I hadn’t seen at the festival, appeared down the road.
“Bjorn? What are you doing here?” Ainar seemed confused that I, the star of the party, was walking away from the festivities all alone.
“I thought I would go see the chieftain. Where is he?”
“He’s in the tent.”
“Is he awake?”
“I’m not sure. When I checked earlier, he was sleeping.”
“I guess you’re just coming back from over there.”
“It’s just... no matter how I look at it, it still bothers me a bit.”

“Hm?” I didn’t waste my breath asking what was bothering her. After all, Ainar had been training under the chieftain ever since she heard the news of my passing. Today must have been a strange day for her. I figured she must have a lot she’d like to say about it.
“Anyway, congratulations, Bjorn! I looked it up, and you are the first warrior to ever become the chieftain of our tribe at such a young age!”
“In other words, I’m the youngest there’s ever been?”
“Yeah! The youngest! Isn’t that incredible?”
Huh, I hadn’t known that, yet at the same time, it didn’t make much of a difference to me.
“Now then, if you’re going to see the chieftain, let’s head over together.”
“But didn’t you just come from over there?”
“Haha! What does that matter? I was on my way to see you anyway!”
“All right, then.”

Ainar and I settled into a brief conversation as we made our way to the chieftain’s tent. We mostly just talked about the duel and my new status as the chieftain. I wondered, were his injuries fully healed by now?

“The elders are spiteful bastards! They scolded me for giving him a potion, saying he would have healed ‘in due time’ even if I didn’t use one! How does that make sense?! It was the same with the coming-of-age ceremony! I told them they should at least send the warriors of our tribe off with shoes on their feet! But those elders are stubborn about sticking to tradition. Even though I was being so reasonable!”
“Ainar.”
“Huh?”
“When someone acts like that, you should call them unreasonable. Not spiteful bastards.”
“Oh... is that so?”
When I corrected Ainar’s language to keep her from getting in trouble in the future, she scratched the back of her head, looking embarrassed.
Step, step.
We walked down the quiet forest path for a bit longer. When the chieftain’s tent finally came into view, Ainair suddenly spoke up again.

“Bjorn.” She slowed down to stand behind me, placing her hands on my shoulders like she was about to push me forward. “Any way I look at it, you are much better than me. You’re smart. Strong. And the other warriors follow you without you even trying.”
Well, sure, but it’s not like you’re all too shabby yourself.
“Ainar—”
I tried to turn around and say something, but she cut me off. “So please take care of me. I know you’ll do a 150 percent better job than me! All the other warriors think the same!”
I didn’t know where she got 150 percent from, but I nodded my head. “All right.”
“Really? Good. Since we’re here, get going. I’m going to head back and celebrate with the rest of the warriors now.”
“Okay. See you later.”
Ainar turned back down the path while I entered the chieftain’s tent.
“You’re here.”
To my surprise, he was awake. Not only that, but he looked completely fine. Was it because Ainar used a potion? All he had were a few bruises and some minor swelling.
Screech.
I didn’t get permission from the owner of the tent, but I acted like the barbarian I was and dragged a chair over to sit down next to him.
“How are your injuries?”
“Nothing I can’t handle, don’t worry.”

“Really?” Well, I was only asking out of courtesy, so I didn’t bother arguing. Those were enough niceties, anyway—I got straight to the point. “When are you going to give me the position of chieftain?”
“Tomorrow, as soon as the sun rises.”
The answer surprised me. “I thought it would take longer since we’ll need to contact the warriors living on the outside.”
“By now, your story has spread across the city. Everyone will return to the holy land on their own.”
Well, he certainly wasn’t wrong. More and more warriors had joined the festivities as the news reached new ears.
“But... Hm. I noticed you look pretty relieved after fighting so hard?” The second question I asked was mostly one of personal curiosity.
“I always felt that this position wasn’t right for me. Ah, and I guess I was right since I lost.”
“I see.”
“So, why did you come to see me?” the chieftain asked, apparently confident I came to visit him for something else.
I smiled as I told him the real reason for my visit. “I want to hear about the king.”
“...The king?”
“Yeah. What kind of man is he?”
After all, I was going to be the chieftain tomorrow, right? It was about time I finally heard some of the dark secrets plaguing this kingdom.
“The king...” The chieftain smiled wryly as he leaned back against the wall. “Just once.”
“Huh?”
“Once. That’s how many times I’ve met him.”
I wasn’t expecting that at all. Given how terrified he’d sounded the time he spoke of the king in front of me, I’d been sure that the chieftain was well-acquainted with him.

“It happened when the War of Holy Relics was coming to an end... about thirteen years ago. Back then, I had just become the chieftain, and I went to a conference held between all the different races, intending to restore our declining tribe to its former glory. That’s when I first met him.” The chieftain’s breathing grew ragged as he stared out into space, lost in his memories of that day.
“That day... what happened?”

“At first, it was nothing unusual, just a regular meeting. The dwarves and the beastpeople were discussing something I didn’t understand. Meanwhile, I was busy arguing with the old man from the Magic Tower who was representing the humans.”
“The Magic Tower? Shouldn’t the king be the one representing the humans?”
“I thought the same. But for as long as I’ve been chieftain, it’s always been someone else representing the humans at these meetings, not the king.”
“I see...” That was news to me. Information about the discussions held between the representatives of each race was something regular warriors in the tribe weren’t privy to.
“Anyway, that day was special.”

Though he was supposedly near impossible to meet in person, the king abruptly showed up at their meeting for a once-in-a-lifetime visit. The chieftain himself was still unsure why he appeared that day.
“I was busy arguing with that old man from the Magic Tower when before I knew it, a man arrived. Nobody there knew who he was. One of us even tried to kick him out, but...”
“He said just one sentence.”
“Kneel, my servants.”

Apparently, the moment those words left his mouth, all the representatives had stood there blankly for a beat, then kneeled before him. They had forgotten every question and every thought they had in their heads.
“We didn’t even know who he was, but somehow, words forced themselves out of our mouths.”
“What words?”
“We greet His Majesty the King.”

The chieftain went on to emphasize how chilling and eerie of an experience it had been. The sense of absolute helplessness he felt. The complete loss of any will to resist orders. Of course, I was more interested in another part of his story.
If he has the ability to control others... does that mean he’s a wizard?

What could be the source of the king’s power? An essence with the power to manipulate beings without touch, or anything similar, didn’t exist in the labyrinth. That was why I thought it might be magic instead.

However, when I mentioned my speculations, the chieftain shook his head in swift rebuttal. “It was nothing like magic or an essence. It was like his voice itself held power. Like it had been written into my very blood and soul the moment I was born that he is the king, my master.”
The more he talked about his experience, the more confused I became. For now, I decided to hear the rest of his story. “So what happened next?”
“Nothing much. He simply glanced us over like he was looking for someone, then said, ‘They’re not here,’ and left. Only then were we able to breathe again.”
That was the entirety of the chieftain’s meeting with the king.
Before I racked my brain to come up with some sort of logical explanation for this, I first had to clarify a few things.
“You’re asking how strong the other representatives back then were? I’m not sure... probably about as strong as me.”

I didn’t want to assume that the king’s manipulation ability was unbeatable, but he did manage to control five high-ranking adventurers who explored the eighth floor or higher with just a few words. There also seemed to be no limits on his ability’s range either.
“Don’t you think I would’ve resisted if I could? Don’t make me laugh. I would rather die than kneel before someone I’ve never even seen before.”
The chieftain was convinced that if the king had ordered him to die at that moment, he would have ended his life right there on the spot.
If it’s not an essence or magic... what kind of trick did the king use?
I didn’t know. Fortunately, there was one thing I could still pin my hopes on.
“Ah, come to think of it, that old man from the Magic Tower only realized who he was and followed suit after the rest of us kneeled.”
Maybe his power didn’t work on humans? It was a possibility, but I couldn’t be certain.
...At any rate, I’ve at least confirmed that the king seems to have some sort of ability.
Though the chieftain didn’t know much, I still felt this wasn’t all that bad a haul. I then moved on to my final question. “How did the king look? Did he look sick?”
“...I can’t remember. I can’t even remember what age he was, whether he was a man or actually a woman, or even the voice that I heard.”

Hmm... Could the king also manipulate memories? No, maybe they used a spell or an item for that. Unlike the power to control others, there were definitely some skills and items that could mess with people’s memories.
“Do you have any more questions about the king?”
“No, that was all.”
“Well, that’s good. Then...”
The chieftain waved his hand in the air as if to dismiss me.
That’s a little weird.
His attitude was really confusing me. “Chieftain, can I ask you one last question?”
“Hurry up and do it.”

“Why are you acting so relaxed? It’s not like you know what kind of chieftain I’ll be, or what I’ll do once you hand over the position.” In fact, the last time we spoke, we had an argument during which the chieftain told me that there would be no place left for us to live if we antagonized the humans and that even if things seemed unfair, we had to suck it up and deal with it. I’d been a bit frustrated with his logic at the time, but in hindsight, it made sense when I looked at it from the chief’s perspective.

“Why would I care about all of that? It’s not like I’m the chieftain anymore.” But today, the chieftain merely laughed like I’d just told a funny joke. “Starting tomorrow, I’m just a regular barbarian.”
Right. He was no longer the chieftain, just a regular warrior.
“And...” that regular warrior now said, a fire in his eyes. “Since ancient times, we’ve always been a step behind the rest. Does that answer your question?”
“...It does.”
“Good, then get out. I’m hungry.”
I exited the chieftain’s tent and headed over to another to sleep.
Just like that, morning came.
“Woohoo!”
I stood before well over ten thousand warriors.
“Warriors, I, Bjorn, son of Yandel, swear this on a warrior’s honor!”
None of them would understand if I said anything too complicated, so I decided to keep this short.
“I will make sure we become stronger, regain everything that we have lost, and go even further beyond!” I declared as I looked out at the wall beyond the forest.
[Your position within your chosen race has changed from Regular Warrior to Chieftain. The special Approval Rating stat now applies to your character.]
That was how I ended up walking the path of a barbarian chieftain.

chapters.title: Chapter 452: Barbarian Revolution (1)
paragraphs: There were several special stats in Dungeon and Stone, some of which were hidden and didn’t affect your General Combat Power. A prime example was the Reputation stat.
Though calling it a stat is a bit of a stretch.

If your Reputation stat was high, people around you began to take notice, which in turn increased your probability of experiencing special events, such as unexpected quests. In other words, this stat raised your base likeability with NPCs you were talking to or meeting for the first time. However, it was more window dressing than anything else.
Honestly, it’s nothing more than a measure of your progress.

Essentially, you could say that cause and effect were reversed in this case. It wasn’t that the player benefitted from being given the stat, but rather that the player was given the stat because they were already well-known and influential. Celebrities didn’t get more famous and well-liked because their Fame stat went up. No, they were simply famous to begin with.

That was, in effect, how the Approval Rating stat worked as well. It raised your influence within your race while decreasing how often fellow members disagreed with you. Because of that, things like the success rate of your policies and the execution rate of your orders increased. The stat was generally useless when you were going down a regular adventurer route, but it became incredibly important if you were pursuing a leadership role.
Well, unless you were a barbarian.
[Your Approval Rating has increased by +1.]
[Your Approval Rating has increased by +1.]
[Your Approval Rating has increased by +1.]
[Your Approval Rating...]
[Your Approval Rating...]

As long as you followed the typical route to becoming the barbarian chieftain, your Approval Rating stat was extremely high from the jump. After all, you had to earn it the good old-fashioned way. Warriors held a great deal of respect for the chieftain’s authority and followed their instructions without question.
The problem is that unlike other races, where you can keep your position indefinitely by maintaining a high Approval Rating, no guarantee will last forever here.

Anyone could challenge me for the position of chieftain at any moment. Even so, that wouldn’t be a major issue for me. It actually worked to my advantage because it meant that no matter what mistakes I made, I’d never lose my position as chieftain so long as nobody could defeat me in combat.
...Still, I should work to keep my Approval Rating high. If it gets too low, these kids will all get depressed.
I sat there lost in thought while Ainar cleaned out the tent I’d be moving into as the new chieftain. After a while, she came over to me and said, “Bjorn! Why are you just standing there?!”
What an uncharacteristically foolish question coming from her. “Because I’m the chieftain.”
“B-But... it’s not fair to make me do it alone!”
“And Ainar, you are now an elder.”
“...Elder? Me?” The news of her promotion smacked Ainar upside the head, leaving her dazed. Hm, was it really that unexpected?
“Of course you are! Where else would I possibly find a more reliable warrior than you, Ainar?”
She choked on her own spittle.

“Aren’t you Ainar, second daughter of Fenelin?! One of the Seven Powerful, the Wild Sword?! I should instead be asking why the former elders and chieftain have been treating you like an ordinary warrior this whole time!”
“Well... I don’t know about that, but...”
What was with her sudden lack of confidence?
“I am Bjorn, son of Yandel! Chieftain of the Barbarians! A baron of the kingdom of Rafdonia! So heed my words!”
When you wanted someone to hear you out, the best thing to do was put your status front and center.
[Your Approval Rating has increased by +1.]
In the end, Ainar didn’t take much convincing. “I-Is that so?”
“Yes.”
“A-All right! Then I’m an elder now!”
“Then can I ask you to finish cleaning? As the chieftain, I have other work I need to take care of. It’s only natural that an elder would assist me.”
“Of course! I’m happy to help out too!”
Ainar went back to cleaning without another word of complaint. I sat in my chair and closed my eyes. Not because I was sleepy, but because I had something to think through.
It’s a lot worse than I thought...

The former chieftain had briefed me on the tribe’s current situation, and things were somehow even worse than I’d imagined. There were issues with its finances, population size, general welfare, infrastructure... Listing out what wasn’t a problem might be an easier task. It was a miracle that the tribe was functioning at all, and I wasn’t sure where to start.
I guess I should have known there were going to be some complications.
After classifying the problems in order of urgency and difficulty, it became clear to me what I needed to do before anything else.
First up: Cabinet Reorganization.
This was the first quest I’d have to tackle as the new chieftain, though I wouldn’t exactly call it anything as formal as a “reorganization.”
“Hey... Bjorn?” Shortly after I’d closed my eyes, Ainar came over and carefully shook me on the shoulder.
“When we’re in the holy land, call me Chieftain.”
“Oh, then... Chieftain...?”
“Good. What is it?”
“I’ve been thinking, and... don’t you think it’s a little unfair for me, an elder, to do all these chores?!”
Tsk. This is the problem with kids who study...
She’d gotten a bit sharper about things like these after reading all those books.
“If you don’t want to do it yourself, get another warrior to do it! Or go get another elder to do it! I... I hate cleaning!”
I laughed at her bold, self-interested declaration. “Fine, then stop cleaning.”
“...Are you going to make another elder do it?”
“No. There are no other elders anyway, just you.”
“...Huh? What do you mean?”
So she didn’t know. I launched into my intro into what typically happened when a new chieftain took power. “All the original elders retired with the former chieftain.”
“What?! Don’t tell me those old timers all left because they didn’t want to recognize you as our leader!”
“Calm down. That’s not what happened.”
At first, I’d also thought they were quitting because they were unhappy that a noble was becoming the chieftain, but it turned out something else was at play.
“You’re the chieftain, yet you’re going back into the labyrinth? Haha! Do your best, then! Don’t die like last time!”

The elders had been taken aback by my declaration that I wasn’t going to quit being an adventurer, but they didn’t seem to care that I was a noble at all. They were honestly just happy that they could finally retire.
“Kahaha, you’re in for a rough time. I guess young warriors enjoy taking the hard road these days.”
“Do your best! And if there’s something you don’t know, don’t bother coming to me! I’m not going to do math anymore!”

It turned out all the former elders were warriors who had fought alongside the former chieftain and reluctantly took up their positions after he begged them to. The miserable old warriors had been complaining every day for years that they wanted to quit, yet somehow, the chieftain had managed to convince them to take up the pen as their weapon of choice.
“So don’t hate them too much for trying to save a potion.”
“I checked, and we really don’t have any money left in this tribe.”

Ainar had complained about and bad-mouthed the elders for not wanting to use a potion on the former chieftain and refusing to give the young warriors better weapons or shoes at their coming-of-age ceremony, but...
“Th-that was...!” She now looked like a young girl who just found out her parents were secretly working part-time jobs through the night to put her through school.
“Anyway, if there are any other warriors who are worthy of the elder role, recommend them to me. You’ll probably know better than I do.”
“That’s... definitely true! After all, Bjorn, you are—”
“Chieftain.”
“...Chieftain, you are busy taking care of the clan.”
I sighed, grateful that she was at least willing to do that much for me. Ainar recommended a few warriors, but her voice trailed off as she scratched her head, deep in thought.
“Ainar, what’s that expression for?” I probed, noticing something was wrong. “You look unsure about something.”
Her shoulders sagged at my question. “I’ve only been listing my close friends that are good at fighting... but I’m not sure they will live up to your expectations...”
“What do you think I’m expecting?”
“Well... none of them can read.”
“Oh, don’t worry about that.”
“Huh? Really?”

“Of course.” I never expected to find anyone who could read to begin with. Apparently, the former elders only began to learn how to read and write after becoming elders. Plus... “I don’t plan to entrust administrative duties to the elders like before.”
How did they all think the barbarians ended up in this situation in the first place? We were never the type of people to read, count, or do admin work.
“I only need the elders to teach our young warriors how to fight and take care of each other.”
“Huh? Then who is going to do everything else? No matter how smart you are, that’ll be too much for you to do on your own.”
I chuckled. “The answer lies inside the castle’s walls. I plan to hire humans.”
I was going to hire others to do the work for me. In other words, the barbarians were outsourcing.

I needed an office worker who was skilled in administrative affairs, and there was one person who fit the bill perfectly: Shavin Emoor, a rank-seven administrative official who just so happened to be a friend of mine.
I heard from Ragna that she was promoted to rank six recently but was fired soon after for some reason.

Of course, my chances of recruiting her weren’t all that high. As far as I could tell, she’d refused Ragna’s offer of work for the sake of preserving their friendship, which meant that she might reject my offer for a similar reason.
At the very least, I’ll be able to get the names of a few good candidates from her.
That was all I needed right now, anyway. Finding talented individuals was great and all, but before that, I needed to pull together the funds to hire them.
What to do about the funds...

That was yet another problem without a solution. The tribe’s savings were nearly at rock bottom. We barely had enough to pay for the weapons at the various coming-of-age ceremonies and meals for the underage warriors.
...First, I need to find a new source of income.

Instead of giving fish to a hungry man, you should teach him how to fish. To change the barbarians, I needed to completely rethink how the tribe made money. It didn’t make sense to expect the warriors who were active in the labyrinth to make donations or leave their estates to the tribe if they died just because we were of the same race.
Money, huh?
No ideas stood out to me. For one, the barbarians had lived on their small plot of land for thousands of years, so there was surely no iron ore left to mine.
And I don’t like the idea of metalwork either.

We might be able to produce high-quality metal by using our muscles to pound the iron, but that was about it. The blacksmiths in the city made armor of a much higher quality than we ever could, so changing our ways to become blacksmiths wasn’t feasible in the first place. It would take time we didn’t have, and our efforts would never allow us to surpass the dwarves.
...Is there really nothing we can do aside from fighting in the labyrinth? Damn, what the hell are barbarians, anyway?

After cursing the situation, something suddenly occurred to me. Why were the barbarians lacking funds when we were all capable of becoming adventurers? Adventurers earned a decent living and then some. Not only that, our warriors were taught from a young age to pay their taxes on time to help the tribe.
“Ainar.”
Since I couldn’t figure it out, I decided to ask a real barbarian for advice, but her response was surprising. “That’s probably because... we are poor.”
“No, I’m saying I can’t understand the reason why you’re poor. Aren’t you all making decent money?”
“No way, that’s just you! After we buy our equipment, drinks, and food, we barely have anything left!”

It was a passable excuse at first glance, but as an expert in all things barbarian, I interpreted her claim in a different light. The problem wasn’t their income, but their spending. They spent overly large sums on themselves and invested mere leftover change into the tribe. That was why we were financially destitute.
“I, um... I promise you we’re not stealing anything.”
“I’m not saying you are. Just tell me where the money you spend goes.”
“...You can’t tell the other warriors I told you.”
“I got it. Hurry up and say it.”
“Well, the other warriors don’t like selling their old equipment even after buying new stuff.”
“...What?”
“It makes sense, right? After using a piece of equipment for so long, you become attached to it... and some warriors even like to hand them down to their children!”
I was rendered speechless.

That was the reason why the tribe had no money. It was completely ridiculous, but there was nothing I could do to fix the issue right away. Collecting equipment had become a barbarian habit, just like how crows collected shiny objects. Even the chieftain wouldn’t have enough sway to change something that was hardwired into their barbarian DNA.
But still.
“I-It’s not all bad, though! I-Isn’t collecting equipment kind of like saving?!”
Ainar’s excuse hit me like a lightning bolt. “...Saving?”
“Y-Yeah! If we become famous later, then we can sell it for more! It’s an investment, but just in a different way!”
“...Investment?”
“But o-of course, I’m not like that! I have a few pieces, but... I made sure that none were the same! They’re all different kinds of equipment, so I can use them whenever I need them and—”
“Ainar! Are you a genius?”
Her rambling had given me a great idea, though Ainar didn’t seem to realize what she had just done.
Yes, this will be revolutionary.
There was no better word for it.
Thanks to the festival, all the barbarians who lived outside the tribe had returned to the holy land. Under the bright sun, I launched right into my spiel, no introduction needed.

“Everyone, I have something to tell you!” As soon as everyone was assembled, I began my speech, or should I say the announcement of my very first policy. “Brave warriors! I am not like the previous chieftains! Instead, I have decided to give you all an opportunity!”
The warriors’ eyes lit up at the word “give.” They were all listening intently, curious as to what I was about to offer.
“An opportunity...?”
“I don’t know what it is, but it sounds like a good thing...?”

All right, I’d succeeded in piquing their curiosity. I had to move quickly before they got distracted, as was the barbarian way. Thanks to Ainar, I was able to come up with a plan that should educate the barbarians on economics while also restoring our funds.
“I am giving you the opportunity to buy land here in the holy land!”
“...Land?”
“He just said he was going to give us something, though? But now he wants us to buy something? With money?”
The barbarians seemed confused about what I was saying. Yeah, I figured they wouldn’t get it at first. I had to start from the beginning and keep things simple for their sake.

“Do you have a house in the city? Probably not, right? No, even if you do, it’s not really yours because the land isn’t yours. Because you are commoners, you can never really own land in the kingdom!” Only nobles had that privilege. “But here in the holy land, things are different. If you buy land here, I will make sure it remains yours, forever.”
With a small property tax, of course.
“Do whatever you want with the land. Write your name in the dirt, build a massive monument or statue—the choice is yours.”
“...Anything we want?”

“Yes! Complete freedom! Do you want to build a house? Go ahead! You no longer need to sleep in a flimsy tent that’ll collapse in the rain! You no longer need to buy a house in the city that will never be yours! Now, you can build your own, so that even your children’s children can live in it forever!”
I’ll let them build as much as they want. I won’t even bother implementing a window tax.
“Th-that sounds like a good thing?” The barbarians slowly started coming around to the idea after hearing that their descendants would be able to keep the land to live on.
However, some only tilted their heads in hesitation.
“But to buy land...”
“I don’t know how much it will be, but that must be expensive!”
“Is land all that valuable? I’d rather buy a weapon I can use...”

A few of the warriors instinctively sensed that something was off, so before the tides could turn, it was time for me to pull out my trump card. “Think about it, warriors! One day, those weapons you buy will rust. But the land you buy is different. It will last forever, and can one day be passed down to your children.”
Of course, that argument would not sway the hearts of the barbarians, whose motto was to live for today.
“Plus, if you buy land, you no longer have to pay to live in an inn or for any other accommodations! Not only you but your children as well! Forever!”
However, said barbarians were also forced to spend a decent amount of money on accommodations every month. Their eyes widened in realization.
“...I-I see!”
“It makes sense! If you have land, you can just sleep here in the holy land!”
They had finally realized the value of owning land.
“But it would be more convenient to live in the city near the labyrinth...”

A select few still expressed reasonable concerns, but they were only a small fraction of the population. I took a moment to memorize their faces. Alongside our tribe’s best fighters, these warriors might prove to be good elders in the future.
It was time to move on to the next phase.

“And more importantly...” I smiled big and wide as the barbarians all listened silently, waiting for the big reveal. Thanks to that, I didn’t have to shout to be heard. “Soon, the land here in the holy land will become expensive!”
Money was a universal motivator that traversed racial boundaries.

“It will become even more expensive as time passes. So even if you decide you want to buy the land later on, you will no longer be able to! Isn’t it obvious?! Once someone buys land, it will be theirs forever! And once all the land has been sold, there will be nothing left for others to live on! So, if you want land, you are going to have to beg others to sell theirs! You will have to pay a hefty price and hope another warrior will sell to you!”
It was the very simple principle of supply and demand.

“Buying land will be difficult then. Who would ever want to sell a valuable piece of land where even their children’s children can continue to live? They will no longer have to spend money on living in the city ever again. Oh, and if you don’t buy land, your children’s children will be angry with you about being forced to sleep in a tent. They’ll say, ‘Why didn’t my ancestors buy land back then?’”
I could see the panic in the warriors’ eyes as they pictured their future grandchildren scolding them. Now that I had taken their offspring hostage, there was no need for further explanation.
“Warriors! I will say this one last time!”
I decided to conclude things like a modern politician: as loudly as I could.
“A warrior never passes up an opportunity that’s right in front of them!”
The answer to our problems was real estate.

chapters.title: Chapter 453: Barbarian Revolution (2)
paragraphs: The name of this project would henceforth be the Holy Land Redevelopment Plan. Even though we had yet to sell a single piece of land, I knew the plan would succeed. Inquiries from the other barbarians were already rolling in.
There’s no need to do any more promotions. Soon enough, all the barbarians who weren’t present will hear about it through word of mouth.
Then all that was left would be to sell.
“Uhm... Bjorn?”
“Chieftain.”
“That’s what I meant to say! Chieftain, why aren’t we selling the land right away? There are already so many warriors who want to buy it?”

The reason for that was simple. “Like you said, there are plenty of warriors who are looking to buy some. The issue is that we don’t have that much land to sell. We won’t be able to sell it to everyone.”
“Then shouldn’t we be selling it now to the first barbarians who want to buy it?!”

I was glad to see that Ainar had accepted her new calling as a merchant, but unfortunately, she still had a lot left to learn. If we sold the land to the very first bidder, then what would we even get for it? None of the barbarians had savings, so we would have to sell the land for an unnecessarily cheap price.
“If there are warriors who want to buy land, tell them to come back on the fifth of next month. I won’t be selling anything until then.”

The fifth of next month was the perfect time to open the market. The barbarians would have just returned from the labyrinth, meaning that would be the time of month they’d have the maximum amount of money on them. I’d decide how much land to sell based on the number of interested barbarians. If one hundred of them made an offer, I could sell it to thirty, give or take a few.
Ainar tilted her head in confusion after hearing my plan. “Huh? Why wouldn’t you just sell it to all of them?”
I kindly began to teach her the ropes. “First off, we can’t sell too much land right away. We still don’t have enough people to take care of the administrative side of things.”
“Secondly, if we sell it all at once, we won’t make that much money.” The concept of real estate hadn’t been properly established in the minds of these barbarian warriors quite yet.
“...Won’t make much money? What do you mean?”
“Think about it. Only thirty of the one hundred were able to buy land. What do you think the rest would do?”
“...They’ll wait for next time?”
“A few of them might, sure. But others will try to buy the land from the owners for a higher price.”
“Oh! That’s definitely true! Right now, those warriors don’t have the money to do that, but later on, they definitely will...”

Man, she really had gotten pretty smart. I took a moment to inwardly admire her growth, then went on to explain the heart of this redevelopment plan. “In the end, the land will eventually become even more valuable than the original selling price. Aren’t weapons the same? The popular items aren’t sold in bulk but instead little by little over time.”
“Oh! Then the first warrior who resells their land will make money for free?”
Finally, Ainar had arrived at what I was trying to say.
“That’s right. And the most important part is they’ll go tell the other warriors how they made money quickly without lifting a single finger.”

Your descendants could inherit the land? The inherent value of having it under your name? Being able to save on rent? All of that was just an excuse to reel them in. The only thing that mattered was convincing them that buying a piece of land was the best move.
“The warriors...” Ainar marveled in a trembling voice. “They’ll go nuts for it, even the ones who said they didn’t see a reason to buy land...”
“Yeah. It’s a quick and easy way for them to make money. All they have to do is buy the land and resell it.”

It was like a money-copying bug. In a way, it was similar to Kharon’s backpack revolution. He may have started it for the sake of protecting a warrior’s honor, but in the end, it always came back to money. Even barbarians loved money.
I should sell some of the land to a select few of them first rather than going through an auction process.

I had no intention of stopping this money-copying bug from being used. Even if the bubble burst later when people started to catch on, it would already be too late. This was still the most efficient way to build up the tribe’s funds in the shortest amount of time.
...Though I should probably avoid the introduction of mortgage loans. I’m sure we’ll have other sources of income to use before it comes time for that anyway.

I was more worried about the near future rather than the distant one. I knew barbarians being introduced to the concept of real estate would grab the attention of the other races. But still, I judged that this was the best option we had.
It doesn’t make a difference if we stand out even more than we do now, so there’s no point in worrying about it. And it’s only right that I put raising the tribe’s status before all else.

It wasn’t like we barbarians would be the first to enter the real estate market in this world either. The dwarves and beastpeople had already sold the majority of their respective holy lands to bolster their funds. Everyone would just think that I copied the other non-human races.
Phew... Now onto finding my administrative team.
There was a lot of work that still needed doing before I could put shoes on the feet of our young warriors.
The same day I spread the good word of real estate to the barbarians, I reentered the city around lunchtime. As soon as I arrived, I went straight to my first meeting.
“It’s been a while, Shavin Emoor.”
I correctly assumed she would be at her house since she was currently unemployed. “...Huh? B-Bjorn?” She was surprised to see me show up at her door unannounced but still welcomed me into her home.
“I’m sorry. I was going to come visit you earlier, but I was busy.”
“Not at all! I’m the one who should be sorry. I just... had no idea you would come here to see me.”
“Of course I would. We’re friends!”
“Besides, I have an offer for you. Well, more like a favor to ask.”
She looked moved when I called her a friend but then grew visibly tense. “A favor to ask...?”

“I heard you lost your job, so I was wondering if you could come and help me. Or maybe recommend some people you know? I need people who are capable of doing administrative work, and I need them to be as trustworthy and reliable as possible.”
“...You must really need some help if you came to me.”
“You were the first person I thought of, actually. I don’t know anyone else who does those sorts of things. It’s only right to ask a friend for help at times like these.”

After listening to my reasonable explanation, Shavin took a moment to think the offer over. But it didn’t take long before she readily agreed to help. “All right. If you are willing to pay me at my previous rate, I will gladly help you. I’ll bring some trustworthy people along too, naturally.”

“How much did you get for working in administration before?” Shavin cautiously revealed her salary, but the pay was much less than I expected, so I pushed to increase it just slightly. Our negotiations didn’t go on much longer than that. “But I’m surprised. I never expected you to agree to help me.”
“Well... I was actually looking for a job.”
“Really? I’m glad this worked out, then. I was worried because I heard you rejected Ragna when she offered you one.”
“Ragna just wanted to support me. This feels like you really need my help.”
“So you didn’t want to be indebted to her since it might strain your friendship.”
“...Haha, that’s one way to put it. From the sound of it, I’m guessing you already met up with her?”
“How do you think I found your house? Oh, and I should mention that it’s supposed to be a secret that Ragna and I met up.”
“A secret... You two sure do live in the world of nobles now.” Shavin looked fascinated by the lives Ragna and I were living. She brewed some tea for us to drink, and we chatted for over an hour.
“I should head back. I have a few things I need to get done before my next quest.”
“Sounds good! I’ll connect with my previous coworkers the day after tomorrow. But even if the rest of them go their own way, I’ll make sure to show up to work. Oh, but where should I go?”
“I’ll come by in the morning three days from now.”
“Huh? You’re going to pick me up? I appreciate the gesture, but you don’t have to...”

While it would’ve been nice if it was a matter of common courtesy, the truth was that humans weren’t allowed to enter our holy land without permission. I intended to escort them to work on their first day, make a pass for them, and more.
“Anyway, I’ll see you then.”
“All right, get home safely.”
