[Abman Urikfried has cast Super Strengthen. The effect of the next active skill used will be greatly amplified proportional to soul power.]
[Abman Urikfried has cast Pierce. The next attack’s piercing power is increased by 10 times.]
[Abman Urikfried has cast Giant Arrow. The size of the next ranged projectile will be greatly increased.]
[Iron Bear Iradun has cast Fire Bear Stance. All attacks will receive a shove (high rank) bonus.]
[Abman Urikfried has cast Master of the Jungle. Iron Bear Iradun’s stats are greatly increased and...]
He didn’t talk to himself. Most self-talk was depressing, and saying those things out loud wouldn’t change reality.
No, it would only make him a more depressed and gloomy person.
That was why he never talked to himself. At least, that was the case until now.
“I’m going nuts.”
For the first time in genuinely such a long while, he mumbled to himself. In front of him was a man who was holding onto his life even as he vomited up liters of blood.

“Please, I want you to get up now... But strictly speaking, the possibility of that will be low. Even while knowing that, I have these harsh thoughts. I... I thought I was allowed to have more stories... But it seems that isn’t the case anymore. What a fickle thing fate is, right? Hah... I don’t know why, but whenever I am with you, I feel like such a bad person.”
He apologized to the man on the ground.
“I’m sorry. I really am different from you. I know that you wouldn’t have even had thoughts like this, but I still can’t make up my mind. However...”
The man quietly closed his eyes before opening them again.
“It still needs to be done.”
Although he knew the man couldn’t hear him, he continued to talk.
“Now, go.”
It felt like if he didn’t, he would become weak again. He thought his determination wouldn’t falter until the final moments, and that needed to be true so that he could be sure of his convictions.
“It feels nostalgic to create another path for you again... But I guess that’s to be expected. I am your scout, after all”
Even while knowing what the right path was, he couldn’t take any other path.
“May the blessing of the twilight star be with us...”
With that, Rotmiller solidified his determination.

chapters.title: Chapter 751: First Point (1)
paragraphs: “They’ve lost track of Baron Yandel...”
The servant who had served him for decades lowered his head with shame and gave the report.
However, the marquess didn’t get angry. He just closed his eyes and let out a long sigh as if to suppress his emotions.
“I see...”
Although he wouldn’t say he wasn’t angry at the plan failing, he needed to be precise about who he targeted with his anger.
For the marquess, that target was himself—and also, the world itself. This world used invisible strings to puppet all events. As if it found enjoyment in those things more than any one person could.
The world doesn’t want him to die...
Thunder was fired. Although he didn’t know what Yandel did, that barbarian blocked the attack, protected everyone, and was consequently put out of commission.
From what he had been told in the reports, it seemed that Yandel was on the brink of death. That was why he thought one more shot of Thunder would do the trick.
“Tell me, what happened?” the marquess demanded.
An unknown magic circle had activated, and when the dust cleared, everyone had disappeared from view.
“We are gathering information on what magic was used as quickly as we can—”
“There is no need for that. I already know what it is.”
“Pardon?”
As the prime minister of Rafdonia, the marquess knew this city better than anyone else.

This city was a huge citadel. The greatest citadel in existence that could respond and react to any situation even while being invaded by outside forces. There were countless ancient magics installed all around the citadel, and a few of them could still be used even now.
“It should be a type of summoning magic circle. One that forcibly pulls anything in a set area to another place.”
Although the marquess was only hearing about the situation on the ground via second-hand reports, he could piece together the events better than anyone else.

“Which means that the culprit would be the Fifth Commander, Baron Wilkins. If it is him, he would’ve received the authority to use the ancient magics in District Seven as soon as wartime measures were put in place.”
The marquess organized the content as if speaking to himself.

“He wouldn’t have been able to prepare for the first impact of Thunder, but he would have been wary of it afterward. Because he would have realized we are aiming for Baron Yandel. He would have done everything he could to block the second attack. However, it should have required quite a long time to activate the magic circle...”
The marquess tapped the table with his finger.
“Did you say there were some who were left behind?”
“Yes. Around a dozen barbarians on the outer edge of the group didn’t disappear.”
“I see... So the magic circle was hurriedly activated after seeing our forces back away from them...” Fire returned to the marquess’s eyes. “Then it isn’t too late.”
“Pardon?”

“This magic circle was last used for rescue purposes during the Iron Wall Rebellion. However, the records also state it wasn’t able to be used properly as it had been activated in a hurry back then as well.”
There was no chance the record was false. While making this plan, he had gone through all the tricks up the palace’s sleeve hundreds, no, thousands of times. Again and again and again.
Knock, knock, knock!
Quick knocks were heard at the door. As the marquess permitted the person to enter, a man rushed inside and gave his greetings.
Eltora Tercerion. The previous third commander, and the son of the marquess.
However, even though this man was his direct blood, the marquess just asked him his business when he came in.
“What is it?”
His tone was even colder than when he treated his servant.
If one looked closely, one would be able to see he was frowning somewhat like someone who was displeased about something, but it didn’t take long for that frown to disappear.
“The Divine Spear, Ainar, has been located causing pandemonium in the District 4 Dimension Square!”
The marquess’s lips curled up at his son’s report.
If the summoning magic had worked perfectly, all the people within the designated area would’ve been moved to the imperial capital. However, this was confirmation that didn’t happen.
Even during the Iron Wall Rebellion, there was trouble because the people who were supposed to be rescued were thrown randomly into all the different districts.
Of course, even with this, if Bjorn Yandel was lucky enough to be transported into the territories of Rafdonian forces, then there was nothing he could do.
It’s too early to give up.
That barbarian was the same as him. If it wasn’t impossible, then that monster would hold onto that slim possibility to obtain victory in the end.
To catch such a monster, there was only one thing that could be done.
“Eltora, send this message to all forces. Tell them to search each and every wardrobe and crate in the districts that our forces currently have control over.”
He would become the very same monster.
“Have you ever felt like fate is messing with you?”
If someone asked him that question, Rotmiller could nod and explain many times when he felt like the premise applied.
When he lost his parents during his childhood.
When he met the benefactor who taught him the skills to survive.
When he learned that he constantly needed to meet different people in the labyrinth because he wasn’t skilled enough to stand on his own.
Even though that was who he was, he was able to join the first chapter of a man who would be remembered as a great hero.
Having grown up in the orphanage of the Reatlas Church, Rotmiller thought all of that was determined by fate.

Meeting people, learning new things, making allies, gaining things he deemed precious, realizing new truths, giving up some things to then obtain more important things, and learning new emotions he never felt before...
If chance continued was fate, then his entire life was just a continued repetition of chance encounters.
Perhaps even now.
“How annoying...”
Rotmiller felt fate’s annoying hand once more.

Could anyone truly blame him? An ancient magic weapon had fallen from the sky and the man who seemed impossible to topple protected everyone and collapsed. Even without having the time to regroup, enemies appeared from all directions, and he had to run away with everyone else.
“Behel—LAAAA!”

The barbarian holding the spear carried the dying hero, and the elf who had a contract with the Elemental Ruler opened the way. The dual-wielding beastwoman quickly leaped here and there to protect those in danger, and the wizard who became the de facto leader of the group quickly cast spells to find a way out of the place.
“Th-the enemies are moving back!”
The enemies who seemed to stick to them like tar quickly moved away like the receding tide.
“It’s Thunder!”
And as that attack appeared in the sky once more, geometric shapes suddenly appeared on the ground they were standing on before shining with bright light.
His memory after that was unclear.
When he regained consciousness, he was in front of a goddess statue.
“Teleportation...?”
When he took a look around, he noticed the temple had been reduced to rubble, and he could see Noarkan soldiers walking out in the streets outside the windows.
And Bjorn Yandel. The man called a hero by all was collapsed in front of him, unconscious.
Thanks to having poured countless highest-grade potions on him, he didn’t seem to have any exposed external injuries. He was just covered in blood. He would soon be able to wake up.
While holding onto that hope, Rotmiller quietly waited, but the situation suddenly turned for the worse.
It wasn’t that Yandel’s condition suddenly worsened.
“Search everywhere! The marquess has commanded us to check every inch of this place, even if we have to rip down the wallpapers!”
If the soldiers he could see sometimes through the windows had just been on patrol, at some point, they began to search the area with a clear motive. The two of them would be exposed soon enough.
“...del! Yandel! Can you hear me?”
Rotmiller hurriedly woke Yandel up, and thankfully, the barbarian woke up from his deep sleep.
“Don’t worry, I won’t have any problem moving—”
For some reason, he began to spout blood from all his pores and collapsed again.
Rotmiller’s mind went blank at the sight.
The enemy would soon find them. They needed to get out of here before that happened. But how...?
He didn’t know.
That was why Rotmiller looked through the interior of the ruined temple and gathered information.

Currently, they were in Reatlas Church’s District Four central branch. They could get to the imperial capital if they just followed the main road in front of the temple. And if they could just get there...
We’ll survive.
However, there was one big problem. How were they going to get there? How was he going to carry this gargantuan and immobile barbarian through the enemies and to their destination?
Thankfully, Rotmiller was used to fighting against reality. Rather than look for a perfect plan, he made the best possible choice he could make.
I need a horse and a cart.
Rotmiller headed to the stable attached to the temple. There was a cart that could be used to transport goods, but there were no horses. It seemed they had all been taken away already.
Neigh!
However, miraculously, his eyes made contact with a horse hanging out outside the fences.

It wasn’t important how the horse was still here. Well, it was probably something like the horse managed to get over the broken fences and was lucky enough to evade getting plundered with the rest of the horses. Anyway, the important part here was that a horse and cart were secured.
“Whoa, whoa. Easy there...”
Since Rotmiller had experience managing a horse in the orphanage when he was young, he grabbed the horse by the reins. He then attached it to the cart so that it could pull it.

He barely managed to move the colossally heavy barbarian onto the cart, bending his body so his feet didn’t poke out the end, and used piles of hay to fill in the missing space. Finally, he placed a huge piece of cloth over the whole thing to turn it into any other transport vehicle.

The problem here was he had no idea if it would work. Would he be able to get to his destination without issue? If he failed here, both of them would die. Maybe it was the right choice for him to do his best to survive by himself.
As those thoughts continued to haunt him, he began to feel frustrated.

Why did it have to be him? This man had countless allies who were more talented and excellent than he was. Even if this man never asked it of them, countless people in the city would go out of their way to help him. So why was it that when he needed help the most...
Why did it have to be me standing next to him?
“I’m going nuts.”
Words of frustration exited his mouth.
He shook Yandel’s body, hoping he would get up and just staring blankly when he didn’t, cursed fate for putting him in this predicament, then felt ashamed at his own powerlessness.
“However...”
Inside this ruined temple, after meeting eyes with the many broken goddess statues scattered around here, he made up his mind.
“It still needs to be done.”
There had always been moments like this in his life.
Even though he was afraid, this was a path he needed to walk down to get through all this.
“May the blessing of the twilight star be with us...”
He got on the horse and went out onto the street where the enemies were, and behind him was the cart connected to the horse.
Naturally, they moved very slowly. Rather than running as fast as it could, this was closer to a leisurely walk.
It wasn’t stealthy either. The wooden wheels creaked whenever they rolled, and every time those sounds echoed out, Rotmiller felt as if his heart was going to burst.
Ba-dump, ba-dump, ba-dump.
Blood rushed to his head as he got feelings of vertigo, but he tried to maintain as calm a mindset as he could.

He wasn’t as strong as those allies of Yandel who went on those grand adventures with him. He wasn’t powerful enough to wade through swathes of enemies with just his might, nor could he escape danger with wit and ingenuity like those talented wizards.
That was why...
Please...
He prayed and prayed some more that this little trick of his would work. That was all he could do.
However, it seemed his efforts paid off. The first Noarkan he met just looked at him for a moment. He didn’t seem to consider him suspicious or try to talk to him.
It seemed that the Noarkan didn’t see anything wrong with him confidently rolling a cart down the street.
He sighed. He’d thought the plan was feasible at best when he first began carrying it out, but when the plan actually worked, all the tension in his body left him.
However, that was just one person.
Rattle, rattle.
With how slow he was moving, there was still a long and painful journey left to go. However, this wasn’t anything new for Rotmiller.
His life was always like this.
Two people, three people...
Only after rolling around in the labyrinth for eight years did he become a rank seven adventurer.
Four people, five people, six people...
He also began much later than the rest as well.
Most entered the labyrinth the day they became an adult, but the first time he first stepped foot into the labyrinth was when he was twenty-six.
Ten people, twenty people, thirty people...

Because he was late, he ran with all his might. However, it still ended with him being left behind, and he needed to endure the pain of being left behind. That was why there was nothing new about this endeavor either.
Going slowly.
He was already used to it to the point of being sick of it. Maybe this was the one thing he was the best at in the world—
“Hey.”
At that moment, the seventy-first Noarkan he met suddenly stopped and approached him.
“Which squad are you from? I’ll need to check what’s in your cart.”

chapters.title: Chapter 752: First Point (2)
paragraphs: One Noarkan approached him to check on the cart. However, it didn’t seem like he was doing this out of a sense of duty or a sense of loyalty to his work. Regardless of the man’s tough-looking appearance, it was just in the way the man spoke.
“What? Why aren’t you saying anything? Do you have something valuable in there?”
Hearing those words, Rotmiller realized it. This man’s goal was to just sate his own greed.
“I only have food.”
He said that in the hopes the man would pull his attention away and go somewhere else, but the Noarkan only grinned at his excuse.
“Food? You should’ve given a more convincing lie. Hey, bro? Don’t be a stranger. Everyone just wants to live their life.”
“What do you want?”
“It’s nothing much. Just share some with me. We’re all suffering out here, hmm?”
Rotmiller let out a sigh in his heart.
How did he end up catching the attention of someone like him? No, maybe he should be glad it was someone like him who came up to talk to him?
Maybe I can end this with just a conversation.
After coming to that conclusion, Rotmiller pulled out a few items of decent value from his Treasure Vault.
“These are all I can give you. So be satisfied with that.”

The things he was handing over were his precious savings, but he didn’t find it a waste to lose them like this. If he could save Bjorn Yandel’s life with just this much, he was getting off pretty cheap.
“Oh, these precious things?”

There was one problem with the method Rotmiller chose as his solution. Having retired as an adventurer and living a pretty worry-free life just teaching people how to be scouts at the barbarian holy land, Rotmiller had forgotten.
The greed of beasts was unending, and there were beasts in this world who spoke the language of humans.
“But bro, I’ve been thinking pretty hard about this...”
If he looked weak, he would be ripped to shreds.
“I don’t think this will be enough.”
The Noarkan’s voice was filled with even more greed and confidence now.
It was very simple. Rotmiller looked like a very easy target, seeing he handed over money after being pushed so gently.
“What’s in there? Gotta be something if that’s what you’re giving me. Let me check for a moment.”
From the perspective of the Noarkan, he had only given up these precious things because there was something even more precious under that cloth.
“Didn’t you hear me? I said, let me check the cart.”

The man went from keeping his distance as he spoke to sizing up Rotmiller to now approaching him with dangerous intent. It seemed he would check the contents of the cart even if he needed to use force.
“Do you really need to check it...?”
“That’s what I said.”
At that, a confident smile spread over the Noarkan’s face, and Rotmiller felt his heart sink.
In the end, this was all he could do.
Rotmiller made his split-second decision and nodded. “Sure, you can look at it. But as I told you, there’s only food in there.”
“Shut up. Do you think I was born yesterday? Let’s see how well you’ve tried to hide it.”

The Noarkan sneered at Rotmiller and approached the cart. However, the moment he reached out with his hand of greed toward the cloth covering the cart, Rotmiller used the dagger he drew from the Treasure Vault and stabbed the man in the neck.
“Ah?” The man didn’t seem to even realize what had happened to him before collapsing to the ground.
Rotmiller slowly scanned the surroundings.
Ba-dump!
All the Noarkans nearby were looking at him. A commotion had been caused, and in the end, a person even died. It was only natural that it drew everyone’s attention.
However, Rotmiller finally realized it.
Although he never fully understood it when he just heard it described in words, he now understood what kind of place Noark was.

Even the Noarkans who had been searching the area around them didn’t hold any suspicion in their eyes as they looked at him. There wasn’t any surprise or fear that a person had died either. There was just a thick layer of greed.
That was why Rotmiller shouted back at them, “The fuck are you looking at? Just piss off and do your work if you don’t want to die as well.”
He shouted to not look weak. However, those slimy gazes didn’t move away.
Rotmiller took the dagger out of the man’s neck.
Damn it, damn it, damn it!

He repeatedly cursed in his heart before sawing at the dead man’s neck. He cut through the skin and separated the hard neck bone to fully decapitate the man’s head off of the body, then stabbed the head onto a spike on the left part of the cart.
“Why? Do you want to be put on the right one?” he said to the audience once again.
The Noarkans finally flung their attention away and went back to what they were doing before.
Rattle, rattle.
With that, the stopped cart began to move again—at a notably faster pace this time.
Rattle, rattle.
As he continued to move forward, he understood why Goblins and Orcs wore ornaments made of bones. They only looked uncomfortable in the eyes of humans. For savages, they were very convenient.
“Who’s that guy?”
“Where is he taking that cart? Should I ask?”
“Leave him be. He looks like he’s lost it.”

The ones who saw him pulled their attention away, not wanting to get caught up in something troublesome. They never even suspected that the Bjorn Yandel they were looking for was being carried away in the very cart of the man confidently rolling past with someone’s head stabbed into a stick.
Rattle, rattle.
And so, after continuing down the street at a faster pace, the cart stopped again when the city walls could be seen in the distance.
“Who are you? I think you have a similar hobby to me. How fun.”
A wizard with a staff stood in the way of the cart. The wizard didn’t seem to care about the head being displayed on the cart, and he really didn’t care either.
“But what are you trying to hide that you did such a cute thing...”
A strong gust of wind began to swirl in front of him. The cloth that was covering the cart couldn’t hold on and was flung into the air. Then, the thing hidden underneath it was exposed to the world.
It was very unfortunate.
“It’s Bjorn Yandel!”
“Bjorn Yandel!”
Everyone in this city knew who he was.
Thanks to the help of the bear that suddenly appeared, Parav was able to escape out to the street.
Boom!
With the destruction of the well connected to the secret tunnel, the threat of being chased was also dealt with. He also saw the faces of the people waiting for him in front of the well.
“Mr. Parav...!”
Starting with Lilith Marrone, who ran up to him with tears in her eyes, the evacuees, including the bear’s wife, came to thank him.
“Haha, hello. Is this our first time meeting? I am Hikurod Murad. I suppose I am higher in seniority than you.”
Even a dwarf shook his hand with a hearty laugh.
“Senior...?”
“Ah! Mr. Murad was an ally of Mr. Yandel in the past!”
Parav nodded at Marrone’s explanation. Now that he thought about it, he had heard something or another about someone that kind of sounded like him maybe?
“Oh!” he exclaimed as realization hit him. “I heard that you were working a forge after retiring...”
“That’s right!” the dwarf said cheerily. “Well, now, I’m in danger of losing my entire life savings! Hahaha!”
“It’s really amazing to be meeting you like this. But why are you here...?”

“It’s because of that friend over there. He said he’d go and try to find his wife on his own, but I couldn’t just send someone alone who’d get lost in his own backyard.” The dwarf gestured with his chin toward the bear husband and wife, and only then did Parav greet the man properly.
“I am Abman Urikfried.”
“Ah! I’ve heard of you! I am Sven Parav.”
“I’ll say this again, but truly, thank you. Call me whenever you are in trouble, whatever it is. I will drop everything to come help you.”
Parav felt a weird emotion at the genuine show of gratitude.

Fate truly was mysterious. It was surprising the woman he saved at that moment was the wife of a previous ally of Yandel, and when he thought about it then, it seemed saving the wife ended up saving his own life.
“But have you two worked together before? Mr. Urikfried, Mr. Murad?” Marrone asked the two of them.
The dwarf answered for both. “Ahaha, we have not. I am quite the senior to this friend here.”
“Is that so? It’s just that you two look really friendly...”
“We became friends through fate. The fact that we both run a store, the fact that we both can hold our drinks...and the commonality in Yandel as well.”
“Ah, I see. I wondered if maybe you two were on the same team before, but it looks like I was mistaken.”
So that was what happened. It made sense.
This very day was also only happening thanks to the relationship of everyone having been allies of Yandel.
“Then who was on the same team as you, Mr. Murad? I know you were with Mr. Yandel, Ms. Karlstein, and that wizard...but I don’t think I’ve heard the last one.”
“Ah, Brown Rotmiller. He was the team’s scout. In a sense, he’s this guy’s direct senior? I heard that he was teaching the young warriors how to be scouts in the holy land...”
“Ah, is that so?”
“Now that I think about it, it’s been quite a while since we’ve seen each other since we’ve both been so busy. After this is over, I’ll need to go over to him and share a drink or two.”
The dwarf smiled with nostalgia in his eyes.
Whoosh!
The whirlwind that blew through the cart lifted the cloth off of it and turned the situation upside down in one fell swoop.
Everyone went silent, including the wizard, who had turned over the cloth with a joking tone before.
“Bjorn Yandel!”
“It’s Bjorn Yandel!”
Then, they began shouting as time started to flow again.
However, Rotmiller was not afraid. Although panic clouded his mind for a moment, he quickly regained his wits and began to think.

District Four was under Noarkan control. However, that didn’t mean the Noarkans had taken control of the city wall between District Four and the imperial capital. The palace still held dominion over the walls, and the Noarkans had set up a battle-line a decent distance from the wall. Also, excluding the area near the gate, the battle-line wasn’t that wide either, so...
If I can just get through this place...
Everything would be fine.
The palace soldiers were probably looking at him from the wall as well. They would send reinforcements through the gates or do anything to save Yandel.
“I’m sorry.”
With that short apology, he stabbed an arrowhead into the butt of the horse he was riding.
Neigh!
The horse sprinted forward at the pain.
The wizard, who had also spaced out after seeing Bjorn Yandel, quickly rolled to the side to avoid getting trampled, and the way was opened.
Of course, the possibility of getting through the rest of the enemies and reaching the city wall was near zero.
But it’s not zero.
Rotmiller naturally learned this while living with the barbarians. Giving up without trying was the most foolish thing.
It was true, really. Failure was better than giving up.
Ba-dump!
Even more so, if there was nothing to lose.
“Yeah! It’s Behel—LAAAA!”
Rotmiller let out the battle cry, the one his ears were familiar with to the point of being sick of it, for the very first time.
“Behel—LAAAAAA!”
As if to respond to his shouting, a true battle cry repeated back.
Having heard the shouts of countless barbarians, Rotmiller immediately recognized who it was.
Huh, this voice is...
Ainar?

chapters.title: Chapter 753: First Point (3)
paragraphs: When living in the barbarian holy land, the one thing you were guaranteed to hear was the relentless refrain of their battle cry, echoing thousands of times per day.
Behela when eating, Behela when splitting firewood.

The barbarians invoked the name of their ancestral god at every turn, a habit so ingrained that Rotmiller had learned to tell them apart by that alone. Battle cries that seemed identical at first gradually began to reveal the unique inflections of their owner, subtle differences that identified each barbarian in their own right.
This particular battle cry had three distinct traits that set it apart as well.
“Behel—LAAAAA!”

First, the opening “be” began quietly and then ramped up into the familiar bellow. Second, the gap between the “hel” and “la” was filled with a deep inhale. Third, and most notably, the battle cry was from a woman.
Ainar...?

The moment he turned his head toward the direction of the sound, Rotmiller found it was just as he suspected. There stood Ainar, standing atop a four-story building with a pair of wings stretched wide behind her. The female warrior held in her hand a green spear—one that looked expensive even from a distance.
“It’s the Divine Spear!” someone in the crowd gasped.
“I could’ve sworn I heard she was near Dimension Square!”
Rotmiller didn’t know why Ainar was here, but what did that matter, really? The important thing was that his chances of getting through this mess had increased.
Boom!
With a great four-story leap from her perch, Ainar jumped from the building and beelined toward the cart.
Neigh!
A moment later, she was running alongside the arrow-in-butt horse, matching pace as she told Rotmiller, “Speak, scout. What do you need me to do?”
In true barbarian fashion, she went straight to the point.
“I’m not too smart, and I don’t know. So tell me—what do I need to do to save Yandel?”
That short sentence conveyed her total trust in his judgment.
Rotmiller felt his breath catch, but he suppressed the rising wave of emotion and found his calm. If she was going to give him her trust, he needed to repay her in kind.
“If we can just reach the city walls, the palace soldiers will help us, so—”
“Keep it simple.”
He took her interruption in stride. “Open the path in front of us!”
“There we go.”

As soon as Rotmiller gave the order, Ainar sprinted forward, spinning and stabbing her giant spear into the enemies in their way. None of them could block her, instead succumbing to defeat as the wings on her back flapped away.
Rotmiller watched it all from behind. For a fleeting moment, he could nearly mistake Ainar for a Valkyrie sent by the heavens to save Bjorn Yandel.
“Behel—LAAAAA!”
They were surrounded by enemies, and yet no one could ever hope to pose an obstacle to the female warrior. It allowed the cart to move at a quick pace. The walls were approaching faster and faster.
If only things could resolve so easily.
One man slunk into their path, clearly intent on barring them from passing.
Rotmiller didn’t know who this man was. However, he watched Ainar’s expression harden when she saw him, losing all trace of the glee at bulldozing through all her enemies.
“You’ll need to go on your own,” she said, her voice low and divorced from all mirth. “I’ll leave Yandel to you, scout.”
She dashed forward—and then, the world went dark as night.
[Roland Banozant has cast Black Demon Eyes.]
Goosebumps crawled along his flesh. Hundreds of frightening eyes peered out at him from the darkness that had settled over the city.
The world came to a halt, freezing everything in place except for two people.
“It was good that I came over.”
Strange lights flickered in the man’s eyes as he spoke. The female warrior met his calm with a stab of her spear and her signature battle cry.
“Behel—LAAAAAA!”
The pressure of the attack sent winds whipping through the air, but her spear missed its target.
Then, against all logic, the void of darkness shattered and time began to move once more.
The confident man faltered, groaning at the unexpected blow as he stumbled backward. Ainar charged him and shouted over her shoulder.
“Go!”
Rotmiller took the cart and pushed forward.

Honestly, he wasn’t actually doing a thing. As soon as the darkness receded, the horse galloped forward as it had been before. The only thing Rotmiller had to do was hold the reins to steer the animal in the right direction.
The cart rattled as it moved, adding to the sounds of a fierce battle. Superhumans were fighting behind him, but Rotmiller didn’t turn around to look.
All he needed to do was to deliver this cart to the city wall. He put everything he had into achieving that.
“Catch him!”
“Stop him!”
Despite his conviction, the other soldiers who had been hiding appeared again to chase him once Ainar disappeared. On top of that, the cart had begun to slow down.
Damn it.
Honestly, it was to be expected. No matter if it was a cart on wheels, the horse couldn’t haul a barbarian of that size and mass indefinitely. It was bound to become exhausted eventually.
Rotmiller let go of the reins and moved onto the cart before raining fire down at the ones chasing him. However, it wasn’t enough.
He wasn’t a strong person, not like Ainar.
“They’re just ordinary arrows!”
“He’s nothing special!”
The very same people who had let Ainar pass without putting up a fight were now taking jabs at Rotmiller’s relative weakness.
Well, he took comfort in the few arrows that did find their mark from his apparently “weakling” skill.
“Get him!”
Still, the gap between the mob and the cart was beginning to narrow.
He knew he would be caught. There was no outrunning them at this pace. A decision clearly needed to be made, but he didn’t have the time to think through all of the variables.
“He’s out of arrows!”
He ran out of arrows to shoot.
Pshwoo!
An enemy projectile hit him square in the right shoulder, taking his ability to use his right arm along with it.
If he stayed on the cart, all it would do was increase the weight the horse needed to pull.
His thoughts hounded him.
Is this really it? When he appeared in the holy land, I thought I had a few more stories left to tell. So is this really how my story ends?
But no, it didn’t have to be. There was one way.
They were chasing Yandel, not him.
If he dropped this heavy barbarian onto the ground, he could live. If he just pushed the barbarian off, he would arrive at the wall and then he would live.
And yet...
I think I understand now.
In those moments he thought he would die in the holy land, Rotmiller hadn’t been able to comprehend what that wizard friend of his was thinking back when he’d made his final decision.
Rotmiller had a guess, but something had eluded him even as death nearly came for him.
He understood now.
No matter how afraid I am—
Just like the barbarians who entered the labyrinth.
Just like the warriors who laughed in the face of hardship.
I can’t run away.
Like a gust of wind carrying away the fog, his mind became clear.
Dwalkie wasn’t a great man but an ordinary one, just like him.

He would have been afraid of death like anyone else. He would have been desperate to live for even a moment longer. He would have thought about his regrets and the mistakes he made as he looked back on his life, and he would have wanted to run away and fix them all.
However, he did not run away. He did the most he could, and that resulted in him saving everyone else.
Yeah...
If it weren’t for him, Rotmiller’s story would have ended a long time ago. It was laughable to even debate it.
He gave his final goodbye to the man who couldn’t even hear him.
“I’m sorry, but you’ll need to go by yourself.”
To the very end, though, Rotmiller was truly ordinary at heart.

In a final act of regret, he pulled out a pen from his Treasure Vault and scribbled something on that man’s palm. The nature of the situation wouldn’t allow him the time to write anything in detail, but the act at least helped him settle one of his many regrets. Depending on how they were read, his last words could be interpreted as the written manifestation of his greedy nature.
But I should be allowed this much, at least.
Rotmiller dropped the pen to take up his short sword, then jumped off the cart to wield it against the enemies. And wield it he did.
“What’s with this bastard?”
Sharp blades cut through his body as the rattling of the cart faded into the distance.
He could tell even without having to look back. That cart was going the right way.
Toward that tall and mighty city wall.
I awoke to a sore body but a clear mind.
It felt like I had just woken up from a deep sleep—like I’d just woken from a long dream, but I couldn’t remember what sort of dream it was.
“Where...”
...was I?
From the look of the ceiling, I could tell I was in the barracks of some camp.

I propped myself up on my elbows to glance around but couldn’t see any other clues as to where I was. Maybe it looked similar enough to what I remembered to be the barracks of the palatial soldiers, but why would I be doing, sleeping there?
“Rotmiller...”
I began to piece together the fragments of memory from before I fell unconscious.
Thunder fell, and I blocked it. Just when I barely regained consciousness, Rotmiller had been next to me.
What happened?
I was confused. I needed information about the situation I was in. With that thought in mind, I was just about to get off the bed when a knight entered the barracks.
It was a familiar face, the one who had disappeared along with Raven after I’d been pulled into the Netherworld by the Corpse Collector.
“Astarota?”
The King’s Knight, Astarota Berun, greeted me with a simple statement. “You’re finally awake.”
“Why am I here?” I demanded. “Where is Raven?”
“How about you ask one at a time?”
Wow, pretty cold to a guy who just woke up. “Where is Raven?”
“Don’t worry, she’s in a safe place. She should be here soon since I’ve sent her word.”
I sighed. “Alright, then. Tell me. Where am I and why am I here?”
“First, this is the imperial capital of Karnon. The reason a noble like you is in the barracks of a random footsoldier is for security.”
“Security?”
“The moment your location is made known, Thunder will fall again.”
I hesitated. “What?”
“It seems the prime minister’s just itching to fire it. Every time your location is discovered, he keeps firing Thunder at you.”
Okay, so it really was the prime minister who fired it.
That was no doubt an important piece of information, but it still didn’t answer my question.
“Astarota, I asked not why I’m in the barracks but what happened while I was unconscious.”
“Ah, is that so?” Astarota hummed nonchalantly before launching into an explanation of everything that had been going on.
It was easy enough to summarize.

A second bolt of Thunder fell, leading Baron Wilkins, the Fifth Commander, to activate the ancient magic installed in the city—a teleportation spell with a long casting time. Because he cast it too early, it didn’t activate properly, meaning our landing location was determined at random.
“So in the end, everyone there was teleported to random locations all over the city?”
“Isn’t that better than everyone dying?”
Well, that was true. “Then did I luck out and land here?”
“Of course not. You landed in the middle of enemy territory in District 4. You, and another man who carried you all the way here while you were unconscious.”
“Another man... Rotmiller! Are you talking about Brown Rotmiller?”
“Probably.”
“What happened to him?”
Astarota responded to my hurried question with casual disinterest. “He’s dead.”
I froze as the answer echoed through my mind. “What?”
“From the eyewitness account of a wall patrol, as soon as the cart you were on slowed down, he jumped off to block the enemies.”
Uh...
“Also, Ainar Fenelin also helped you escape with him, and she was captured by the enemies as a prisoner.”
Rotmiller died and Ainar was captured?
My brain refused to function with the influx of information. Astarota noticed and smirked.
“Despite appearances, you really are too soft. I’ll be outside while you sort this out. Oh, and one last thing...” When I only stared at him in silent bafflement, he continued, saying, “Your palm.”
With that, Astarota left the barracks, leaving me to my distress where I sat alone at the edge of the bed.
Finally registering his seemingly random parting words, I lifted my arm and flipped my palm face up. A hastily written message was written on it.
Reading the words dragged me straight back to reality.
Please be nice to Ms. Shavin. She’s a good woman.
This wasn’t a dream.

chapters.title: Chapter 754: First Point (4)
paragraphs: “Pardon me, Elder. Could I trouble you with a question?”
A white-haired old man leisurely sipped his tea at the question. “Not a problem at all. Go on.”
“Why did you try to stop him? My paltry thoughts do not allow me to understand.”
“Which part don’t you understand?”

At the old man’s counter question, the man in a wolf mask answered, “In exchange for him reaching the holy land, a rank seven adventurer by the name of Brown Rotmiller died and Sven Parav became a saint in return. Ah, but not a complete one yet, of course.”
“Hmm?”

“As a result of this, the man lost a useless scout in return for an ally who will become a great asset to him in the future, and yet you tried to stop him from reaching the holy land. I was curious as to why.”
“Ah, so it was that...”
The old man gave a seemingly benevolent smile. However, if one looked closely, one would be able to see a devilish playfulness lurking in his eyes.
“It’s not fun if I just tell you,” he concluded.
“Pardon?”
“Mull over it by yourself. Why do you think I did that?”
After receiving another question in return, the wolf-masked man thought for a moment before carefully saying, “I am debating between three ideas.”
“Go on.”
“One is that you had already predicted how he would act, Elder.”

“I knew he would do the opposite of whatever I said to do, so I told him not to go to the holy land...is wrong. If that were the case, why would I have sent you to give him a useless piece of advice? He would’ve headed that way on his own, even if I didn’t do anything.”
“That is true... I questioned that as well.”
“Then what is the second idea?”
“Second... No matter which way he went, Brown Rotmiller would have died anyway.”
“Oh?”
“Of course, that doesn’t explain why you tried to send that man to District Seven... However, my guess is that perhaps you didn’t want Sven Parav to become a saint.”
“That’s an interesting thought,” the old man allowed, intrigued. “Keep going.”
“Well... You have said in the past that Sven Parav is a soul born with a divine presence. One that even allows an evil god with whom he’s never formed a contract to converse with him.”
“I did.”

“So perhaps you didn’t want to see Sven Parav join hands with the evil god. In a certain light, a priest of Karui is stronger than a saint. Though in the end, he would have been helpful to that man all the same.”
The old man gave a proud smile. “I was right to ask for your thoughts. That was quite the insightful line of thought you had.”
“Are you saying that is wrong as well?”
“It is wrong. If he headed for District Seven, Sven Parav would’ve died.”
“I see...” The wolf-masked man sulked like he had missed a test question, but then continued to speak. “My third idea was that Brown Rotmiller is more valuable than a saint Sven Parav...”
He didn’t believe this even as he said it. Really, how could a rank 7 scout who had already retired be better than a paladin who was about to become a saint?
“Correct.”
“Pardon?”
“Your third idea matches my conclusion. Brown Rotmiller would have ultimately proven much more useful along his journey.”
The wolf-masked man couldn’t understand it. However, having observed the fates of countless people since he began following the elder, he offered up another theory to bolster the idea.
“So Sven Parav will actually become a negative influence in his journey.”
He spoke with certainty. There was no other explanation. The blessing would actually be a curse. There had been quite a few cases of the sort—fate was a mysterious and capricious beast, after all.
“Wrong again.”
The wolf-masked man choked out an involuntary response, and the elder turned his gaze toward the window.
“Sven Parav will accomplish great deeds along his journey, just as we expect.”
“Even so...you chose Brown Rotmiller over him.”
“It is foolish to judge a person’s future only by their present. People become great not by their origin, but by their efforts. This is a world where even a beggar can become a king one day.”
“Did Rotmiller perhaps have the potential to become that great?”

The old man smirked at the binary way of thinking, shaking his head. “He doesn’t have such talent. However, the worth of all is determined by how they are recorded.” Then with a hint of regret tinging his voice, he revealed, “If Brown Rotmiller survived, he would’ve left an even greater mark on this world.”
Of course, in this world, that future no longer existed.
From my perspective, I had just closed and opened my eyes.
It didn’t feel real at all—not anything I personally experienced but just second-hand information sent my way after everything was already said and done.
I couldn’t shake the hope that maybe, just maybe, they’d gotten some of the details wrong.
Please treat Ms. Shavin nicely. She’s a good woman.
But it was all real.
Ainar Fenelin had been captured by the enemy and Brown Rotmiller, my first scout, had died.
Those were the immutable truths.
My fists clenched as my thoughts raced.
Just what went wrong?
Before I went to the holy land, Wolf had told me that if I went to District Seven, X would die, and if I went to the holy land, Y would die. That was why I assumed X would be Rotmiller.
In the end, I headed for the holy land as I initially planned, and I was able to save X—Rotmiller—from danger.
But Rotmiller was Y all along...?
Because I’d gone to the holy land, Rotmiller died.

There was no point in entertaining useless trains of thought, like I’d practically killed him by making that choice. There were things I could do and things I couldn’t do. I was clear with the distinction between the two of them, and I wasn’t the type to fall into depression because of failure either.
Yeah, I wasn’t.
But then, why did I feel like crap?
The violence inscribed deep within my savage body began to boil up.
I wanted to fight so that I didn’t have to think. I wanted to crush and break everything I saw.
Still, I held back. The barbarian body I was in was different from Hansu Lee. A flash of temper wouldn’t end with just a broken set of a mouse and keyboard.
A wise warrior needed to know when to fight and the right moment to explode with this emotion.
At that moment, someone pushed aside the curtain at the front of the barracks and entered. It was a welcome face: Arua Raven.
But what was this?
The moment our eyes met, Raven’s mouth slammed shut. Her face drained of color as her small and pale body began to shake like a willow tree.
What was it? Did something bad happen to her?
The thoughts and the desires I had just barely suppressed began to bubble up again.
“S-sorry.”
Then, I watched as Raven avoided eye contact and I realized what had happened.
“I-I’ll be outside for now... Until you calm down...”
Raven was afraid of me.
I let out a deep exhale as if expelling all the poison built up in my body, then stopped Raven as she moved to leave the barracks in a panic. “Don’t go, I’ve calmed down.”
Raven carefully turned around and let out her own sigh—one of relief. After a long, hesitant pause, she mustered words of comfort. “I heard what happened...”
I didn’t answer her. If I did, the things I’d just barely managed to suppress would come back up again. However, I needed to at least ask one thing.
“Do you know what happened to Rotmiller’s body?”
“Um... I think it’d be best if you didn’t know...”
“Don’t worry about that and just tell me. I’ve calmed down.”
“Uh... I-I still don’t think you should—”
“I said I’m fine.”
Raven just stared at me silently without a single ounce of belief in her eyes. Only when the curtain to the barracks flapped open a few moments later to reveal Astarota did I get my answer.
“The Noarkan soldiers cut off his head and took it. If they get confirmation that he was your ally, it would be acknowledged as an achievement.”
Ba-dump!
“It seems you were thinking of using the Stone of Revival, but it unfortunately won’t work.”
My heart was beating, so fast that I wondered if it was even within healthy limits.
I clenched my jaw hard to the point where I thought maybe my teeth would start cracking.
“But how about you do something about that killing intent of yours? I’m fine...” Astarota trailed off. “But this one here might pass out.”
I glanced over to Raven. She was stiff as a board, so I reigned in my temper with a sigh, then pulled out a new topic to distract myself.
“What happened to you two? And where’s Vivian?”
“After you disappeared with the Corpse Collector, the captain of Orcules appeared. A battle ensued... Anyway, the short story is that we ran away first.”
“What?”

“Let me correct that. We didn’t run away but stepped away at the appropriate time.” He then stated that it was to protect Raven and if it had been a fair fight, he definitely could have defeated him, but at the end of the day, only Astarota knew the truth.
In any case, what happened after that went something like so:

The captain entered the battle to aim for me but changed his target to Astarota when he realized he was the King’s Knight. While the captain was chasing after Astarota, I escaped the Netherworld just in the nick of time. After losing his tail, Astarota entered the imperial capital and recuperated from his injuries.
Oh, and Vivian came with him but was thrown in jail.
“That woman’s of no use anymore. I thought about executing her but kept her alive just in case.”

After regrouping, he thought about looking for me to group back up again but lost my location due to the ancient magic. Sometime later, he heard word that I had entered the imperial capital unconscious and quickly came over to check on me.
“Now that’s that, I want to ask you something. Where will you go now?”
At Astarota’s question, I closed my eyes for a moment. What did I need to do now?
It didn’t take long for me to come to a decision.
“We first need to save Ainar...”
“I see.” Astarota nodded. He then asked me, “But how?”
I didn’t respond.
“I’ve told you this before, but I’ve only heard news that she was captured as a prisoner. We have no information on where she is being held or if she’s even alive or not.”
Right. Then I first needed to gather information. “Astarota, I have a request.”
“Go on.”
“Could you gather my scattered allies? Even just the ones in districts under the palace’s reach would do.”
“You don’t even need to make that request. It’s already underway.”
“Okay, I see...”
Even though he always seemed pretty inflexible, he was smart with the way he handled work.
“If you need anything or you’ve made a plan of action, call for me.”

Astarota then left the barracks, and I quietly sat at the edge of the bed, thinking over all of the information I had to see if I missed anything. Every few minutes, I called Astarota to see if any new information came in.
Where Ainar was.
If more of my allies had been thrown into the middle of enemy territory.
If the marquess’s location had been determined.
Given we were in times of war, I could only rely on the information network of the military, and my heart continued to squeeze as no useful news reached me.
No, wait...
But the information I was so desperately looking for came from a completely unexpected source.

As I thought about the marquess, I was reminded of Ragna, and as I thought about Ragna, I thought about her right hand, Hyeonbyeol. Thinking about Hyeonbyeol in turn reminded me of that so-called “love paper” I received from her.
No way...

I hurriedly took out the “love paper,” only to find that there actually was a message written on it. The contents could be summarized into two pieces of intel: Ainar’s supposed current location and...
Ainar Fenelin, Alminus Central Bank underground vault. Planned for execution.
...Ainar’s current fate.

chapters.title: Chapter 755: First Point (5)
paragraphs: Alminus Central Bank was the nexus of the world’s wealth, and when factoring in all the treasures stashed away in its secret collection of private vaults, it was a bona fide dragon’s hoard. With so much wealth. gathered in one place, the security in place was well configured. It was the perfect place to sequester a person of interest, much better than the Public Peace Agency or the prison beneath the Adventurer’s Guild.
“But don’t you think this is a little too on the nose?”
Thus, when I explained the situation to Raven, her response was about what I expected.

“Harin Savy? First of all, I don’t know why you have a love paper with someone like that, but that woman’s the right hand of Countess Peprok. You know, the one who’s clearly in the marquess’s faction? This is a trap no matter how I look at it. I don’t really want to say this, but...” Raven trailed off, letting the silence hang between us. “Why do you think they took Ms. Ainar and didn’t just kill her on the spot?”

I had to admit that her worries aligned with my own. Raven wasn’t aware that Harin Savy was actually Hyeonbyeol, nor did she know the relationship we had, and yet even I didn’t think Hyeonbyeol had sided with the marquess and was deliberately feeding me false information.
A trap is still a trap, though.

The problem wasn’t the informant named Hyeonbyeol but the fact the information made its way to me at all. If the Noarkans had truly wanted to keep information about Ainar top secret, it wouldn’t have gotten to me.
And considering how the marquess operates...

There was no “chance” of it being a trap—it was a certainty. The fact that Ainar had been captured alive only confirmed it, just as Raven said. I had assumed they would use her as leverage to negotiate with me, but an execution? It was laughably transparent.
And yet, maybe this is it.

Maybe it was my chance. The information had come to me through Hyeonbyeol, and the palace hadn’t caught wind of it either, not yet—meaning the Noarkans probably couldn’t even imagine I had gotten my hands on the intel.
There was no avoiding the trap, but if I was right and the trap hadn’t been fully laid yet...
We need to hurry.
Time was of the essence.

Across the street from the Alminus Central Bank stood a building that had once been the headquarters of the Alminus Business. Far from the hub it was supposed to be, it had long since been looted and reduced to ruins.
In that shell of bygone commerce, a woman hid in silence.
“Ms. Emily...?”
“Be quiet. I’m thinking.”
Amelia Rainwales gazed out the window. Yet even though she didn’t spare him a glance, the man beside her seemed to know what she was thinking by her expression alone.

“Even you wouldn’t be able to make it, Ms. Emily... I won’t suggest that we should go to District Three or the imperial capital where it’s safe, but please, won’t you hide and rest? At least until you recover from your injuries?”

Auyen’s voice was heavy with worry and sincerity. There was no telling how people would react to learning he had once been a plunderer. However, he considered Amelia and Yandel his benefactors, the ones who had raised him from that life. He couldn’t stand idly by and let one of his saviors actively put herself in harm’s way.
“Besides...” he added, tone hardening to brook no argument. “You don’t even have an arm anymore.”

Amelia had suffered a grave injury to her right arm during the Noarkans’ pursuit. It wasn’t as if her arm had been severed entirely, but in a way, that might have been the more fortunate turn of events. The arm had been torn asunder, split clean down the middle right down to the muscles and bones, and due to a specific essence of Amelia’s, she couldn’t use potions to heal either.
“We’ve just barely stopped the bleeding,” Auyen pressed, his voice edging on pleading. “What could you possibly hope to accomplish in that condition?”
He had tried everything up until outright dropping to his knees, practically begging her to stop. Still, Amelia didn’t so much as blink.
“I said I’m thinking.”

Her unflinching calm only made Auyen all the more nervous. He had spent enough time by her side to know what “thinking” truly meant for her. She wasn’t deliberating whether to act—her decision had already been made. The only thing left to contemplate was how.
“Do you think Captain Yandel would approve of what you are doing right now?” he blurted, playing his last, final card—the strong he had in his deck.
That, at last, got her attention.

Amelia’s gaze shifted from the window to him. She didn’t say a word, but the sheer intensity of her silent stare was overwhelming. Even so, despite the tremors raking his body, Auyen refused to look away.
“Auyen Rockrobe,” she said then, finally breaking her silence. “You’re crossing the line.”
“I have no choice. If I want to bring someone who’s crossed the line back over, I need to cross it myself.”
His resolve hung in the air, undeterred by the cold fury that threatened to snuff it out. Then, with a sigh of resignation, Amelia relented.
“Even I know that this is dangerous, but it can’t be helped,” she said softly, her tone unexpectedly gentle.
“Why can’t it be helped?”
“Because... Because I don’t want Ainar Fenelin to die.”
It was, in many ways, what had led them here to their current problem.

Ainar had been captured and just so happened to be transported along the very street where the two of them had been hiding. After secretly trailing the convoy, they both then watched as Ainar was moved into the bank.

“Why are you assuming that they will kill her? They’ve taken her prisoner, which means they’re not planning to kill her anytime soon. Right, they have to be scheming up something—like using her to negotiate with the palace or the captain.”
“That’s one possibility.”
“Alright, then for now—”
“But what if they don’t?” she continued, cutting him off before he could get the words out. “What if we keep waiting because we assume she has more time, and then because we did, she dies?”
Auyen faltered, his words caught in his throat. “Even if that happens... Mr. Emily, surely you know that no blame would fall on you.”

It wasn’t empty comfort—he truly meant every word. Yet, even as he said it, his eyes drifted away, unable to meet her own for a reason he couldn’t name. She noticed—of course she did—and a faint smirk tugged at her lips.
“There’s no need for that,” she assured. “You’re not wrong.”
She had once thought the same way, as so many others like them did. They both knew what it meant to live to survive, no matter the cost.
“Pardon? Oh! Then that must mean—!”
“Enough.”

Amelia ended the conversation there. Communicating had never come easy to her, and she doubted she could persuade him with words alone if she tried. Truthfully, she didn’t even know where to begin explaining her stance.
“I’ll be careful. Stay here and keep yourself hidden.”
Her parting words weren’t a request but a demand. Auyen no longer tried to oppose her.
“Okay. Please be safe...”
Amelia didn’t reply. One moment she was there, and the next, she was gone from his sight.

Left alone in the empty third-floor office, Auyen peered out the window at the bank’s main entrance, scanning for any sign of her. However, no matter how long he stared, Amelia was nowhere to be seen.
It was to be expected, really. There was no way she would just prance through the front door. And even if she had, she was so stealthy that his eyes would never have caught her.
“I pray for your safety...”

Although he wasn’t a religious man, Auyen closed his eyes to pray. When all that was left in the room was him and a prayer, he kept his vigil, observing the bank from afar, just in case something happened.
Time slipped by him until, suddenly, a voice startled him from behind.
“What the—? Someone really is here.”
“I told you, didn’t I? I detected a life force.”
Auyen whirled around, panicked. He had been too wary of what was going on outside to notice the intruders from within.
Smack!
A blunt instrument struck his head, and he collapsed to the floor. As his consciousness began to fade, he heard the Noarkans conversing.
“So, who is this guy?”
“Isn’t this one of Yandel’s allies that got separated?”
“Eh, doesn’t seem like it. Not if he went down from one hit.”

“Well, he’s either a civilian hiding in District Four or one of the adventurers who got beaten earlier today. From what I heard, a few mid-sized clans were mixed in with those hundreds of barbarians.”
“Hmm, he must be one of them, then.”
They were trying to figure out who he was. Fortunately—or unfortunately, for that matter—they didn’t realize he was a member of the Anabada Clan.
Now if only that gave him a way out.
“So then, what do we do?”
“What else? We take him back to HQ, same as always. Aren’t they getting desperate, anyway? Heard they’re running out of fuel for the magic weapon.”
“Ugh, we’re so far from headquarters, though.”
“They’ll still pay us for him. And this guy looks like he’s eaten a few essences too. Come on, it’ll be enough for some petty cash.”
“Fine, fine. Let’s do it. I don’t think we’ll find any more around here either—”
The man then stopped mid-sentence.
“Wait a sec. He’s still awake.”
Crack!
That was the last thing Auyen remembered.
Greed begets ruin.
Auyen Rockrobe had always agreed with that saying. After all, the only reason he had survived this long was because he had never let greed take root in his heart.
“Next.”
He gave up his dream of becoming a great adventurer. Instead, he learned navigation.
“Next.”
Although he ended up in a cruel clan that worked him like a slave, he was grateful simply to have enough food to eat and time to sleep, and so had never once entertained thoughts of anything more.
“Next.”
It had been the same when he was taken in by the barbarian. Even while confined underground and deprived of sunlight, he was content just to be alive and didn’t dare dream of escape.
“Next.”

The result of his temperance was that they slowly began to accept him—and in doing so, they saved him. Sure, he had been humiliated—being called Rockrock or Nguyen, for example—but that was fine. Whenever they ate the food he prepared for them, whenever they praised him for doing good work and fulfilling his duty, he felt something within him begin to fill, a well he thought would remain forever dry.
Well, he did feel more like an employee who did odd jobs than an actual ally of Yandel, but still...
“Next.”
So what? Were heroes really all that perfect?
“Next.”

Of course not. People like him had their place too. He knew he was contributing to their journey in his own way, and that belief drove him to work more diligently than ever before. He studied cookbooks when out shopping, grew adept at handling horses, and continued his navigation studies so he could be useful just in case, for that small chance the Anabada Clan ever operated on the sixth floor or needed to sail again.
He must have forgotten, if only for a moment.
“Next.”
Greed begets ruin. A snake cannot become a dragon just because it journeyed alongside one.
This, too, must be fate...

Auyen considered his current predicament to be natural. How could he not? He was obviously just a burden, a leech who didn’t know his place yet followed along after them. It was only fitting that things ended this way.
“Didn’t you hear me say next?”

A soldier in armor grabbed him by his back collar and shoved him forward toward a huge machine. It was as crude and plain in form as it was in function: a pillar extending down into a vat where people were being thrown indiscriminately one after another for reasons he had no business knowing.
So... This is how I die.
To a man who had spent his life suppressing his desires, resignation came as easy as breathing.

He didn’t even consider resisting, not even when the grip on his neck began to choke him. He could take one or two people with him, sure, but what then? He would be tortured, interrogated, and meet an even more gruesome end.
No, letting that machine take him seemed like a much cleaner way to go.
“Wait, stop.”

Just as his head was shoved over the seemingly bottomless pit, someone approached and spoke, a brief reprieve of borrowed time. The one who stopped his execution was a man clad in a knight’s uniform. He stepped forward, grasping Auyen’s chin even as his neck was still held from behind, then nodded to himself.
“Looking again, I’m certain of it. Auyen Rockrobe... Even if he doesn’t look the part, he’s a member of the Anabada Clan.”
“A-are you sure?”
“I don’t know where you found him, but I’ll take him from here. His Lordship will decide his fate personally.”
With that, he was handed over to the knight and dragged away. When he shook himself out of his stupor, he found himself under the scrutiny of a middle-aged man exuding an unsettling authority.
Auyen knew who it was the moment he saw him.
“I brought him as you said, Lord Marquess.”
“And is he unbound because...?” came the immediate retort from the marquess.

Almost rushing to excuse his choice, the knight defended, “While he is an ally of Yandel, he is merely the navigator of the group. His estimated combat ability is below that of an Orc, so you needn’t worry, my lord.”
“I see...”
The marquess seemed satisfied by the explanation and didn’t comment further.
For a moment after, Auyen’s mind was blank. Then, realization dawned.
They don’t know.

Of course, he thought. It was only natural. Although the palace knew Yandel had obtained that essence, they couldn’t possibly imagine he would give it to Auyen. And since he never had any opportunity to use it before, there had been no threat of the information leaking.
Could it be?
This could be an opportunity...
“Speak if you wish to live.”
There was no hesitation. It was an altogether new experience for Auyen, who agonized over the smallest decisions, such as which eggs to buy at the market. But this time, he didn’t even need to think.
“How much value do you hold to Bjorn Yandel?”
The question had barely left the marquess’s lips when Auyen activated his ability.

Instantaneous activation and so impossible to dodge. Impossible to block as well, with commendable destructive capabilities at its core. Low soul power cost, a short cooldown—and a skill Yandel had once praised.
It was none other than the ability of the rank three monster, Bellarios.
[Auyen Rockrobe has cast Shatter.]
Power surged from his hand and out toward the target, and then—
The mastermind of the war. The former prime minister of Rafdonia. Marquess Tercerion.
He was a man whom Auyen would have never dreamed of crossing paths with under normal circumstances—and now, he was also an enemy for the ages, a traitor whom everyone in the city wanted to kill.
That once great man collapsed, blood spilling from his lips.

chapters.title: Chapter 756: Hostage (1)
paragraphs: “So you’re saying... that Marquess Tercerion coughed up blood, collapsed, and now he’s on the verge of death?”
The despair that the castellan of Noark felt when he received the report went beyond words. No, despair could come later. His first reaction was utter disbelief. Who could truly blame him, though?
“How does this make sense?”

Countless knights and wizards were in the marquess’s security detail, each groomed by the marquess from a very young age to be a proverbial human golem, brainwashed to erase the very concept of betrayal from their minds. Once, the Noarkan castellan had even envied the marquess and told the man that perhaps he wouldn’t need to be so afraid if he had. those types of people around him. And yet now...
“They got past that iron-wall defense?”
That airtight security had been breached.
“Even if he’s an ally of Yandel, isn’t he just a rank-seven navigator?”

The castellan simply couldn’t believe it, no matter how often he heard it. Even if the supposedly rank-seven navigator had come to possess a rank-three essence, what was the marquess thinking? He’d brought the man right under his very nose without even putting an essence sealer on him!
“Well,” ventured the subordinate hesitantly. “I suspect that they were extremely confident in their own information.”
“Let’s assume say that the marquess might have fallen for it. None of the guards around him questioned that decision, not even once?”
The subordinate shut his mouth at the castellan’s rage, and not because he had nothing to say either.

As he himself served a lord, he could assume the guards of the marquess would have predicted the navigator might try to assassinate the marquess. However, they would have expected a fireball or a thrown weapon at best. With the marquess standing so closely by their side, they probably assumed they would have seen the navigator’s attempt and stopped him in the act—maybe even get themselves the chance to say something cool like, “A pointless act... Are you unharmed, my lord?”
Hmm, that’s...
It wasn’t a bad plan. Especially if no one got injured.

The marquess would be satisfied with the skills of his subordinates and be confident he didn’t waste his money on them, and his subordinates would feel more confident in asking for a raise the following month. But alas...
Maybe it’s because they’re the marquess’s close aides? They’re both smart and treacherous. I’ll need to keep them in mind for later.

The Noarkan castellan might have sympathized more with their feelings had things not turned out this way, but there was no room for that now. What should have stayed as an “attempt” had gone had succeeded—the marquess might very well have been assassinated this day.
Those fools...

The marquess’s entourage would be nothing more than a band of fools now. However, he wasn’t going to join their ranks by voicing such thoughts aloud. Why should he? The castellan wasn’t angry at him, and nothing good would come from a superior knowing the thoughts of a subordinate like him.

As he expected, the castellan let out a deep sigh. The castellan was also an intelligent man, and he didn’t vent his anger at involved personnel either. Instead, he allowed just a hint of his frustration to leak through as he asked the servant, “Then tell me. I understand that the assassination attempt succeeded, but what do you mean he’s on the verge of death?”
It was a reasonable question for the castellan to have. The marquess wasn’t a poor commoner who couldn’t get access to the healing of priests.
One was either dead or alive. Being “on the verge of death” made no sense.
“Well...”
At the castellan’s question, the servant clenched his eyes shut as he braced for what was to come.
“To be correct, he isn’t on the verge of death.”

And in truth, he had never said that sequence of words. Although the servant noticed that there had been a misunderstanding, he didn’t cut off the castellan. There was no reason to do so, not with the mood as it was, so he remained quiet. Even so, the servant continued with his explanation before the castellan could fault him for the uncomfortable situation caused by the mistake.
“The marquess possesses an artifact that can save his life but it forces him to be unconscious for two days.”
He omitted the artifact’s number and name because that wasn’t important at the moment.

“I don’t know if I should be relieved...” The somewhat intelligent higher-up of his finally understood the full scope of the situation and asked, “And does the authority to wield the magic weapon still only lie with the marquess?”
“Yes.”
“So it means we can’t use Thunder for two days.”
The ancient weapon, deemed to hold more strategic value than even the captain of Orcules, was turned into a mere pile of scraps—all because of a single rank-seven navigator.
“Then what happens to the plan?”
Though the plan was clearly identified, the
subordinate who had served this one superior of his for decades at this point understood what he meant.
“The authority to use the Divine Spear Ainar to capture Bjorn Yandel has temporarily been transferred to the eldest son Eltora Tercerion.”
“And what if something happens to him in the meantime?”

That would complicate the situation. Even the meticulous marquess wouldn’t have selected a substitute for his already temporary proxy. The true answer was “We don’t know”—unless, of course, someone intervened.
“If that is the case...”

This was an externally caused problem rather than an internal problem, meaning the alliance treaty could be reinterpreted altogether. Knowing this, the subordinate summarized that thought into one, simple sentence.
“Then you could temporarily wield his authority, Lord Castellan.”
“I see...”
Hearing the answer he wanted, the castellan visibly relaxed. Only then did he ask a question he was personally curious about.
“Then what happened to that navigator?”
“Well...”
After realizing his boss had lightened up a little, the servant began to talk with a freer tone.
His first thought when he awoke in the middle of a dark underground prison was this:
Why am I alive?
In a world where failing to pay taxes was an offense punishable by death, an endless struggle to survive each waking moment was the expected state of affairs.
As a resident of such a world, Auyen Rockrobe understood the value of life—or rather, he knew how precious his life was better than anyone else. And yet...
How am I alive?
Rather than being relieved that he was alive, he was confused.
To be sure, he was certainly relieved. But still, confusion loomed larger.

Understandably so, really. It was like watching a huge meteor fall upon the ground, only to wake up unscathed. The survivor’s thoughts would surely trend toward not surprised glee but utter bafflement.
He replayed the events leading up to when he fell unconscious.
The moment the marquess fell over while coughing up blood.
“M-my lord...!”
Some high-ranking servants, who seemed to be wizards or priests, ran up to the marquess in worry.
“A-an assassin...!”
The knights, whose only jobs were to use their strength, ran up to him and overpowered him. He then fell flat on the ground as his entire body was restrained.
And “entire body” was no exaggeration either. Arms, legs, neck, ankles, left thumb, middle finger, ears—the pile of knights bound his body as if trying to seal a great demon.

Well, thinking back on it, it was understandable. They couldn’t just stand around when the marquess collapsed. The thought of standing aside simply because other knights were present wouldn’t have crossed their minds.
Auyen couldn’t even breathe under the crushing weight of the dozen or so knights, and his consciousness began to fade then. And when he opened his eyes, he was here.
Really, why am I alive?
One odd thing about consciousness was that even when dying from suffocation, the mind could clearly absorb information.
“The marquess has fallen unconscious...!”
“This damn bastard...!”
“Why are you just apprehending him? Kill him now!”
Rage and hatred against him, the assassin. That was the reason he couldn’t believe he was truly alive.
Only a cold chill swept through this underground prison in answer to his confusion.

Auyen continued to ponder the reason for his survival, that question evolving from wondering why he was alive to wondering why they kept him alive. Soon enough, his question was answered by a stranger who personally came into this supposed underground prison to relieve him of his confusion.
“I am Eltora Tercerion.”
The man revealed himself to be the marquess’s son.
“I have something to request of you.”
At first, Auyen wondered if he was going to request that he die a painful death after enduring horrific torture...
“Please, save me.”
However, Auyen was instead left fumbling for words at the man’s request.
What was going on?
The act of waiting might seem passive at first, but it carried a certain nuance to it depending on how one saw it.
Just look at the dictionary:
Passive: the subject is moved by an external force.
Active: the subject moves of its own accord.
If someone waited out of their own free will, then they would be actively waiting. On the other hand, if someone threatened them with a knife and told them to wait, they would be waiting passively.
Amelia Rainwales was of the former.

Her body had still not fully recovered, and when she came in to assess the situation, she could tell her rescue target was still fine. The best decision here would be to wait for a better opportunity than to act in the moment.
Of course, she would be forced to act if she detected suspicious movement before then.
Having made her decision, Amelia waited. She didn’t feel bored or anything of that sort. With countless experiences in infiltration and assassination under her belt, she was used to waiting.
Hooooonk!
She was a little angry that her rescue target was so relaxed that she was even snoring in her sleep, but it didn’t change what she needed to do.
She hid her breathing and erased her presence She opened her ears, overheard conversations, and slowly built up information in her mind.
Although the information seemed trivial, it could still be used to make better judgments down the line. And some of the information was indeed useful.
Like this particular bit of intel.
“I don’t know why we were told to watch that woman. Rather than waste manpower like this, couldn’t we just kill her?”
“Tsk, aren’t you being too shortsighted?”
“Shortsighted... What does that mean?”
“It means you can only see things close to you. Think about it. Why do you think the higher-ups captured the Divine Spear alive and imprisoned her like this?”
“Just tell me...”
“The Divine Spear is bait. To catch an even bigger fish.”
“By a bigger fish... Ah! To catch the Giant!”
“That’s right. If not for that, we wouldn’t be wasting so much power on observing just one captured barbarian.”
After hearing that theory, the man didn’t say anything else. He just looked at the one who told him all this for a while before asking, “Did you think of all this by yourself?”
“Haha, how could I? I just heard from someone who was assigned to this mission. They seemed to have been at the headquarters before this.”
“Did you hear about shortsighted or whatever from him too?”
“Isn’t it obvious? Those learned folks all use such difficult words...”

Having hidden herself in the ceiling, Amelia couldn’t ignore what she just overheard. From how the conversation had proceeded, it wasn’t just a “theory” the two of them had cooked up but the official plan.
So it was bait to draw out Yandel...
While she was glad she came to save Ainar by going against Auyen’s advice, she also felt pressed for time. The situation was now a race against time.

She needed to do something before Yandel fell into the trap. It was obvious that that barbarian would charge in to save his ally the moment he heard about it even if he knew it was a trap. It would be best if she could deal with the situation before he got here. There was no doubt about it.
But how?
The answer to her conundrum came from an unexpected source.
“Leave for a moment. I have some business with that woman.”
The two guards who boasted about their great security detail stepped away at the command of one man, and then he entered the area where Ainar was being held.
Eltora Tercerion...!

Ameila’s eyes glistened as she crouched in the darkness. While she might not know what business that guy had with Ainar, it was naturally nothing good. He was the son of the marquess, perhaps the greatest evil of the era. It was obvious he was scheming something—
Auyen...?
Damn it, he got captured.
After confirming who was walking next to the marquess’s son, Amelia’s lip pinched shut as she ran through simulations in her mind.
If I act now while he doesn’t even know I’m hiding above him...
She could not only simply cut his neck open, she could subdue him. And the fact that she could subdue him meant that she could threaten and control him as well.
There won’t be a better opportunity than this.
With that thought, it didn’t take long for her to move into action. Momentary decisions worked best when paired with intuition, anyway.
Now.
Amelia undid her stealth, jumped from the ceiling, and swooped down. Her target looked up and noticed her at that moment, but it was already too late to respond to her blade.
